NAMES.name: normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_beam_tracing_point
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless magnetic-surface label obtained from normalized enclosed
toroidal flux, evaluated at each beam-tracing point to map the propagation
path onto nested plasma surfaces.
NAMES.long:
This quantity assigns the magnetic surface intersected by each beam-tracing
point a dimensionless, radial-like toroidal-flux label. It describes the
location of the propagation point in nested equilibrium flux surfaces, not a
physical distance or a local vector component.

The normalized toroidal flux coordinate is defined by

$$
\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}} = \sqrt{\frac{\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}} - \Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}}}{\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,boundary}} - \Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}}}}
$$

where $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ is the normalized toroidal flux coordinate,
$\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the enclosed toroidal magnetic flux of the magnetic
surface through the beam-tracing point, $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}}$ is its
value at the magnetic axis, and $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,boundary}}$ is its value
at the equilibrium boundary.

The quantity is evaluated pointwise at each beam-tracing position for which
the nested equilibrium flux surfaces define the coordinate. It applies to
the magnetic surface associated with each propagation point and is not
aggregated over the beam path, nor does it represent a particle-population
property.

This is the beam-tracing-point evaluation of the [normalized toroidal flux
coordinate](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate). It differs from
[normalized toroidal flux coordinate at a measurement
position](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_measurement_position),
which assigns the same magnetic-surface coordinate to a specified physical
measurement location rather than to a beam-tracing point.

sources.leaf_definition: Normalised toroidal flux coordinate
sources.parent_definition: Position of the ray/beam along its path

NAMES.name: normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_ece_channel_emission_position
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless magnetic-surface label assigned to an electron-cyclotron
emission location, locating that emission on nested toroidal-flux surfaces.
NAMES.long:
The normalized toroidal-flux coordinate at an electron-cyclotron-emission
channel's emission position is the magnetic-surface label assigned to the
location from which the channel's emission originates.

The coordinate is defined by

$$
\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}} = \left(\frac{\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}} - \Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}}}{\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,boundary}} - \Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}}}\right)^{1/2}
$$

where $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ is the normalized toroidal-flux coordinate,
$\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the toroidal magnetic flux of the magnetic surface
passing through the emission position, $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}}$ is that
flux at the magnetic axis, and $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,boundary}}$ is that flux
at the equilibrium boundary.

This quantity is a point evaluation for one electron-cyclotron-emission
channel position, applying to the magnetic surface intersecting that
position. It has no sum, average, or integration over channels,
line-of-sight points, or emission locations, and it is not a cylindrical
radial distance.

It is the emission-position specialization of the [normalized toroidal flux
coordinate](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate): within the normalized
interval, it is zero at the magnetic axis and reaches one at the equilibrium
boundary. Its locus differs from the [normalized toroidal flux coordinate at
measurement
position](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_measurement_position),
which is evaluated at a measurement position rather than an
electron-cyclotron emission position.

sources.leaf_definition: Normalized toroidal flux coordinate of the measurement
sources.parent_definition: Radiation temperature from the closest channel to the magnetic axis, together with its radial location

NAMES.name: normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_measurement_position
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless toroidal-flux surface label assigned to a physical measurement
position, locating that position between the magnetic axis and equilibrium
boundary.
NAMES.long:
The normalized toroidal flux coordinate at a measurement position is the
label of the equilibrium magnetic surface passing through that position. It
maps the physical location onto nested toroidal-flux surfaces rather than
representing a cylindrical distance, local vector component, path average,
or region integral.

The coordinate is defined by normalizing enclosed toroidal flux between the
magnetic axis and the equilibrium boundary:

$$
\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}(\mathbf{x}_m) = \left[\frac{\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}(\mathbf{x}_m) - \Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}}}{\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,boundary}} - \Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}}}\right]^{1/2}
$$

where $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}(\mathbf{x}_m)$ is the normalized toroidal
flux coordinate at measurement position $\mathbf{x}_m$,
$\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}(\mathbf{x}_m)$ is the enclosed toroidal magnetic flux
of the equilibrium surface through that position, $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}}$
is its value at the magnetic axis, and $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,boundary}}$ is its
value at the equilibrium boundary.

This quantity applies to one physical measurement position and carries no
population or species attribution. Within the normalized interval, it is
zero at the magnetic axis and one at the equilibrium boundary; it is not an
average over multiple positions and must not be interpreted as the distinct
label evaluated at a beam-tracing point or emission position. It is the
position-specific evaluation of the parent [normalized toroidal flux
coordinate](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate), while the
corresponding beam-location quantity is evaluated at a different locus.

NAMES.name: normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_of_measurement_position
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless magnetic-surface label assigning the Doppler reflectometer
measurement location to a normalized toroidal-flux surface between the
magnetic axis and boundary.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the normalized toroidal-flux coordinate of the physical
position at which the Doppler reflectometer measurement is associated. It
maps that measurement location to a nested magnetic surface rather than
describing a cylindrical distance or a local vector component.

The coordinate is defined by

$$
\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{m}}) = \left[\frac{\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{m}})-\Phi_{\mathrm{axis}}}{\Phi_{\mathrm{boundary}}-\Phi_{\mathrm{axis}}}\right]^{1/2}
$$

where $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{m}})$ is the normalized
toroidal-flux coordinate at the measurement position,
$\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{m}}$ is that physical measurement position,
$\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{m}})$ is the toroidal magnetic flux
enclosed by the magnetic surface passing through the position,
$\Phi_{\mathrm{axis}}$ is its value at the magnetic axis, and
$\Phi_{\mathrm{boundary}}$ is its value at the last closed flux surface.

The scope is one local magnetic-surface label evaluated at the Doppler
reflectometer measurement position; it is not an average, integral, or
aggregate over a propagation path, channel set, or plasma region. Within the
region between the magnetic axis and the last closed flux surface, the value
is zero at the axis and one at the boundary. It excludes the toroidal angle
of the position and any signed displacement from a reference location.

This is the measurement-position specialization of the [normalized toroidal
flux coordinate](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate); the parent
defines the same surface label independently of the measurement locus.

NAMES.name: poloidal_angle_of_measurement_position
NAMES.short:
Geometric poloidal angle locating a measurement position around the magnetic
axis in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) cross-section, increasing
clockwise.
NAMES.long:
The poloidal angle of a measurement position is the geometric angular
coordinate of a physical point about the magnetic axis in the poloidal
cross-section of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. It
identifies the point's position around the magnetic axis, rather than a
field-line or toroidal angle.

Taking zero on the outward radial direction from the magnetic axis, the
angle is defined by

$$
\theta_{\mathrm{meas}} = \operatorname{atan2}\!\left[-\left(Z_{\mathrm{meas}}-Z_{\mathrm{axis}}\right),\,R_{\mathrm{meas}}-R_{\mathrm{axis}}\right]
$$

where $\theta_{\mathrm{meas}}$ is the poloidal angle of the measurement
position, $\operatorname{atan2}$ is the two-argument arctangent that
preserves the angular quadrant, $R_{\mathrm{meas}}$ and $Z_{\mathrm{meas}}$
are the major-radius and vertical coordinates of the measurement position,
and $R_{\mathrm{axis}}$ and $Z_{\mathrm{axis}}$ are the corresponding
coordinates of the magnetic axis.

This quantity is evaluated pointwise at the designated measurement position
and is not a line average, flux-surface average, or signal-weighted
aggregate. It is the measurement-position specialization of
[poloidal_angle](name:poloidal_angle_of_flux_surface), and it is distinct
from
[toroidal_angle_of_measurement_position](name:toroidal_angle_of_measurement_position),
which locates the same point around the symmetry axis.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the position advances clockwise from the
outward radial direction in the poloidal cross-section, viewed from the
right-hand side of the symmetry axis.

NAMES.name: radiative_temperature_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.short:
Temperature-equivalent radiation energy scale of electron-cyclotron
emission, evaluated at the magnetic axis, the degenerate innermost magnetic
surface where the poloidal magnetic-flux gradient vanishes. It is a
brightness-temperature quantity, not necessarily the local kinetic electron
temperature.
NAMES.long:
Temperature-equivalent radiation energy scale of electron-cyclotron
emission, evaluated at the magnetic axis. The magnetic axis is the
degenerate innermost magnetic surface of the equilibrium, the locus in the
poloidal cross-section where the gradient of the [poloidal magnetic
flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux) vanishes; evaluation at this locus does
not imply that the radiative temperature has an extremum there.

The blackbody-equivalent radiation energy scale is defined by matching the
radiation field's specific intensity to the Planck spectral intensity:

$$
I_\nu = \frac{2 h \nu^3}{c^2}\left[\exp\!\left(\frac{h\nu}{T_\mathrm{rad}}\right)-1\right]^{-1}
$$

where $I_\nu$ is the radiation specific intensity, $\nu$ is the radiation
frequency, $h$ is the Planck constant, $c$ is the speed of light, and
$T_\mathrm{rad}$ is the [radiative temperature].

This quantity is restricted to the radiation field associated with
electron-cyclotron emission at the magnetic-axis locus. For layer-resolved
electron-cyclotron emission, the axis value is the radiative temperature of
the resonance layer whose effective emission location is closest to the
magnetic axis; the aggregation convention is nearest-layer selection, not a
spatial average over neighboring layers. Ordinary-mode and
extraordinary-mode electron-cyclotron emission are polarization-specific
variants; the unqualified quantity does not select a polarization mode and
is not a sum or mean over modes.

It is the radiation-field member of [temperature at the magnetic
axis](name:temperature_at_magnetic_axis) and the magnetic-axis counterpart
of [radiative temperature]. It must not be identified with the local kinetic
[electron temperature at the magnetic
axis](name:electron_temperature_at_magnetic_axis) except in the limiting
case of optically thick thermal emission, where the brightness temperature
approaches the electron thermal energy scale.

NAMES.name: wavelength_of_wave_beam
NAMES.short:
Vacuum spatial period of a probing electromagnetic wave propagating as a
diagnostic beam, defining its spectral wavelength.
NAMES.long:
Vacuum wavelength of a wave beam is the spatial period of its
electromagnetic phase in vacuum, assigned to the beam’s carrier radiation.
It characterizes the beam itself rather than a spectral transition or an
instrument-response feature.

The vacuum wavelength $\lambda_0$ is related to the beam’s temporal
frequency $f$ by:

$$
\lambda_0 = \frac{c}{f}
$$

where $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum and $f$ is the temporal
oscillation frequency of the electromagnetic wave.

This quantity applies to a probing electromagnetic wave beam and describes
its vacuum propagation property, independent of plasma-induced changes in
phase velocity. It is assigned to the beam as a whole and is not a sum,
average, or integral over beams, paths, channels, or spectral components. It
excludes the in-medium wavelength and wavelengths associated with filters,
detector pixels, or spectral transitions.

This beam-specific specialization of [vacuum electromagnetic wavelength]
supplies the wavelength used to characterize the beam’s propagation and its
interaction with plasma. For a vacuum plane wave, the magnitude of its [wave
vector] satisfies the equivalent relation $|\mathbf{k}| = 2\pi/\lambda_0$,
where $\mathbf{k}$ is the vacuum wave vector.

NAMES.name: derivative_with_respect_to_normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_of_area_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short:
Rate of change of the area enclosed by a closed magnetic flux surface’s
poloidal cross-section as its signed poloidal magnetic-flux label varies.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the local geometric derivative of the area enclosed by a
closed magnetic flux surface’s poloidal cross-section with respect to the
surface’s signed poloidal magnetic-flux label.

The defining relation is

$$
\frac{dA}{d\psi}
$$

where $A$ is the enclosed poloidal cross-sectional area and $\psi$ is the
signed poloidal magnetic flux labeling the nested surface.

The derivative applies to each closed flux surface in the nested equilibrium
region and is not a volume or toroidal-surface average. It describes the
poloidal cross-sectional area only; it excludes the total area of the
three-dimensional toroidal surface and derivatives with respect to a
toroidal-flux coordinate.

This is the derivative specialization of the geometric quantity [area of a
flux surface]. It is mathematically analogous to the derivative of enclosed
volume with respect to poloidal magnetic flux, [derivative with respect to
poloidal magnetic flux coordinate of volume of flux
surface](name:derivative_with_respect_to_poloidal_magnetic_flux_coordinate_of_volume_of_flux_surface),
with area replacing volume.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the enclosed poloidal cross-sectional area
increases in the direction of increasing signed poloidal magnetic flux
$\psi$; for positive plasma current, this direction is toward the magnetic
axis because $\psi$ decreases outward.

sources.leaf_definition: Radial derivative of the cross-sectional area of the flux surface with respect to psi
sources.parent_definition: Equilibrium profiles (1D radial grid) as a function of the poloidal flux

NAMES.name: derivative_with_respect_to_toroidal_flux_coordinate_of_area_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short:
Rate of change of the poloidal cross-sectional area enclosed by a nested
magnetic flux surface as the dimensionful toroidal-flux coordinate varies.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the radial rate of change of the poloidal cross-sectional
area enclosed by a closed magnetic flux surface, parameterized by the
dimensionful toroidal flux coordinate. It describes how neighboring
flux-surface cross sections change along that coordinate.

For a nested family of flux surfaces, it is defined by

$$
\frac{dA}{d\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}}
$$

where $A(\rho_{\mathrm{tor}})$ is the poloidal cross-sectional area enclosed
by the flux surface labeled by $\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}$, and
$\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the dimensionful toroidal flux coordinate.

The scope is the enclosed poloidal cross-sectional area of a closed magnetic
flux surface in an equilibrium, with no averaging or summation over flux
surfaces. It is a local geometric derivative along the nested-surface
family, not the area of the three-dimensional toroidal surface.

This quantity is a derivative specialization of [area of a flux surface]. It
is distinct from the [derivative with respect to normalized poloidal flux
coordinate of area of a flux
surface](name:derivative_with_respect_to_normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_of_area_of_flux_surface),
which uses a normalized poloidal-flux coordinate, and from the [derivative
with respect to toroidal flux coordinate of volume of a flux
surface](name:derivative_with_respect_to_toroidal_flux_coordinate_of_volume_of_flux_surface),
which differentiates enclosed volume rather than cross-sectional area.

NAMES.name: electron_density
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short:
Free-electron number density per physical volume, with included populations
and spatial aggregation specified by applicable qualifiers or loci.
NAMES.long:
Free-electron number density is the amount of unbound electron population
occupying a local physical volume. It is the zeroth velocity-space moment of
the electron distribution.

For a kinetic description, the defining relation is:

$$
n_e(\mathbf{r},t)=\int f_e(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{v},t)\,d^3\mathbf{v}
$$

where $n_e$ is the free-electron number density, $\mathbf{r}$ is position,
$t$ is time, $f_e$ is the electron velocity-distribution function,
$\mathbf{v}$ is electron velocity, and $d^3\mathbf{v}$ is the differential
volume element in velocity space.

The unqualified quantity denotes a local physical-volume density without
selecting a thermal, fast, suprathermal, or complete-population component.
Its aggregation convention is local rather than line-averaged or
volume-averaged; population-qualified and spatially aggregated forms are
narrower instances of this general electron-density concept.

Bound electrons and ion populations are excluded. The quantity is distinct
from [thermal electron density](name:thermal_electron_density), which
excludes fast and suprathermal electrons, and from [total electron
density](name:total_electron_density), which explicitly combines the
specified electron populations.

The [line-averaged electron density](name:line_averaged_electron_density) is
the path integral of local electron density divided by the complete chord
length, while [volume-averaged electron
density](name:volume_averaged_electron_density) is the corresponding average
over the plasma volume. Electron density also provides the denominator in
the [ratio of total ion density to electron
density](name:ratio_of_total_ion_density_to_electron_density).

NAMES.name: elongation_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short:
Ratio of the vertical to horizontal semi-axes of a nested magnetic flux
surface’s poloidal cross-section, independent of its overall size.
NAMES.long:
Elongation is the shape ratio of an individual nested magnetic flux surface,
describing how extended its poloidal cross-section is vertically relative to
horizontally.

For a given flux surface, the elongation is defined by

$$
\kappa = \frac{a_v}{a_h}
$$

where $\kappa$ is the elongation, $a_v$ is the vertical semi-axis of the
poloidal cross-section, and $a_h$ is its horizontal semi-axis.

The quantity applies separately to each nested magnetic flux surface and is
a shape ratio rather than an integrated, summed, or averaged quantity. It is
not restricted to the outermost surface; the distinct [elongation of the
plasma boundary](name:elongation_of_plasma_boundary) refers specifically to
the last closed plasma boundary.

The [radial derivative of elongation of a flux surface] describes the change
of $\kappa$ across nested surfaces, whereas this quantity gives the
elongation at one surface.

NAMES.name: elongation_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless ratio of the plasma boundary’s vertical half-height to its
minor radius, quantifying the elongation of its cross-sectional shape.
NAMES.long:
Plasma-boundary elongation is the ratio of the vertical half-height to the
minor radius of the outermost closed plasma cross-section, describing its
vertical shaping relative to a circular cross-section.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major
radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, the elongation
is defined by

$$
\kappa = \frac{Z_{\max}-Z_{\min}}{2a}
$$

where $\kappa$ is the plasma-boundary elongation, $Z_{\max}$ and $Z_{\min}$
are the maximum and minimum vertical coordinates of the boundary, and $a$ is
the minor radius, defined as the radial half-width of the boundary
cross-section.

This quantity applies specifically to the plasma boundary rather than to an
arbitrary nested magnetic flux surface. Its geometric aggregation uses the
full vertical extent and radial half-width of the boundary cross-section; it
is not a local field value and is not averaged over the boundary. It
therefore excludes the corresponding elongation of an interior flux surface.

The quantity is the boundary-locus specialization of [elongation of a flux
surface](name:elongation_of_flux_surface), which applies the same geometric
ratio to a general nested magnetic flux-surface cross-section.

NAMES.name: equilibrium_weight_of_flux_loop
NAMES.short:
Nonnegative factor that sets the relative contribution of an individual
flux-loop poloidal-flux residual to an equilibrium objective function.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the nonnegative relative weight assigned to the residual of
one flux loop’s measured and equilibrium poloidal magnetic flux. It controls
how strongly that individual constraint influences the equilibrium
objective, rather than defining a magnetic flux itself.

The contribution associated with one flux-loop constraint is defined by

$$
J_{\mathrm{FL}} = \frac{1}{2} w_{\mathrm{FL}}^2 \frac{(\psi_{\mathrm{rec}}-\psi_{\mathrm{meas}})^2}{\sigma_{\mathrm{FL}}^2}
$$

where $J_{\mathrm{FL}}$ is the objective-function contribution of the
flux-loop constraint, $w_{\mathrm{FL}}$ is this equilibrium weight,
$\psi_{\mathrm{rec}}$ is the equilibrium poloidal magnetic flux at the
constraint location, $\psi_{\mathrm{meas}}$ is the corresponding measured
poloidal magnetic flux, and $\sigma_{\mathrm{FL}}$ is the standard deviation
assigned to that measurement error.

The weight applies to one flux-loop poloidal-flux constraint and is not
itself summed over sensors; the objective function aggregates the separate
contributions from individual constraints. It excludes the flux value, the
residual, and the measurement-error standard deviation, which are distinct
physical or statistical quantities.

The constrained flux is the [poloidal magnetic flux at the constraint
position](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_constraint_position), while the
sensor-specific weighting convention parallels the [equilibrium weight of a
poloidal magnetic-field
probe](name:equilibrium_weight_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe) with a
different sensor object.

sources.leaf_definition: Weight given to the measurement
sources.parent_definition: Set of flux loops

NAMES.name: equilibrium_weight_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless factor that controls the relative contribution of a poloidal
magnetic-field probe residual to the equilibrium objective function.
NAMES.long:
The equilibrium weight of a poloidal magnetic-field probe is a dimensionless
factor assigned to the residual of one probe constraint in an equilibrium
reconstruction objective.

For constraint index $i$, the objective contribution is defined through

$$
J = \frac{1}{2}\sum_i w_i^2\frac{(q_i^{\mathrm{rec}}-q_i^{\mathrm{meas}})^2}{\sigma_i^2}
$$

where $J$ is the equilibrium objective function, $w_i$ is the weight of
constraint $i$, $q_i^{\mathrm{rec}}$ is its reconstructed poloidal
magnetic-field value, $q_i^{\mathrm{meas}}$ is its measured value, and
$\sigma_i$ is the standard deviation of its measurement error.

This quantity applies to a single poloidal magnetic-field probe constraint
and does not represent the probe field, its residual, or the measurement
uncertainty. It is not an aggregate over multiple probes; the objective
function aggregates the individually weighted constraint contributions. The
analogous [equilibrium weight of an interferometer
beam](name:equilibrium_weight_of_interferometer_beam) applies the same
weighting role to a different constraint observable.

NAMES.name: faraday_angle
NAMES.short:
Faraday rotation of a probing wave’s polarization plane caused by electron
density and the magnetic-field component along its plasma path.
NAMES.long:
The Faraday angle is the signed rotation of a probing electromagnetic wave’s
polarization plane caused by propagation through magnetized plasma. For an
equilibrium state, it is the angle predicted from the electron density and
magnetic field encountered along the beam path.

In the cold, weakly dispersive magnetoionic approximation, the
plasma-induced rotation is defined by

$$
\theta_F = \frac{e^3\lambda^2}{8\pi^2\epsilon_0 m_e^2 c^3} \int_{\mathcal{L}} n_e(\ell) B_{\parallel}(\ell)\,d\ell
$$

where $\theta_F$ is the Faraday rotation angle, $e$ is the elementary-charge
magnitude, $\lambda$ is the probing-wave vacuum wavelength, $\pi$ is the
circle constant, $\epsilon_0$ is the vacuum permittivity, $m_e$ is the
electron mass, $c$ is the speed of light, $\mathcal{L}$ is the segment of
the beam path crossing the plasma, $\ell$ is distance along that path,
$n_e(\ell)$ is the local electron number density, and $B_{\parallel}(\ell)$
is the signed magnetic-field component along the beam direction.

The quantity applies to the electron contribution accumulated along one
probing beam through the plasma. Its aggregation is a line integral along
that path, not a local rotation rate, flux-surface average, or sum over
multiple beams; optical rotation produced outside the plasma is excluded.
The equilibrium-derived value is the rotation predicted by the reconstructed
plasma state and is distinct from a directly observed angle or from a
residual between prediction and observation.

Faraday angle describes rotation of the polarization plane, whereas
[polarization ellipticity of a polarimeter
beam](name:polarization_ellipticity_of_polarimeter_beam) describes the
signed shape of the polarization ellipse through its axis ratio; the two
quantities are not interchangeable.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the polarization plane rotates according to
the right-hand rule about the beam propagation direction from its incident
reference orientation.

NAMES.name: flux_surface_averaged_major_radius
NAMES.short:
Flux-surface-averaged nonnegative perpendicular distance from the toroidal
symmetry axis to points on a nested magnetic flux surface, giving the mean
major-radius coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Major radius is the nonnegative perpendicular distance from the toroidal
symmetry axis to a geometric point or specified location. For this
flux-surface-averaged quantity, that distance is averaged over each nested
magnetic flux surface in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame,
where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical
height.

The flux-surface average of major radius is defined by

$$
\langle R\rangle_\psi = \frac{\oint_\psi R\,dl/B_p}{\oint_\psi dl/B_p}
$$

where $\langle R\rangle_\psi$ is the averaged major-radius coordinate,
$\psi$ is the magnetic-flux label identifying the surface, $l$ is poloidal
arc length along that surface, and $B_p$ is the magnitude of the poloidal
magnetic field. The contour integral extends around the complete poloidal
intersection of the nested magnetic flux surface.

This quantity applies to a complete magnetic flux surface and aggregates the
local [major radius] using the flux-surface weighting defined by the inverse
poloidal-field magnitude. It is therefore distinct from pointwise major
radius and contains no point-specific or localized evaluation.

The quantity is the flux-surface-averaged counterpart of [major radius]. It
must not be confused with [flux-surface-averaged inverse of major
radius](name:flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_major_radius), which averages
the reciprocal $1/R$ rather than averaging $R$ itself; consequently, it is
not generally the reciprocal of that neighboring average.

sources.leaf_definition: Flux surface averaged R
sources.parent_definition: Equilibrium profiles (1D radial grid) as a function of the poloidal flux

NAMES.name: flux_surface_averaged_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude
NAMES.short:
Flux-surface average of the squared magnitude of the total equilibrium
magnetic field, providing a geometric coefficient for equilibrium and
neoclassical transport relations.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the surface-averaged squared strength of the total magnetic
field on a nested magnetic flux surface. It is a geometric metric
coefficient used in equilibrium descriptions and in bounce-averaged and
neoclassical transport relations.

The flux-surface average is defined by

$$
\left\langle B^2 \right\rangle_\psi = \frac{\displaystyle\oint_{S(\psi)} \frac{B^2}{\lvert\nabla\psi\rvert}\,dS}{\displaystyle\oint_{S(\psi)} \frac{1}{\lvert\nabla\psi\rvert}\,dS}
$$

where $B^2$ is the [square of the magnetic-field
magnitude](name:square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude), $\psi$ is the poloidal
magnetic-flux label of the surface, $S(\psi)$ is the closed magnetic flux
surface with that label, $\nabla\psi$ is the gradient of the flux label, and
$dS$ is the surface-area element.

The quantity applies to the total equilibrium magnetic field, including all
of its components, and is aggregated over each closed flux surface with the
inverse-$\lvert\nabla\psi\rvert$ weighting shown above. It is not the
pointwise value of $B^2$, the square of a flux-surface-averaged
magnetic-field magnitude, or a single magnetic-field component.

It is the flux-surface-averaged form of
[square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude](name:square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude).
It differs from
[flux_surface_averaged_magnetic_field_magnitude](name:flux_surface_averaged_magnetic_field_magnitude),
which averages the field magnitude before squaring, and from
[flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude](name:flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude),
which averages its reciprocal.

sources.parent_definition: Equilibrium profiles (1D radial grid) as a function of the poloidal flux

NAMES.name: gap_at_outboard_midplane
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the signed major-radius separation between a measurement
position and the magnetic separatrix after the position is mapped along its
flux surface to the outboard midplane. It applies pointwise to the selected
position and separatrix rather than to an average or to the separation
between two separatrices.

With the mapped position and separatrix evaluated at the outboard midplane,
the separation is defined by

$$
\Delta R_{\mathrm{sep,mid}} = R_{\mathrm{pos,mid}} - R_{\mathrm{sep,mid}}
$$

where $\Delta R_{\mathrm{sep,mid}}$ is the mapped separatrix distance,
$R_{\mathrm{pos,mid}}$ is the major-radius coordinate of the mapped
measurement position, and $R_{\mathrm{sep,mid}}$ is the major-radius
coordinate of the separatrix at the outboard midplane.

The quantity refers to one measurement position, its associated magnetic
flux surface, and one selected separatrix. It is a signed major-radius
separation in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, with no
flux-surface, spatial, species, or time aggregation. It is not the shortest
geometric distance, a plasma-wall clearance, or the distance between inner
and outer separatrices.

The flux-surface assignment can be expressed through the [normalized
poloidal flux coordinate at measurement
position](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_at_measurement_position),
while the two terms in the difference are outboard-midplane radial
coordinates of the type defined by [radial coordinate at outboard
midplane](name:radial_coordinate_at_outboard_midplane). The mapping
therefore converts the original position into a common outboard-midplane
comparison before the major-radius difference is taken.

NAMES.name: inverse_of_major_radius
NAMES.short:
Reciprocal major-radius coordinate for a geometric point or specified
location, serving as a positive geometric factor in toroidal equilibrium
relations.
NAMES.long:
Reciprocal major radius is the inverse of the perpendicular distance from
the toroidal symmetry axis to a geometric point or specified location. It is
a geometric quantity used to represent the radial dependence of toroidal
equilibrium relations.

$$
R^{-1} = \frac{1}{R}
$$

where $R$ is the [major radius], namely the radial coordinate in the
right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

At the parent level, the quantity is evaluated pointwise or at a specified
geometric location and has no averaging or integration implied. It is
positive wherever the major radius is positive, and it is distinct from the
major radius itself because it reverses the radial dependence rather than
specifying the distance from the symmetry axis.

A flux-surface-averaged instance applies the flux-surface averaging
operation to this reciprocal quantity;
[flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_major_radius](name:flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_major_radius)
is the corresponding geometric coefficient obtained by averaging over a
magnetic flux surface.

NAMES.name: flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_major_radius
NAMES.short:
Flux-surface average of reciprocal major radius, providing a geometric
equilibrium coefficient for toroidal geometry in flux-coordinate equations.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the geometric average of the reciprocal major radius over a
complete magnetic flux surface. It is an equilibrium metric coefficient
independent of plasma species, population, magnetic-field component, and
physical transport process.

For a magnetic flux surface identified by the label $\psi$, the defining
flux-surface average is:

$$
g_{1/R}(\psi) =
\left\langle \frac{1}{R} \right\rangle_\psi =
\frac{\displaystyle\oint_{\mathcal{S}(\psi)}
\frac{dS}{|\nabla\psi|}\,\frac{1}{R}}
{\displaystyle\oint_{\mathcal{S}(\psi)}
\frac{dS}{|\nabla\psi|}}
$$

Here $g_{1/R}$ denotes the metric coefficient, $R$ is the major-radius
coordinate, $\psi$ is the magnetic flux-surface label, $\mathcal{S}(\psi)$
is the corresponding closed magnetic flux surface, $dS$ is its surface-area
element, and $\nabla\psi$ is the spatial gradient of the flux-surface label.
The coordinate $R$ belongs to the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$
frame, where $\phi$ is the toroidal angle and $Z$ is the vertical
coordinate.

The aggregation is over the entire closed flux surface using the
flux-surface weighting shown in the defining relation; this is not the local
reciprocal radius at a point. The quantity is distinct from the flux-surface
average of reciprocal squared major radius, [flux-surface-averaged inverse
square of major
radius](name:flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_square_of_major_radius).

It is the flux-surface-averaged specialization of [inverse major
radius](name:inverse_of_major_radius): the averaging operator is applied to
the local reciprocal-major-radius quantity without introducing a species,
field-component, or process restriction.

NAMES.name: inverse_of_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude
NAMES.short:
Reciprocal square of total magnetic-field strength, providing a positive
magnetic-geometry factor for equilibrium and flux-surface-averaged transport
relations.
NAMES.long:
The inverse square of total magnetic-field strength is a local
magnetic-geometry factor that increases as the total field weakens and
remains positive wherever the field magnitude is nonzero.

It is defined as the reciprocal of the [square of magnetic-field
magnitude](name:square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude):

$$
B^{-2} = \frac{1}{B^2} = \frac{1}{\lvert \mathbf{B} \rvert^2}
$$

where $\mathbf{B}$ is the total magnetic-field vector and $B$ is its
magnitude.

The quantity applies to the full magnetic field in an equilibrium plasma,
including all vector components and without restriction to a particle
population. At the parent level it is a local quantity with no flux-surface
or volume aggregation; it is distinct from the squared field magnitude
itself and from the reciprocal square of any selected field component.

The [flux-surface-averaged inverse square of magnetic-field
magnitude](name:flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude)
is obtained by applying a flux-surface average to this local factor. The
averaging is a separate aggregation operation and does not alter the
reciprocal-square transformation.

NAMES.name: flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude
NAMES.short:
Flux-surface average of the reciprocal square of total magnetic-field
strength, a geometric coefficient in neoclassical and flux-surface-averaged
transport relations.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the flux-surface average of the reciprocal square of the
total magnetic-field strength on a nested magnetic surface. It captures
field-strength geometry independently of the magnetic-field direction.

The defining relation is

$$
\left\langle \frac{1}{|\mathbf{B}|^2} \right\rangle_\psi
=
\frac{\displaystyle \int_{S(\psi)} |\mathbf{B}|^{-2}\,\frac{dS}{|\nabla\psi|}}
{\displaystyle \int_{S(\psi)} \frac{dS}{|\nabla\psi|}}
$$

where $\mathbf{B}$ is the total magnetic-field vector, $|\mathbf{B}|$ is its
magnitude, $\psi$ is the flux-surface label, $S(\psi)$ is the magnetic
surface labeled by $\psi$, $dS$ is its surface-area element, and
$\nabla\psi$ is the spatial gradient of the flux-surface label.

The quantity applies to the complete magnetic flux surface and uses the
inverse-$|\nabla\psi|$ weighting shown in the defining relation. It is not a
pointwise inverse-square field value and has no selection by magnetic-field
direction, component, species, or source.

It is the flux-surface-averaged transformation of the parent [inverse square
of magnetic-field
magnitude](name:inverse_of_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude), with the
reciprocal square formed locally before averaging. It is distinct from
[flux-surface-averaged magnetic-field
magnitude](name:flux_surface_averaged_magnetic_field_magnitude) and
[flux-surface-averaged square of magnetic-field
magnitude](name:flux_surface_averaged_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude),
because nonlinear inversion and squaring do not commute with surface
averaging.

NAMES.name: inverse_of_square_of_major_radius
NAMES.short:
Geometric inverse-square-major-radius coefficient for toroidal plasma
equilibrium, including flux-surface-averaged forms used in magnetic-geometry
relations.
NAMES.long:
This quantity represents the reciprocal-square major-radius dependence of a
geometric coefficient in toroidal plasma equilibrium. It characterizes the
metric scaling associated with the distance from the machine symmetry axis.

For the direct inverse-square form, the coefficient is defined by

$$
K_R = \frac{1}{R^2}
$$

where $K_R$ is the inverse-square-major-radius coefficient and $R$ is the
major radius in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

The quantity applies to toroidal equilibrium geometry and is not the major
radius itself or its direct square. It denotes the inverse-square geometric
factor; any aggregation over a magnetic flux surface is an additional
operation rather than part of the unaggregated quantity.

The [flux-surface-averaged inverse-square-major-radius
coefficient](name:flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_square_of_major_radius)
is the corresponding instance obtained by averaging this inverse-square
factor over a magnetic flux surface. The quantity is therefore the
reciprocal-square counterpart of
[square_of_major_radius](name:square_of_major_radius), with the inverse
relationship supplying the geometric scaling.

NAMES.name: flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_square_of_major_radius
NAMES.short:
Flux-surface average of reciprocal squared major radius, providing a
geometric metric coefficient for parallel-gradient and neoclassical
transport calculations.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the flux-surface average of the reciprocal square of the
major radius on a nested equilibrium magnetic flux surface. It is a positive
geometric metric coefficient used in parallel-gradient operators and
neoclassical and gyrokinetic transport equations.

It is defined by

$$
g_{m1}(\psi)=\left\langle \frac{1}{R^2}\right\rangle_{\psi}
$$

where $g_{m1}$ denotes this metric coefficient, $R$ is the major radius
measured from the toroidal symmetry axis, $\psi$ is the poloidal magnetic
flux labeling the surface, and $\langle\cdot\rangle_{\psi}$ denotes the
flux-surface average on that surface.

The quantity applies to the entire magnetic flux surface and has no species,
field-component, or source-process restriction. Its aggregation convention
is a flux-surface average of the local reciprocal-square geometric factor;
it is not the reciprocal square of a flux-surface-averaged major radius.

It is the flux-surface-averaged form of the pointwise [inverse of square of
major radius](name:inverse_of_square_of_major_radius). It differs from the
related [flux-surface-averaged inverse of major
radius](name:flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_major_radius), which averages
the first reciprocal power of $R$ rather than its reciprocal square.

NAMES.name: magnetic_field
NAMES.short:
Local total magnetic-induction vector in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ,
Z) frame, where R is major radius, φ is toroidal angle, and Z is vertical
height; it does not select a source contribution, perturbation state,
component, magnitude reduction, or evaluation locus.
NAMES.long:
Local total magnetic-induction vector is the magnetic flux-density vector at
a point, carrying both the local field direction and field strength. It is
the unqualified parent quantity before selecting a source contribution,
perturbation state, component, scalar reduction, spatial aggregation, or
evaluation locus.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, the vector resolves
into radial, toroidal, and vertical components as

$$
\mathbf{B} = B_R\hat{\mathbf{R}} + B_\phi\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}} + B_Z\hat{\mathbf{Z}}
$$

where $\mathbf{B}$ is this local total magnetic-induction vector; $B_R$ is
its radial projection, $B_\phi$ is its [toroidal magnetic-field
component](name:toroidal_magnetic_field), and $B_Z$ is its [vertical
magnetic-field component](name:vertical_magnetic_field); and
$\hat{\mathbf{R}}$, $\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}$, and $\hat{\mathbf{Z}}$ are
the corresponding basis vectors. The frame is right-handed with
$\hat{\mathbf{R}} \times \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}} = \hat{\mathbf{Z}}$; $R$ is
major radius measured from the symmetry axis, $\phi$ is toroidal angle
increasing counterclockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{\mathbf{Z}}$, and
$Z$ is vertical height.

The quantity applies wherever a local magnetic induction is defined,
including confined plasma and surrounding vacuum regions, and no particle
species or population is selected or aggregated. It is pointwise and
vector-valued: it is not the [magnetic field magnitude], a
[flux-surface-average magnetic field], or an extremum such as the [maximum
magnetic field](name:maximum_magnetic_field). No cylindrical component,
source contribution, perturbation state, or named locus is implied by the
unqualified name.

When a [magnetic vector potential](name:magnetic_vector_potential)
$\mathbf{A}$ is used, $\mathbf{B} = \nabla \times \mathbf{A}$; $\mathbf{A}$
is the magnetic vector potential and $\nabla \times$ is the curl operator,
and a gage change affects $\mathbf{A}$ without changing $\mathbf{B}$.
Source-qualified fields such as the [vacuum magnetic
field](name:vacuum_magnetic_field) and [plasma magnetic
field](name:plasma_magnetic_field) are vector contributions of the same kind
and add vectorially when they belong to the same electromagnetic state; the
[toroidal vacuum magnetic field](name:toroidal_vacuum_magnetic_field) is the
toroidal projection of the vacuum contribution. The [reference magnetic
field](name:reference_magnetic_field) is a reference total
magnetic-induction vector of the same kind, not a source-specific
contribution; the [toroidal magnetic field at the magnetic
axis](name:toroidal_magnetic_field_at_magnetic_axis) is the toroidal
projection evaluated at the magnetic-axis locus.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the vacuum toroidal magnetic-field component
is directed along increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed
cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: magnetic_flux
NAMES.short:
Magnetic flux is the signed scalar surface integral of the magnetic field
through an oriented surface. Its sign is set by the chosen surface
orientation, while specializations identify the particular surface, field
contribution, or averaging convention.
NAMES.long:
Magnetic flux is a signed scalar associated with an oriented surface. It
represents the net normal component of the magnetic field threading that
surface; the flux itself is not a vector and is not directed, although its
sign depends on the surface orientation.

The magnetic flux $\Phi$ through an oriented surface $S$ is defined by the
surface integral:

$$
\Phi(S) = \int_S \mathbf{B} \cdot d\mathbf{A}
$$

where $\Phi(S)$ is the magnetic flux through $S$, $S$ is the oriented
surface, $\mathbf{B}$ is the [magnetic-field vector](name:magnetic_field),
$d\mathbf{A}=\hat{\mathbf{n}}\,dA$ is the oriented area element,
$\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is the chosen unit normal to $S$, and $dA$ is the scalar
surface-area element.

The unqualified quantity denotes the net integral over the specified
oriented surface with no source restriction and no averaging. More specific
flux quantities supply the surface family, source contribution, projection,
or weighting that narrows this definition.

Magnetic flux is distinct from the local magnetic field, from a
magnetic-field component or magnitude, from a flux-coordinate label
normalized from a flux, and from a time derivative such as loop voltage.
[Poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux) and [toroidal magnetic
flux](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux) are specializations obtained by choosing
different surfaces and orientations for the same integral; source-restricted
or weighted quantities, such as [poloidal-current-weighted average external
magnetic
flux](name:poloidal_current_weighted_average_external_magnetic_flux), retain
the magnetic-flux meaning while restricting the included magnetic field or
applying the stated averaging convention.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the net magnetic-field projection through the
specified surface is along the chosen orientation of its area element.

NAMES.name: external_magnetic_flux
NAMES.short:
External magnetic flux is the signed surface integral of the magnetic field
generated by sources outside the plasma current distribution over an
oriented surface.
NAMES.long:
External magnetic flux is the signed surface integral of the magnetic field
generated by sources outside the plasma current distribution over an
oriented surface. It is the source-separated member of the [magnetic
flux](name:magnetic_flux) family.

The defining surface integral is:

$$
\Phi_{\mathrm{ext}}(S) = \int_S \mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{ext}} \cdot d\mathbf{A}
$$

where $\Phi_{\mathrm{ext}}(S)$ is the external magnetic flux associated with
the oriented surface $S$, $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{ext}}$ is the magnetic-field
vector produced by sources outside the plasma current distribution, and
$d\mathbf{A}$ is the oriented surface-area element.

The scope is the external-source contribution integrated over the complete
surface specified by a concrete specialization. At this parent level, no
poloidal or toroidal projection, spatial locus, or averaging weight is
imposed; the quantity is a signed surface aggregate, not a local
magnetic-field value, a flux-surface average, or a contribution generated by
the plasma current itself.

The child [average external magnetic
flux](name:average_external_magnetic_flux) is a concrete poloidal
specialization with averaging over the plasma cross-section. The related
[current-weighted average external magnetic
flux](name:current_weighted_average_external_magnetic_flux) uses
plasma-current weighting for that aggregation; both remain source-separated
instances of external magnetic flux.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the net external magnetic field points along
the positive normal of the oriented integration surface in the right-handed
cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: magnetic_flux_due_to_diamagnetic_drift
NAMES.short:
Vector magnetic-flux contribution of the pressure-gradient-driven
diamagnetic response in a plasma equilibrium, defined relative to the
corresponding reference magnetic field.
NAMES.long:
The diamagnetic magnetic-flux contribution is the vector magnetic flux
associated with the pressure-gradient-driven diamagnetic response in a
plasma equilibrium, measured relative to a corresponding reference field
without that response.

For an integration surface $S$, the contribution is defined by

$$
\boldsymbol{\Phi}_{\mathrm{dia}} = \int_S \Delta \mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{dia}}\,dS
$$

where $\boldsymbol{\Phi}_{\mathrm{dia}}$ is the diamagnetic magnetic-flux
vector, $\Delta \mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{dia}}$ is the equilibrium magnetic-field
difference attributable to the pressure-gradient-driven diamagnetic
response, and $dS$ is the scalar surface-area element on $S$.

This quantity applies to the plasma equilibrium as a whole at the surface
used to define the magnetic flux. It retains the vector component
information and the aggregation over the selected surface; it is not
restricted to a single axis projection, species, normalization, or spatial
region.

The reference-field subtraction excludes magnetic flux already present
without the diamagnetic response and distinguishes this contribution from
the total equilibrium magnetic flux. The [toroidal magnetic flux due to
diamagnetic drift](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux_due_to_diamagnetic_drift) is
the toroidal component of this general vector quantity.

Components are resolved in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame,
where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical
height.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when a resolved magnetic-flux component points
along the corresponding positive basis direction of the right-handed
cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame; the toroidal component is positive toward
increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: magnetic_shear_at_flux_surface
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless logarithmic radial gradient of the safety factor on a magnetic
flux surface, measuring how magnetic-field-line pitch changes across
neighboring surfaces.
NAMES.long:
Magnetic shear at a magnetic flux surface is the local logarithmic radial
variation of the safety factor, expressing the change in magnetic-field-line
pitch between neighboring nested surfaces.

It is defined by

$$
s(\rho_\mathrm{tor}) = \frac{\rho_\mathrm{tor}}{q(\rho_\mathrm{tor})}\frac{dq(\rho_\mathrm{tor})}{d\rho_\mathrm{tor}}
$$

where $s$ is magnetic shear, $\rho_\mathrm{tor}$ is the toroidal-flux radial
coordinate labeling the magnetic flux surface, and $q$ is the safety factor
on that surface.

The quantity applies to the equilibrium magnetic geometry of the specified
magnetic flux surface without restricting the surface to a particular plasma
region, species, or particle population. It is a local value associated with
one surface, not a sum, volume integral, or average over multiple surfaces.

It is distinct from the corresponding values at special loci such as the
[magnetic axis](name:magnetic_shear_at_magnetic_axis), [plasma
boundary](name:magnetic_shear_at_plasma_boundary), or [internal transport
barrier](name:magnetic_shear_at_internal_transport_barrier). The expression
relates magnetic shear directly to the logarithmic derivative of the safety
factor with respect to the toroidal-flux radial coordinate.

NAMES.name: maximum_magnetic_field
NAMES.short:
Largest value attained by a selected magnetic-field quantity over its
specified evaluation domain, without fixing its source, projection,
magnitude, or locus.
NAMES.long:
The maximum magnetic-field quantity is the extremal value of a selected
magnetic-field quantity evaluated over a specified domain. It is a
domain-level reduction of the local [magnetic field](name:magnetic_field),
rather than the local magnetic-field vector itself.

The maximum operation can be represented abstractly as

$$
M = \max_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{D}} Q(\mathbf{x})
$$

where $M$ is the resulting maximum magnetic-field value, $Q(\mathbf{x})$ is
the selected local magnetic-field quantity, $\mathbf{x}$ is an evaluation
point, and $\mathcal{D}$ is the specified evaluation domain.

This parent fixes the maximum aggregation over the domain but imposes no
particular magnetic-field source, physical state, projection, magnitude
selection, population, or plasma or vacuum region. The result is one
extremal value for the selected domain, not a local value, average,
integral, or mode-resolved quantity.

It is distinct from the local [magnetic field](name:magnetic_field) and does
not by itself determine whether the selected quantity is a total field,
source contribution, signed component, or field magnitude. The child
[maximum magnetic-field magnitude](name:maximum_magnetic_field_magnitude)
specializes this parent by selecting the magnitude of the total local
magnetic-field vector before applying the maximum operation.

NAMES.name: maximum_magnetic_field_magnitude
NAMES.short:
Largest magnitude of the magnetic-field vector over a specified evaluation
domain, distinguishing total field strength from any signed field component.
NAMES.long:
The maximum magnetic-field magnitude is the greatest total field strength
attained within the physical evaluation domain associated with the quantity.

The defining extremum is

$$
B_{\max} = \max_{\mathbf{x}\in D} \left\lVert \mathbf{B}(\mathbf{x}) \right\rVert
$$

where $B_{\max}$ is the maximum magnetic-field magnitude,
$\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{x})$ is the magnetic-field vector at spatial point
$\mathbf{x}$, and $D$ is the specified evaluation domain.

The domain may be a nested magnetic flux surface or a coil-conductor
surface, as established by the physical context. The maximum operation
aggregates the field magnitude over all points in $D$ and returns its
largest value; it does not represent a spatial average or a particular field
component.

This quantity selects the modulus of the magnetic-field vector before
applying the maximum operation. It is therefore the magnitude-specific child
of [maximum magnetic field](name:maximum_magnetic_field), whose parent
concept leaves the scalar field being maximized unspecified. It excludes
maxima of signed toroidal, poloidal, radial, or other individual
magnetic-field components.

NAMES.name: mhd_energy
NAMES.short:
Global plasma stored energy obtained from the volume integral of total
kinetic pressure, including thermal and fast-particle pressure
contributions.
NAMES.long:
MHD plasma stored energy is the global energy content assigned to the plasma
by integrating its equilibrium-reconstructed total kinetic pressure over the
full plasma volume. It includes thermal and fast-particle contributions
rather than representing only one pressure population.

The defining relation is

$$
W_{\mathrm{MHD}} = \frac{3}{2}\int_{V_{\mathrm{plasma}}} p_{\mathrm{tot}}\,dV
$$

where $W_{\mathrm{MHD}}$ is the MHD plasma stored energy, $p_{\mathrm{tot}}$
is the total kinetic pressure determined by the equilibrium reconstruction,
$V_{\mathrm{plasma}}$ is the complete plasma volume, and $dV$ is the
differential volume element.

This is a global volume-integrated quantity over all included plasma
populations. It is distinct from [thermal plasma
energy](name:thermal_plasma_energy), which integrates thermal pressure only,
and from [diamagnetic energy](name:diamagnetic_energy), which is restricted
to pressure perpendicular to the local magnetic field. The factor $3/2$
defines the stored-energy convention used for the total kinetic-pressure
integral.

NAMES.name: minor_radius_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short:
Half the difference between the maximum and minimum major-radius coordinates
of the last closed plasma-boundary contour, defining its horizontal
cross-sectional size.
NAMES.long:
The minor radius is the effective horizontal semi-axis of the last closed
plasma-boundary contour and characterizes the radial extent of the plasma
cross-section.

The minor radius $a$ is defined by

$$
a = \frac{R_{\max} - R_{\min}}{2}
$$

where $a$ is the minor radius, $R_{\max}$ is the maximum major-radius
coordinate on the boundary contour, and $R_{\min}$ is the minimum
major-radius coordinate on that contour.

This quantity applies to the complete last closed plasma-boundary contour
and is determined from its global major-radius extrema. It is a nonnegative
geometric size parameter, not a local major-radius coordinate such as the
[radial coordinate at the outboard
midplane](name:radial_coordinate_at_outboard_midplane) and not a
flux-surface average.

The [elongation of the plasma boundary](name:elongation_of_plasma_boundary)
uses this minor radius as the horizontal reference semi-axis when forming
the boundary's vertical-to-horizontal shape ratio.

NAMES.name: non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field
NAMES.short:
Non-axisymmetric magnetic-field vector of the local vacuum induction
generated by external coils, with its toroidally averaged component removed.
NAMES.long:
The non-axisymmetric magnetic field $\mathbf{B}_{\rm NA}$ is the vector part
of the external-coil vacuum [magnetic induction](name:magnetic_field) that
varies with toroidal angle after its toroidally averaged component is
removed. It retains the full field direction rather than selecting a
cylindrical component or a magnitude.

The non-axisymmetric component is defined by

$$
\mathbf{B}_{\rm NA}(R,\phi,Z) = \mathbf{B}_{\rm vac}(R,\phi,Z) - \left\langle \mathbf{B}_{\rm vac} \right\rangle_\phi(R,Z)
$$

where $\mathbf{B}_{\rm NA}$ is the non-axisymmetric magnetic induction,
$\mathbf{B}_{\rm vac}$ is the magnetic induction generated by external coil
currents with plasma-current contributions omitted, and $\langle
\mathbf{B}_{\rm vac} \rangle_\phi$ is its average over the toroidal angle.
The variables $R$, $\phi$, and $Z$ are respectively major radius, toroidal
angle, and vertical height in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$
frame.

This quantity is a local vector field defined for the external-coil vacuum
contribution, without restriction to a particular plasma population or
spatial region. Its aggregation convention is the removal of the
toroidal-angle average, so only non-axisymmetric toroidal variation remains.

It excludes the toroidally symmetric vacuum field, magnetic induction
generated by plasma currents, and any scalar magnitude reduction. It
therefore does not represent the full local [magnetic
induction](name:magnetic_field) when those omitted source contributions are
present.

The vector is the common parent for its cylindrical projections: the [radial
non-axisymmetric magnetic
field](name:radial_non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field), [toroidal
non-axisymmetric magnetic
field](name:toroidal_non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field), and [vertical
non-axisymmetric magnetic
field](name:vertical_non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field) each resolve this same
vector along one direction of the right-handed cylindrical frame.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when a resolved component points along its
corresponding positive basis direction in the right-handed cylindrical
$(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: normalized_plasma_internal_inductance
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless li_3 parameter measuring poloidal magnetic-field peaking
through a plasma-volume integral normalized by total plasma current and a
reference major radius.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the normalized internal inductance of the plasma current
distribution. It characterizes the peaking of the poloidal magnetic field
generated by the total plasma current, rather than a ratio formed only from
a boundary field.

Under the li_3 definition,

$$
l_i = \frac{2}{R_0\mu_0^2 I_p^2} \int_{V_p} B_p^2\,dV
$$

where $l_i$ is the normalized internal inductance, $R_0$ is the reference
major radius, $\mu_0$ is the vacuum permeability, $I_p$ is the total signed
plasma current, $B_p$ is the magnitude of the poloidal magnetic field, $V_p$
is the plasma volume, and $dV$ is a differential volume element.

This is a global equilibrium quantity. The aggregation is a volume integral
of the squared poloidal-field magnitude over the entire plasma volume,
normalized by the square of the total plasma current; it does not select a
separate species, charge state, orbit class, or localized position.

It is distinct from the dimensional [plasma inductance]: the present
quantity includes the reference-radius and vacuum-permeability normalization
in the defining expression and is not a local inductance, a flux-surface
average, or a boundary-field ratio.

If $L_p$ denotes the [plasma inductance], the normalized quantity is related
by $l_i = 2L_p/(R_0\mu_0)$. Thus, under the same reference normalization, a
larger value indicates a more strongly concentrated poloidal-field energy
distribution associated with the plasma current.

NAMES.name: normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless radial label equal to the square root of toroidal magnetic
flux normalized between the magnetic axis and equilibrium boundary.
NAMES.long:
The normalized toroidal flux coordinate is a dimensionless label for nested
magnetic surfaces, increasing outward from the magnetic axis toward the
equilibrium boundary. It is a magnetic-surface coordinate, not a cylindrical
distance or a local vector component.

$$
\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}} = \left(\frac{\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}} - \Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}}}{\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,boundary}} - \Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}}}\right)^{1/2}
$$

where $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ is the normalized toroidal flux coordinate,
$\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the toroidal magnetic flux enclosed by the labeled
surface, $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}}$ is its value at the magnetic axis, and
$\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,boundary}}$ is its value at the equilibrium boundary used
for normalization.

The coordinate applies to nested magnetic surfaces and to mapped physical
locations assigned to those surfaces. It is zero at the magnetic axis and
one at the chosen equilibrium boundary; each value is a single surface
label, with no summation, averaging, species aggregation, or mode
aggregation. Locus-specific quantities such as the [normalized toroidal flux
coordinate at a beam-tracing
point](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_beam_tracing_point) and
the [normalized toroidal flux coordinate at a measurement
position](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_measurement_position)
are evaluations of this same coordinate.

This quantity is distinct from the dimensionful [toroidal flux
coordinate](name:toroidal_flux_coordinate), because it is normalized to the
axis-to-boundary interval and transformed by a square root. It also differs
from the [normalized poloidal flux
coordinate](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate), which uses poloidal
rather than toroidal magnetic flux, and from the [normalized minor radius of
a flux surface](name:normalized_minor_radius_of_flux_surface), which is
based on geometric extent rather than enclosed toroidal flux.

NAMES.name: normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_constraint_position
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless magnetic-surface label assigning an equilibrium constraint
position its normalized toroidal-flux radius between the magnetic axis and
last closed flux surface.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the normalized toroidal-flux radial label assigned to the
spatial point at which an equilibrium constraint is defined. It identifies
the nested magnetic flux surface passing through that point, rather than the
constrained current, density, pressure, or other physical observable.

The label is defined by

$$
\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}} = \sqrt{\frac{\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}} - \Phi_{\mathrm{axis}}}{\Phi_{\mathrm{LCFS}} - \Phi_{\mathrm{axis}}}}
$$

where $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ is the normalized toroidal-flux coordinate,
$\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the enclosed toroidal magnetic flux of the flux
surface through the constraint position, $\Phi_{\mathrm{axis}}$ is its value
at the magnetic axis, and $\Phi_{\mathrm{LCFS}}$ is its value at the last
closed flux surface.

This quantity is evaluated pointwise at an equilibrium constraint position,
with no spatial averaging, flux-surface integration, or summation over
different constraint types. It is independent of whether the associated
constraint concerns a current, density, pressure, or another equilibrium
observable, and it is not the observable value or its uncertainty.

It is the constraint-position specialization of the [normalized toroidal
flux coordinate](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate): the same
magnetic-surface label is evaluated at the position associated with an
equilibrium constraint. The normalization assigns zero at the magnetic axis
and unity at the last closed flux surface when the enclosed toroidal flux
varies monotonically between those surfaces.

NAMES.name: plasma_beta
NAMES.short:
Plasma beta is a dimensionless measure of total plasma pressure relative to
a magnetic-pressure scale, with the pressure aggregation, field reference,
and any additional normalization supplied by each specialized plasma-beta
definition.
NAMES.long:
Plasma beta is a dimensionless equilibrium measure of the total pressure
content of the confined plasma relative to a magnetic-pressure scale. It
names the common plasma-pressure-to-magnetic-pressure concept without
selecting a particular magnetic-field reference, pressure aggregation, or
additional normalization.

The generic specialization relation is

$$
\beta_\star = \mathcal{N}_\star\!\left(\frac{2\mu_0\,p_{\mathrm{plasma},\star}}{B_{\mathrm{ref},\star}^{2}}\right)
$$

where $\beta_\star$ is a specialized plasma beta, $\star$ labels the
specialized definition, $p_{\mathrm{plasma},\star}$ is the plasma-pressure
measure prescribed by that definition, $B_{\mathrm{ref},\star}$ is the
corresponding magnetic-field reference, $\mu_0$ is the vacuum permeability,
and $\mathcal{N}_\star$ is any additional normalization operation prescribed
by that definition. Where no additional normalization is prescribed,
$\mathcal{N}_\star$ is the identity operation.

The scope is the confined plasma in an equilibrium state. Its aggregation
convention is not fixed at the parent level: each specialized plasma-beta
name supplies the pressure aggregate, the included plasma populations, and
the plasma region over which that aggregate is formed. This parent excludes
species-resolved pressure measures, local beta values, and any fixed choice
of toroidal, poloidal, vacuum, or total magnetic-field reference unless that
choice is made by a specialized name.

Concrete plasma-beta names specialize this parent by fixing
$p_{\mathrm{plasma},\star}$, $B_{\mathrm{ref},\star}$, and
$\mathcal{N}_\star$. The child [normalized toroidal plasma
beta](name:normalized_toroidal_plasma_beta) is a specialized plasma beta
with a toroidal-field pressure scale and an additional normalization;
related axis-specific beta quantities such as [poloidal
beta](name:poloidal_beta) and [toroidal beta](name:toroidal_beta) fix their
magnetic-pressure scale according to their own definitions.

NAMES.name: normalized_toroidal_plasma_beta
NAMES.short:
Normalized toroidal plasma beta, conventionally denoted β_N, is the ratio of
toroidal plasma beta times plasma minor radius and reference toroidal
magnetic field to total plasma current, including the conventional factor
100.
NAMES.long:
Normalized toroidal plasma beta, conventionally denoted $\beta_N$, is the
ratio of toroidal plasma beta times plasma minor radius and reference
toroidal magnetic field to total plasma current, including the conventional
factor 100. It is a whole-plasma equilibrium beta metric based on the
volume-averaged total perpendicular plasma pressure entering toroidal beta.

The defining relation is:

$$
\beta_N = 100\,\beta_{\mathrm{tor}}\,\frac{a B_0}{I_p}
$$

where $\beta_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is
[beta](name:normalized_toroidal_plasma_beta), the unnormalized toroidal
plasma beta; $a$ is the plasma minor radius; $B_0$ is the reference toroidal
magnetic field; and $I_p$ is the total plasma current. The factor $100$ and
the prescribed numerical normalization of $a$, $B_0$, and $I_p$ are part of
the definition.

The scope is the whole plasma. The pressure population is the total
perpendicular plasma pressure represented by $\beta_{\mathrm{tor}}$, with
the volume averaging inherited from
[beta](name:normalized_toroidal_plasma_beta); it is not restricted to
thermal pressure.

This quantity is distinct from [beta](name:normalized_toroidal_plasma_beta),
which is the unnormalized toroidal pressure ratio, and from a
thermal-pressure-only normalized toroidal beta. Within the global
beta-metric family, $\beta_N$ rescales
[beta](name:normalized_toroidal_plasma_beta) by plasma size,
reference-field, and current factors, whereas
[poloidal_beta](name:poloidal_beta) uses a poloidal-field/current
normalization.

NAMES.name: plasma_current
NAMES.short:
Net toroidal electric current carried by the entire plasma column, obtained
by integrating toroidal current density over its enclosed poloidal
cross-section.
NAMES.long:
Plasma current is the net electric current carried by the full plasma
population, represented as the toroidal current crossing a poloidal
cross-section in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$
is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

$$
I_p = \int_{A_p} j_\phi\,\mathrm{d}A
$$

where $I_p$ is the total plasma current, $A_p$ is the enclosed poloidal
cross-sectional area, $j_\phi$ is the toroidal component of the electric
current density, and $\mathrm{d}A$ is the differential area element.

The quantity includes the algebraic sum of toroidal currents from all
charged plasma species and charge states over the complete enclosed plasma
cross-section. It is a global total rather than a local current density, a
species-resolved contribution, or a current restricted to a particular
physical mechanism.

It is the area integral of the toroidal projection of [current
density](name:current_density). The narrower [toroidal total
runaway-electron current](name:toroidal_total_runaway_electron_current)
represents only the runaway-electron contribution and is not the full plasma
current.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the net plasma current flows in the direction
of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical
$(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: plasma_pressure
NAMES.short:
Plasma pressure is the isotropic kinetic pressure of the plasma, the scalar
part of the kinetic pressure tensor used in equilibrium force balance. The
unqualified quantity denotes an equilibrium scalar pressure, not a
first-order pressure perturbation.
NAMES.long:
Plasma pressure is the isotropic kinetic pressure of the plasma, the scalar
part of the kinetic pressure tensor in a fluid or magnetohydrodynamic
description. It represents equilibrium mechanical stress from the plasma
populations included in the pressure model and is not a perturbation
amplitude.

The scalar pressure is the one-third trace of the kinetic pressure tensor:

$$
p = \frac{1}{3}\operatorname{tr}\mathbf{P}
$$

where $p$ is the plasma pressure, $\mathbf{P}$ is the kinetic pressure
tensor, and $\operatorname{tr}$ denotes the tensor trace. For locally
isotropic Maxwellian populations, an included population $s$ contributes
$n_s k_B T_s$, where $n_s$ is the number density of population $s$, $T_s$ is
its temperature, and $k_B$ is the Boltzmann constant.

The unqualified quantity applies to equilibrium scalar kinetic pressure; it
is additive over the included plasma populations and does not imply
normalization, volume integration, or selection of only a bulk-thermal,
fast-particle, or perturbed population subset. It excludes magnetic
pressure, dynamic ram pressure, anisotropic pressure components, and any
individual component of the pressure tensor.

[Total plasma pressure](name:total_plasma_pressure) is the specialization in
which all represented equilibrium kinetic pressure contributions are
included, while [thermal plasma pressure](name:thermal_plasma_pressure) is
restricted to bulk thermal electron and ion populations. [Perturbed plasma
pressure](name:perturbed_plasma_pressure) denotes a first-order variation
about an equilibrium pressure and is not part of the equilibrium quantity
defined here. In magnetohydrostatic equilibrium, the pressure gradient
satisfies $\nabla p = \mathbf{j} \times \mathbf{B}$, where $\nabla p$ is the
spatial gradient of plasma pressure, $\mathbf{j}$ is the electric current
density, and $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field; on nested magnetic flux
surfaces this pressure may be expressed as a function of the [poloidal
magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux) $\psi$, where $\psi$ is the
poloidal magnetic flux.

NAMES.name: poloidal_angle_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short:
Pointwise geometric angle locating a position around a magnetic flux-surface
cross-section, measured clockwise from its low-field-side midplane.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal angle is the geometric angular coordinate assigned pointwise to
each position on the poloidal cross-section of a specified magnetic flux
surface. It is measured from the geometric center of that cross-section
rather than from magnetic-field-line distance.

At a point on the surface, the angle $\theta$ is defined by

$$
\theta = \operatorname{atan2}\!\left(-(Z-Z_0),\,R-R_0\right)
$$

where $\theta$ is the poloidal angle, $\operatorname{atan2}$ returns the
signed principal angle, $R$ is the major-radius coordinate, $Z$ is the
vertical coordinate, and $(R_0,Z_0)$ is the geometric center of the
flux-surface cross-section. These coordinates belong to the right-handed
cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $\phi$ is the toroidal angle.

The quantity applies to individual points on one magnetic flux surface and
has no averaging or summation over the surface. The surface is identified by
a constant [poloidal magnetic flux at a flux
surface](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_flux_surface) value; the angle
therefore parameterizes position around that surface rather than assigning
one unique angle to the entire surface. It is a geometric angle, distinct
from a straight-field-line poloidal angle.

This quantity specializes [poloidal
angle](name:poloidal_angle_of_flux_surface) by making the flux-surface locus
explicit and provides the angular coordinate used to distinguish positions
around the surface's poloidal cross-section.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the point advances clockwise from the

NAMES.name: poloidal_beta
NAMES.short:
Poloidal beta is a dimensionless measure of total plasma pressure relative
to the magnetic-pressure scale of the plasma-current-generated poloidal
field.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal beta is a dimensionless equilibrium measure of the total pressure
content of the confined plasma relative to the magnetic-pressure scale
generated by the plasma current. It characterizes pressure relative to the
poloidal magnetic field rather than the toroidal magnetic field.

The defining relation is

$$
\beta_p = \frac{4\int_V p\,dV}{R_0\,\mu_0\,I_p^2}
$$

where $\beta_p$ is poloidal beta, $p$ is the total plasma pressure, $V$ is
the confined plasma volume, $dV$ is a differential volume element, $R_0$ is
the reference major radius, $\mu_0$ is the vacuum permeability, and $I_p$ is
the total toroidal plasma current.

The pressure integral extends over the entire confined plasma volume and
aggregates the pressure of all included plasma populations, so this quantity
is global rather than local or species-resolved. It excludes any separate
normalization based on minor radius or reference toroidal magnetic-field
strength.

As the poloidal-field member of the
[beta](name:normalized_toroidal_plasma_beta) family, poloidal beta uses a
current- and major-radius-based poloidal magnetic-pressure scale. It is
distinct from [toroidal_beta](name:toroidal_beta), which normalizes pressure
to a toroidal magnetic-field scale, and from
[normalized_toroidal_plasma_beta](name:normalized_toroidal_plasma_beta),
which applies an additional engineering normalization.

NAMES.name: poloidal_current_function
NAMES.short:
Major-radius-weighted toroidal magnetic-field function used in axisymmetric
equilibria and vacuum fields; in ideal-MHD plasma it is constant on each
magnetic flux surface.
NAMES.long:
The poloidal current function is the major-radius-weighted toroidal magnetic
field that defines the equilibrium $F$-function. It provides a common
description for the toroidal field in axisymmetric plasma equilibria and in
current-free vacuum magnetic fields.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, the defining relation is

$$
F(R,Z) = R B_\phi(R,Z)
$$

where $F$ is the poloidal current function, $R$ is major radius measured
from the machine symmetry axis, $B_\phi$ is the toroidal component of the
magnetic field, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

For an axisymmetric ideal-MHD plasma equilibrium, $F$ is a flux function: it
is constant on each nested magnetic flux surface and can therefore be
expressed as a function of the poloidal magnetic-flux coordinate. The
quantity describes the full toroidal magnetic field represented by the
equilibrium; it is not a surface or volume integral, an average, or a
restriction to a particular current source.

The [vacuum poloidal current
function](name:vacuum_poloidal_current_function) is the corresponding
external-coil contribution in a current-free vacuum region, whereas the
unqualified quantity denotes the general $F$-function. The [product of the
poloidal current function and its derivative with respect to the poloidal
magnetic flux
coordinate](name:product_of_poloidal_current_function_and_derivative_with_respect_to_poloidal_magnetic_flux_coordinate_of_poloidal_current_function)
is a distinct Grad–Shafranov source term formed from $F$ and its flux
derivative.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when $B_\phi$ points in the direction of
increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical
$(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.
