NAMES.name: poloidal_length_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short:
Poloidal arc length of a closed magnetic-flux-surface contour in an
equilibrium poloidal cross-section, measuring the perimeter of that selected
surface.
NAMES.long:
The poloidal length is the perimeter of the closed contour formed by one
selected magnetic flux surface in a poloidal cross-section. It is a
geometric property of the surface boundary, rather than its enclosed area,
volume, or toroidal circumference.

The contour length is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$
frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is
vertical height:

$$
L_{\mathrm{pol}} = \int_{\theta_a}^{\theta_b} \sqrt{\left(\frac{dR(\theta)}{d\theta}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{dZ(\theta)}{d\theta}\right)^2}\,d\theta
$$

Here $L_{\mathrm{pol}}$ is the poloidal length, $\theta$ is any smooth
parameter along the contour, $R(\theta)$ and $Z(\theta)$ are its cylindrical
coordinate functions, and $\theta_a$ and $\theta_b$ are parameter values at
the same contour point after one complete circuit. The contour is taken at
fixed toroidal angle $\phi$.

The quantity applies to one magnetic flux surface and includes the complete
closed poloidal contour, with no averaging or summation over multiple
surfaces. It excludes local arc segments and geometric quantities associated
with the enclosed region. The selected surface may be labeled by the
[normalized poloidal flux
coordinate](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate).

Unlike [elongation of a flux surface](name:elongation_of_flux_surface),
which describes a scale-independent cross-sectional shape ratio, the
poloidal length retains the absolute geometric scale of the contour.

NAMES.name: poloidal_magnetic_field
NAMES.short:
Poloidal magnetic-field strength of the local total induction, formed from
radial and vertical components in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z)
frame.
NAMES.long:
Local total poloidal magnetic induction is the magnitude of the total
magnetic-field vector projected into the poloidal plane spanned by the
radial and vertical directions. It represents the local poloidal field
strength without selecting a source contribution, perturbation state, or
named evaluation locus.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major
radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, the defining
relation is

$$
B_p = \sqrt{B_R^2 + B_Z^2}
$$

where $B_p$ is the poloidal magnetic-field strength, $B_R$ is the radial
component of the local total [magnetic induction](name:magnetic_field), and
$B_Z$ is its vertical component. The radial direction follows increasing
$R$, and the vertical direction follows increasing $Z$.

The quantity is pointwise and applies wherever the local total magnetic
induction is defined, including confined plasma and surrounding vacuum. It
has no particle-species or population aggregation and is not spatially
averaged, integrated, or summed over a region. When associated with a
field-sensing location, it denotes the local measured field strength rather
than a value defined as a reconstructed equilibrium estimate.

Unlike the signed [radial magnetic-field
component](name:radial_magnetic_field) and [vertical magnetic-field
component](name:vertical_magnetic_field), this quantity is the nonnegative
magnitude of their combined poloidal projection. Together with the [toroidal
magnetic-field component](name:toroidal_magnetic_field), it specifies the
decomposition of the local total magnetic induction into poloidal and
toroidal parts.

NAMES.name: poloidal_magnetic_flux
NAMES.short:
Poloidal magnetic flux is the signed surface integral of the magnetic field
over a surface bounded by a closed toroidal contour of a nested magnetic
flux surface. It labels nested magnetic flux surfaces and is complementary
to toroidal magnetic flux.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal magnetic flux is the signed surface integral of the magnetic field
over a surface bounded by a closed toroidal contour of a nested magnetic
flux surface. It is the poloidal member of the [magnetic
flux](name:magnetic_flux) family and is the flux function used to label
nested magnetic flux surfaces in an axisymmetric equilibrium.

The poloidal magnetic flux $\psi$ associated with a closed toroidal contour
$C$ is defined by the magnetic-flux integral over an oriented surface $S_C$
whose boundary is $C$:

$$
\psi(C) = \int_{S_C} \mathbf{B} \cdot d\mathbf{A}
$$

where $\psi(C)$ is the poloidal magnetic flux associated with $C$, $C$ is
the closed toroidal contour, $S_C$ is the oriented surface with $\partial
S_C=C$, $\mathbf{B}$ is the [magnetic-field vector](name:magnetic_field),
$d\mathbf{A}=\hat{\mathbf{n}}\,dA$ is the oriented area element,
$\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is the unit normal set by the surface orientation, and
$dA$ is the scalar surface-area element.

The unqualified quantity denotes the net integral over the whole chosen
toroidal-boundary surface, including all magnetic-field contributions, with
no source separation, weighting, or averaging. It applies to the equilibrium
magnetic configuration wherever the scalar flux function is defined; on
nested closed magnetic flux surfaces, all points on the same surface share
the same $\psi$ value.

Poloidal magnetic flux is distinct from the local magnetic field, from
magnetic-field components or magnitudes, from a normalized flux coordinate
derived from $\psi$, and from a time derivative such as loop voltage. It is
complementary to [toroidal magnetic flux](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux),
which uses the poloidal cross-section enclosed by a flux surface rather than
a toroidal-boundary surface; [poloidal magnetic flux at flux
surface](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_flux_surface) is the evaluation of
$\psi$ on a specified flux surface.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the net magnetic-field projection through the
toroidal-boundary surface is along the right-hand-rule area orientation for
a boundary contour directed toward increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the
right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_flux_surface
NAMES.short:
Signed poloidal magnetic flux assigned to a nested magnetic surface, serving
as the equilibrium label for its position in the plasma.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal magnetic flux at a flux surface is the signed magnetic flux through
a horizontal disk centered on the toroidal symmetry axis and bounded by that
surface. In an axisymmetric equilibrium, it is constant over each nested
magnetic surface and provides its absolute, unnormalized flux label.

The poloidal flux at cylindrical coordinates $(R,Z)$ is defined by

$$
\psi(R,Z) = \int_0^R B_Z(R',Z)\,2\pi R'\,dR'
$$

where $\psi$ is the poloidal magnetic flux, $R$ is major radius, $Z$ is
vertical height, $R'$ is the integration radius, and $B_Z$ is the vertical
magnetic-field component, all expressed in the right-handed cylindrical
$(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

This quantity applies to nested equilibrium magnetic surfaces within the
plasma and represents the signed physical flux itself, not a flux-surface
average, species sum, or normalized radial coordinate. It is distinct from
the magnetic flux linked by a [poloidal magnetic flux of a flux
loop](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_of_flux_loop), which is defined by an
oriented diagnostic-loop surface rather than by an equilibrium flux surface.

The [normalized poloidal flux
coordinate](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate) is obtained by
shifting and scaling this poloidal-flux label between its magnetic-axis and
plasma-boundary values; the present quantity retains the absolute label.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when $B_Z$ points in the $+Z$ direction through
the integration disk.

NAMES.name: poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.short:
Signed poloidal magnetic flux evaluated at the magnetic axis, providing the
inner reference value for normalized poloidal-flux coordinates.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal magnetic flux at the magnetic axis is the signed value of the
poloidal flux function at the central extremum associated with nested
magnetic surfaces.

The defining evaluation is

$$
\psi_\mathrm{axis} = \psi(R_\mathrm{axis}, Z_\mathrm{axis})
$$

where $\psi_\mathrm{axis}$ is the poloidal magnetic flux at the magnetic
axis, $\psi$ is the poloidal magnetic-flux function, $R_\mathrm{axis}$ is
the major-radius coordinate of the magnetic axis, and $Z_\mathrm{axis}$ is
its vertical coordinate. The coordinates are expressed in the right-handed
cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is
toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height; $Z_\mathrm{axis}$ is the
[vertical coordinate of the magnetic
axis](name:vertical_coordinate_of_magnetic_axis).

This quantity applies specifically to the equilibrium magnetic field at the
magnetic axis rather than to an arbitrary point or a plasma region. It is a
single point evaluation with no species selection, regional aggregation, or
flux-surface averaging.

The value is an unnormalized flux reference and is distinct from [poloidal
magnetic flux at the plasma
boundary](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary), which supplies
the outer reference value. Together, these two endpoint values define the
flux interval used by the [normalized poloidal flux
coordinate](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate).
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the poloidal flux is oriented so that the
vertical magnetic field through the defining horizontal disk points in the
$+Z$ direction.

NAMES.name: poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short:
Signed poloidal magnetic flux evaluated on the last closed flux surface,
providing the outer reference for normalized poloidal-flux coordinates.
NAMES.long:
The poloidal magnetic flux at the plasma boundary is the signed magnetic
flux through a horizontal disk whose edge lies on the last closed flux
surface. It is the outer boundary value of the poloidal magnetic-flux
function for the confined plasma.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major
radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, the boundary
value for an axisymmetric equilibrium is

$$
\psi_b = \psi(R_b,Z_b) = \int_0^{R_b} B_Z(R',Z_b)\,2\pi R'\,dR'
$$

where $\psi_b$ is the poloidal magnetic flux at the plasma boundary,
$\psi(R_b,Z_b)$ is the poloidal magnetic-flux function at a selected
boundary point, $(R_b,Z_b)$ are that point's cylindrical coordinates, $B_Z$
is the vertical magnetic-field component, $R'$ is the integration variable
representing major radius, and $\pi$ is the circle constant.

This quantity applies specifically to the last closed flux surface bounding
the confined plasma. It is a single boundary value of the flux function,
with no averaging over the boundary or enclosed plasma implied; it is
distinct from the value at the magnetic axis given by [poloidal magnetic
flux at the magnetic axis](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis).

The boundary value supplies the outer endpoint for [normalized poloidal flux
coordinate](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate), while the
magnetic-axis value supplies the corresponding inner endpoint. The poloidal
flux function is constant along a given closed flux surface in the
axisymmetric equilibrium description.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when $B_Z$ on the defining horizontal disk points
in the $+Z$ direction.

NAMES.name: poloidal_magnetic_flux_of_flux_loop
NAMES.short:
Signed poloidal magnetic flux linked by an individual flux loop, defined by
the magnetic field threading an oriented surface bounded by that loop.
NAMES.long:
Signed poloidal magnetic flux of a flux loop is the magnetic flux linked by
an individual flux loop and threading an oriented surface whose boundary is
that loop. It is the finite-surface flux linkage associated with the loop as
a whole, not a local magnetic-field component.

The loop-linked flux is defined by the surface integral of the
magnetic-field vector over a spanning surface of the loop:

$$
\Phi_{\mathrm{loop}} = \int_{S_{\mathrm{loop}}} \mathbf{B} \cdot d\mathbf{S}
$$

where $\Phi_{\mathrm{loop}}$ is the signed poloidal magnetic flux of the
flux loop, $S_{\mathrm{loop}}$ is an oriented spanning surface bounded by
the flux loop, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic-field vector, and $d\mathbf{S}$
is the directed surface element on that surface.

The scope is one specified flux loop and the total flux through its complete
spanning surface; no averaging over multiple loops or loop segments is
implied. The quantity is distinct from a point-locus evaluation such as
[poloidal magnetic flux at a sensor attachment
point](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_of_flux_loop), which evaluates a flux
function at a specified position rather than integrating over a finite
loop-bounded surface.

The defining surface is any oriented spanning surface with the same loop
boundary and orientation; the absence of magnetic monopoles makes the linked
flux independent of the particular spanning surface. This quantity is
related to [poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux) as a
loop-bounded flux linkage, and it must not be identified with [toroidal
magnetic flux](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux), which uses a different
flux-surface geometry; a reconstructed counterpart, [reconstructed poloidal
magnetic flux of flux loop], shares the same magnetic quantity but
represents a distinct value type when that distinction is made.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the magnetic-field vector has a positive net
projection on the oriented surface element selected as positive for the flux
loop.

NAMES.name: poloidal_plane_cross_sectional_area_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short:
Geometric area enclosed by a closed magnetic-flux-surface contour in a
fixed-toroidal-angle poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ,
Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Geometric area enclosed by a closed magnetic-flux-surface contour in a
fixed-toroidal-angle poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,
\phi, Z)$ frame is the poloidal-plane cross-sectional area of that flux
surface. It characterizes the planar section enclosed by one closed magnetic
flux surface.

The area is defined by the planar contour integral

$$
A_{\mathrm{pol}} = \frac{1}{2}\left|\oint_{\mathcal{C}} \left(R\,dZ - Z\,dR\right)\right|
$$

where $A_{\mathrm{pol}}$ is the poloidal-plane cross-sectional area,
$\mathcal{C}$ is the closed poloidal contour of the flux surface at fixed
toroidal angle $\phi$, $R$ is major radius measured from the toroidal
symmetry axis, $Z$ is vertical height, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle in the
right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, and $dR$ and $dZ$ are
differentials along the contour. The absolute value makes the area
independent of the contour traversal orientation.

This quantity applies to the nested family of closed magnetic flux surfaces
from the magnetic axis to the plasma boundary; its limiting value at the
magnetic axis is zero. It is an individual-surface geometric measure at
fixed toroidal angle, not an average over toroidal angle, not an aggregate
over multiple flux surfaces, and not a measure of open field-line regions.

It is distinct from the [surface area of flux
surface](name:surface_area_of_flux_surface), which is the area of the
toroidal surface generated by the flux-surface contour. At the last closed
flux surface, the corresponding boundary quantity is the [poloidal-plane
cross-sectional area of plasma
boundary](name:poloidal_plane_cross_sectional_area_of_plasma_boundary); it
is also distinct from the [volume of flux
surface](name:volume_of_flux_surface), which measures the toroidal volume
enclosed by the same nested surface.

NAMES.name: poloidal_plane_cross_sectional_area_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short:
Area enclosed by the last closed magnetic flux surface in a poloidal plane,
defining the equilibrium plasma cross-sectional size at the plasma boundary.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the geometric area enclosed by the last closed magnetic
flux surface (LCFS), which forms the plasma boundary, in a poloidal
cross-section.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, the enclosed area is
defined by

$$
A_{\rm LCFS} = \iint_{\mathcal{S}_{\rm LCFS}} dR\,dZ
$$

where $A_{\rm LCFS}$ is the LCFS cross-sectional area, $\mathcal{S}_{\rm
LCFS}$ is the region enclosed by the LCFS contour at fixed toroidal angle
$\phi$, $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, $Z$ is vertical
height, and $dR\,dZ$ is the poloidal-plane area element.

This is a global equilibrium quantity for the complete plasma-boundary
contour. It is not a local surface element, a flux-surface average, or the
area of a toroidal surface formed by revolving the contour.

It is the plasma-boundary specialization of [poloidal plane cross-sectional
area of a flux
surface](name:poloidal_plane_cross_sectional_area_of_flux_surface), whose
corresponding area is defined for an arbitrary closed magnetic flux surface;
the LCFS is the outermost such surface enclosing the plasma.

NAMES.name: product_of_poloidal_current_function_and_derivative_with_respect_to_poloidal_magnetic_flux_coordinate_of_poloidal_current_function
NAMES.short:
Grad–Shafranov equilibrium source term equal to the poloidal current
function multiplied by its derivative with respect to poloidal magnetic
flux.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the flux-function product that represents the
toroidal-field contribution to the Grad–Shafranov equilibrium balance. It is
formed from the poloidal current function and its variation across nested
magnetic flux surfaces.

The defining expression is

$$
F\,\frac{dF}{d\psi}
$$

where $F$ is the [poloidal current
function](name:poloidal_current_function), equal to the
major-radius-weighted toroidal magnetic field, and $\psi$ is the signed
[poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux) labeling the nested
equilibrium flux surfaces.

This quantity applies to an axisymmetric equilibrium and is evaluated as a
function of the poloidal-flux label. It has no species, population, region,
or mechanism restriction, and its aggregation convention is the direct
product of two flux-function quantities: it is neither a flux-surface
average nor a sum over surfaces. It is distinct from the undifferentiated
poloidal current function and from the product $F^2$.

Within the Grad–Shafranov equation, this term supplies the magnetic
contribution associated with the variation of the poloidal current function
and therefore participates in the balance determining toroidal current
density and plasma pressure. The derivative factor distinguishes it from the
parent [poloidal current function](name:poloidal_current_function) itself.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the poloidal current function and its
derivative with respect to signed poloidal magnetic flux have the same sign;
the poloidal current function is positive when the toroidal magnetic field
points toward increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed
cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

sources.leaf_definition: Derivative of F w.r.t. Psi, multiplied with F
sources.parent_definition: Equilibrium profiles (1D radial grid) as a function of the poloidal flux

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_at_inboard_midplane
NAMES.short:
Major-radius coordinate of a magnetic flux surface at its inboard midplane
intersection, locating the high-field-side point relative to the toroidal
symmetry axis.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the major-radius coordinate of the point where a magnetic
flux surface intersects the inboard midplane, identifying the
high-field-side location of that surface relative to the toroidal symmetry
axis. It is a locus-specific form of the [radial
coordinate](name:radial_coordinate).

For a magnetic flux surface $\mathcal{S}$, the inboard-midplane radial
coordinate is defined by

$$
R_{\mathrm{in}}(\mathcal{S}) = R\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{in}}(\mathcal{S})\right)
$$

where $R_{\mathrm{in}}(\mathcal{S})$ is the quantity defined here,
$R(\mathbf{x})$ is the major-radius coordinate of spatial position
$\mathbf{x}$, $\mathcal{S}$ is the specified magnetic flux surface, and
$\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{in}}(\mathcal{S})$ is its inboard midplane
intersection. The coordinates are expressed in the right-handed cylindrical
$(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and
$Z$ is vertical height.

The scope is one coordinate value for each specified magnetic flux surface
at its inboard, high-field-side midplane intersection. It is not a
flux-surface average, a poloidal or toroidal average, or the corresponding
outboard-midplane coordinate; the latter is represented by [radial
coordinate at outboard
midplane](name:radial_coordinate_at_outboard_midplane). Unlike [radial
magnetic field](name:radial_magnetic_field), this quantity describes the
location of a surface and not a magnetic-field component.

This quantity specializes [radial coordinate](name:radial_coordinate) by
fixing the evaluation locus to the inboard midplane. Comparing it with the
outboard-midplane value characterizes the horizontal extent and radial
placement of the same magnetic flux surface.

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_at_outboard_midplane
NAMES.short:
Major-radius coordinate of the low-field-side intersection between a
magnetic flux surface and the equatorial midplane.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the major-radius coordinate $R$ of the point where a
specified magnetic flux surface intersects the equatorial midplane on its
outboard, low-field side. It gives the outboard radial extent of that
surface rather than a distance across the plasma or an average over the
surface.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, with unit-vector basis
$(\hat{R},\hat{\phi},\hat{Z})$, the major-radius coordinate is related to
the right-handed Cartesian basis $(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$ by:

$$
R = \sqrt{x^2+y^2}
$$

Here $R$ is the perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis,
$\phi$ is the toroidal angle, $Z$ is the vertical coordinate, and $x$ and
$y$ are the horizontal Cartesian coordinates measured from that axis.

The quantity applies to one specified magnetic flux surface, identified by
its poloidal magnetic-flux label $\psi$, where $\psi$ denotes the flux
function labeling nested magnetic surfaces. It is evaluated only at the
outboard intersection with the equatorial midplane; it excludes the inboard
intersection and any flux-surface average.

It is a locus-specific specialization of the [radial
coordinate](name:radial_coordinate), obtained by evaluating $R$ at the
outboard midplane. The corresponding [inboard-midplane radial
coordinate](name:radial_coordinate_at_inboard_midplane) describes the
distinct high-field-side intersection of the same type of magnetic surface.

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_closest_wall_point
NAMES.short:
Major-radius coordinate R of the first-wall point nearest the plasma
boundary, measured from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed
cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the major-radius coordinate of the wall point selected as
closest to the plasma boundary. It identifies that point’s perpendicular
distance from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical
$(R, phi, Z)$ frame.

The defining geometric relation is

$$
R_{\mathrm{cw}} = \left\lVert \mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{cw},\perp} \right\rVert
$$

where $R_{\mathrm{cw}}$ is the radial coordinate of the closest wall point
and $\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{cw},\perp}$ is the perpendicular displacement
vector from the toroidal symmetry axis to that point.

The scope is the single wall point selected by its minimum proximity to the
plasma boundary. This is a pointwise geometric coordinate with no
plasma-population dependence and no averaging, summation, or integration. It
is not the wall-to-boundary separation distance, nor is “closest” a
statement that the point has the smallest major radius among all wall
points.

This quantity is a locus-specific instance of [radial
coordinate](name:radial_coordinate), restricted to the closest wall point
rather than an arbitrary geometric reference position.

sources.leaf_definition: Major radius
sources.parent_definition: Position and distance to the plasma boundary of the point of the first wall which is the closest to plasma boundary

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_conductor_cross_section
NAMES.short:
Major-radius coordinate of the designated reference point associated with a
conductor cross-section, measured from the toroidal symmetry axis.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the major-radius coordinate $R$ assigned to the designated
reference point of a conductor cross-section. It locates the cross-section
in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame without describing the
cross-section's shape or extent.

The coordinate is defined from the horizontal Cartesian coordinates of the
reference point:

$$
R = \sqrt{x^2+y^2}
$$

where $R$ is the perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis, and
$x$ and $y$ are the horizontal coordinates in the right-handed Cartesian
$(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$ basis, with $\hat{z}$ aligned with the vertical
direction.

The quantity applies to one conductor cross-section and represents one
designated reference location for that cross-section. It is not summed over
conductors, averaged over the cross-sectional area, or resolved pointwise
along the cross-sectional outline.

Unlike the [radial outline of a coil conductor
element](name:radial_outline_of_coil_conductor_element), which assigns
radial coordinates to outline points, this quantity identifies the
cross-section's reference geometry. It does not specify the reference
point's vertical coordinate, toroidal angle, dimensions, or outline shape.

This is a conductor-cross-section specialization of the parent [radial
coordinate](name:radial_coordinate); the parent definition supplies the
general major-radius meaning, while this name fixes the locus to a conductor
cross-section.

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_control_surface
NAMES.short:
Major-radius coordinate of each point on a control-surface outline, measured
as perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis in the
right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The radial coordinate of a control-surface outline point is its major-radius
location, measured as perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry
axis. It identifies the point's position in the right-handed cylindrical
$(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

The defining geometric relation is

$$
R = \sqrt{X^2 + Y^2}
$$

where $R$ is the major-radius coordinate, and $X$ and $Y$ are the Cartesian
coordinates perpendicular to the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed
Cartesian $(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$ basis. The cylindrical angle $\phi$ is
the toroidal angular coordinate and $Z$ is the vertical coordinate of the
same point.

This quantity applies to each point defining the control-surface outline.
The control surface is defined by an outline in a poloidal plane and extends
in the toroidal direction with axisymmetric geometry; this quantity is the
local coordinate of an outline point, not a surface average or an integrated
surface property. It is distinct from displacement along a flux-surface
normal, which describes a different geometric direction.

This entry specializes [radial coordinate](name:radial_coordinate) by
restricting its locus to a point on a control-surface outline while
retaining the same major-radius definition.

sources.leaf_definition: Major radius
sources.parent_definition: Set of points defining the surface in a poloidal plane. The surface then extends in the toroidal direction in an axisymmetric way

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_current_center
NAMES.short:
Major-radius coordinate of the plasma-current centroid, obtained by
normalizing the toroidal-current first moment over the poloidal plasma
cross-section by total plasma current.
NAMES.long:
The radial coordinate of the current center is the major-radius location of
the centroid of the toroidal plasma-current distribution. It identifies a
current-weighted position and is distinct from the geometric centroid or the
magnetic axis.

The coordinate is defined by the toroidal-current first moment:

$$
R_c = \frac{\displaystyle\int_{D_p} R\,j_\phi\,dS}{I_p}
$$

where $R_c$ is the major-radius coordinate of the current center, $R$ is the
major-radius coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$
frame, $j_\phi$ is the toroidal component of the plasma [current
density](name:current_density), $dS$ is an element of poloidal
cross-sectional area, $D_p$ is the plasma current-carrying poloidal
cross-section, and $I_p$ is the total toroidal plasma current, equal to the
corresponding integral of $j_\phi$ over $D_p$.

The quantity applies to the full plasma-current distribution and uses a
current-weighted first-moment aggregation over the poloidal cross-section.
It excludes weighting by particle density, pressure, magnetic-field
strength, or geometric area alone; the resulting position is therefore not a
generic geometric center.

This quantity is a locus-specific instance of the general [radial
coordinate](name:radial_coordinate), evaluated at the current center. Its
vertical counterpart, [vertical coordinate of the current
center](name:vertical_coordinate_of_current_center), supplies the
corresponding vertical position needed to locate the current centroid in the
cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_dr_dz_zero_point
NAMES.short:
Radial coordinate of the dR/dZ zero point is the R coordinate, in the
right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, of a plasma-boundary or separatrix
point where R is locally stationary with respect to Z.
NAMES.long:
Radial coordinate of the dR/dZ zero point is the $R$ coordinate, in the
right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, of a specified point on a
plasma-boundary or separatrix contour where $R$ is locally stationary with
respect to $Z$. In this frame, $R$ is major radius measured from the
toroidal symmetry axis, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical
height.

The coordinate is defined by the stationary-radius condition on the
specified contour:

$$
R_{\mathrm{dR/dZ=0}} = R(P_0), \qquad \left.\frac{dR}{dZ}\right|_{C,P_0} = 0
$$

where $R_{\mathrm{dR/dZ=0}}$ is the radial coordinate of the dR/dZ zero
point, $P_0$ is the specified dR/dZ zero point, $C$ is the plasma-boundary
or separatrix contour on which $P_0$ lies, $R(P_0)$ is the major-radius
coordinate of $P_0$, $Z$ is the vertical-height coordinate, and $dR/dZ$ is
the derivative of the contour coordinate $R$ with respect to $Z$ along $C$.

The scope is a single specified geometric point on the contour; the value is
not an average over the contour, over toroidal angle $\phi$, or over all
stationary points. If several points on the contour satisfy $dR/dZ=0$, the
definition does not by itself impose an inboard, outboard, upper, or lower
selection rule; each specified zero point has its own radial-coordinate
value.

This quantity is only the cylindrical $R$ coordinate of the point, not a
flux-surface-normal displacement or a flux-label coordinate. Together with
the [vertical coordinate of the dR/dZ zero point], it locates the point in
the poloidal $(R, Z)$ cross-section at fixed $\phi$ of the right-handed
cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It is distinct from the [radial coordinate
of an X-point](name:radial_coordinate_of_x_point), which locates a magnetic
null on a separatrix rather than a radial extremum of a boundary or
separatrix contour.

sources.leaf_definition: Major radius

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_geometric_axis
NAMES.short:
Major-radius coordinate locating the midpoint of the plasma boundary's
radial extrema, thereby specifying the horizontal position of its geometric
axis.
NAMES.long:
The radial coordinate of the geometric axis is the major-radius position of
the plasma cross-section's geometric center, defined from the extrema of the
plasma boundary in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

The geometric-axis coordinate is defined by

$$
R_{\mathrm{geo}} = \frac{R_{\max} + R_{\min}}{2}
$$

where $R_{\mathrm{geo}}$ is the major-radius coordinate of the geometric
axis, and $R_{\max}$ and $R_{\min}$ are the maximum and minimum major-radius
coordinates of the plasma boundary, respectively.

This quantity applies specifically to the geometric axis of the plasma
cross-section and uses the midpoint aggregation of the boundary's radial
extrema. It is distinct from the [radial_coordinate](name:radial_coordinate)
of an arbitrary point or reference position and from the radial coordinate
of the magnetic axis; its vertical counterpart is the [vertical coordinate
of the geometric axis](name:vertical_coordinate_of_geometric_axis).

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_magnetic_axis
NAMES.short:
Major-radius coordinate locating the magnetic-axis O-point in the
right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame around which nested closed flux
surfaces are organized.
NAMES.long:
The radial coordinate of the magnetic axis is the major-radius location of
the O-point, the local extremum of the poloidal magnetic flux around which
nested closed magnetic flux surfaces are organized.

In terms of a right-handed Cartesian basis $(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$ with
$\hat{z}$ vertical, its major-radius coordinate is defined by

$$
R = \sqrt{x^2+y^2}
$$

where $R$ is the major-radius coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical
$(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, and $x$ and $y$ are the Cartesian coordinates
perpendicular to the toroidal symmetry axis.

This is a point value evaluated at the magnetic axis in the plasma poloidal
cross-section; it is not a flux-surface average, region integral, or
coordinate of an arbitrary magnetic or physical contour. It is distinct from
[radial_coordinate_at_inboard_midplane](name:radial_coordinate_at_inboard_midplane),
which locates a flux-surface intersection with the inboard midplane.

This quantity is the magnetic-axis specialization of
[radial_coordinate](name:radial_coordinate): the parent applies to general
points or reference positions, whereas this quantity fixes the locus to the
magnetic-axis O-point.

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_measurement_position
NAMES.short:
Major-radius coordinate locating a measurement position by perpendicular
distance from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical (R,
φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The radial coordinate of a measurement position is the major-radius location
of that position, defined by its perpendicular separation from the toroidal
symmetry axis. It identifies a single generic measurement location,
independent of the instrument or plasma quantity associated with that
location.

The defining geometric relation is

$$
R_{\mathrm{meas}} = \left|\mathbf{r}_{\perp,\mathrm{meas}}\right|
$$

where $R_{\mathrm{meas}}$ is the major-radius coordinate of the measurement
position, $\mathbf{r}_{\perp,\mathrm{meas}}$ is its perpendicular
displacement from the toroidal symmetry axis, and the vertical bars denote
the magnitude of that displacement. The coordinate is expressed in the
right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius,
$\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The scope is one measurement position; no averaging, summation, or
integration over positions is implied. This quantity applies to a generic
measurement position and does not identify a particular diagnostic object,
line of sight, toroidal angle, or vertical coordinate. Unlike
[radial_coordinate_of_line_of_sight](name:radial_coordinate_of_line_of_sight),
it is not restricted to a line-of-sight reference point.

This quantity is the measurement-position specialization of the broader
[radial_coordinate](name:radial_coordinate); the same perpendicular-distance
definition is used, with the locus narrowed to a measurement position.

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_strike_point
NAMES.short:
Major-radius location of an individual magnetic strike point where a
separatrix leg intersects a divertor target, expressed in the right-handed
cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The radial coordinate of a strike point is its major-radius location
relative to the toroidal symmetry axis, at the intersection of a separatrix
leg with a divertor target.

The major-radius coordinate is defined from the strike point's horizontal
Cartesian position by

$$
R_{\mathrm{sp}}=\sqrt{x_{\mathrm{sp}}^2+y_{\mathrm{sp}}^2}
$$

where $R_{\mathrm{sp}}$ is the strike-point major-radius coordinate, and
$x_{\mathrm{sp}}$ and $y_{\mathrm{sp}}$ are its horizontal Cartesian
coordinates in the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$ basis,
with $\hat{z}$ vertical and coincident with $\hat{Z}$.

This quantity applies to one specified magnetic strike point at a time, with
no summation, averaging, or other aggregation. The same definition covers
inner and outer divertor strike points without combining them or selecting
one branch by the name alone.

It excludes the vertical location of the strike point, which is given by the
[vertical coordinate of the strike
point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_strike_point). As a component of
[radial_coordinate](name:radial_coordinate), it supplies the major-radius
coordinate needed with the vertical coordinate to locate the strike point in
the poloidal $(R,Z)$ plane. The related [radial coordinate of the
X-point](name:radial_coordinate_of_x_point) instead identifies the
separatrix's magnetic null rather than its divertor intersection.

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_x_point
NAMES.short:
Major-radius coordinate locating the main X-point, the poloidal
magnetic-field null that defines the separatrix in an equilibrium.
NAMES.long:
The major-radius coordinate of the main X-point is the perpendicular
distance from the toroidal symmetry axis to the poloidal magnetic-field null
that defines the separatrix. It identifies the radial location of this
specific equilibrium feature in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$
frame.

The coordinate is defined geometrically by

$$
R_{\mathrm{X}} = \sqrt{x_{\mathrm{X}}^2 + y_{\mathrm{X}}^2}
$$

where $R_{\mathrm{X}}$ is the major-radius coordinate of the main X-point,
and $x_{\mathrm{X}}$ and $y_{\mathrm{X}}$ are its horizontal Cartesian
coordinates in the right-handed $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ basis, with
$\hat{z}$ aligned with the vertical direction $\hat{Z}$. The subscript
$\mathrm{X}$ identifies the main X-point.

This quantity applies specifically to the main X-point and represents one
coordinate of that point rather than its complete position. It is a single
geometric value, not an average, integral, or sum over a flux surface or
region; it excludes coordinates of secondary X-points and other equilibrium
features.

It is a locus-specific specialization of the [radial
coordinate](name:radial_coordinate), which assigns the same major-radius
concept to arbitrary geometric positions. The X-point condition
distinguishes it from the [radial coordinate of the magnetic
axis](name:radial_coordinate_of_magnetic_axis), which locates the
poloidal-field O-point rather than the separatrix-defining null.

NAMES.name: radial_derivative_of_poloidal_magnetic_flux
NAMES.short:
Rate of change of signed poloidal magnetic flux with the dimensionful
toroidal-flux radius labeling nested equilibrium flux surfaces.
NAMES.long:
The radial derivative of poloidal magnetic flux is the rate at which the
signed poloidal magnetic flux changes across nested equilibrium magnetic
flux surfaces. It is a metric coefficient relating the poloidal-flux and
toroidal-flux coordinate descriptions.

The defining relation is

$$
\frac{d\psi}{d\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}}
$$

where $\psi$ is the [poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux),
and $\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the dimensionful toroidal-flux radius that
labels the nested surfaces.

This quantity is evaluated as a function of the toroidal-flux radius, with
one derivative value associated with each nested equilibrium surface. It is
not a surface integral or average, and it is distinct from a derivative with
respect to the cylindrical major radius, minor radius, or a normalized flux
coordinate.

Relative to [poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux), this
quantity describes how the flux label changes in the outward
toroidal-flux-radial direction. It has the same independent coordinate as
the [derivative with respect to toroidal flux coordinate of area of flux
surface](name:derivative_with_respect_to_toroidal_flux_coordinate_of_area_of_flux_surface),
but differentiates poloidal magnetic flux rather than enclosed surface area.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the poloidal magnetic flux increases as
$\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}$ increases outward from the magnetic axis toward the
plasma boundary.

sources.leaf_definition: Derivative of Psi with respect to Rho_Tor

NAMES.name: radial_magnetic_field
NAMES.short:
Radial magnetic-field component of the local total induction, resolved along
increasing major radius in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The radial magnetic field $B_R$ is the signed component of the local total
[magnetic induction](name:magnetic_field) resolved along the radial
direction. It represents directional field strength rather than the full
magnetic-induction vector or its magnitude.

The radial component is defined by

$$
B_R = \mathbf{B} \cdot \hat{R}
$$

where $\mathbf{B}$ is the local total magnetic induction, $\hat{R}$ is the
unit vector in the direction of increasing major radius, and $B_R$ is the
resulting radial component.

This quantity is defined locally in the right-handed cylindrical
$(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and
$Z$ is vertical height. It does not select a plasma, vacuum, perturbed, or
other source contribution, and it has no restriction to a particular region
or species. The named quantity is the local projection, not a spatial
average; any finite-volume average is a separate aggregation.

The radial direction is the cylindrical $\hat{R}$ direction and is distinct
from the normal to a magnetic flux surface and from the direction
perpendicular to the magnetic field. It is distinct from the [toroidal
magnetic field](name:toroidal_magnetic_field) and [vertical magnetic
field](name:vertical_magnetic_field), which are projections onto the other
cylindrical directions. Together with those components, it resolves the
local magnetic induction; its radial and vertical components form the
[poloidal magnetic field](name:poloidal_magnetic_field).
NAMES.sign:
Positive when $B_R$ points in the direction of increasing
major radius $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: reference_major_radius
NAMES.short:
Nonnegative perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis to a
designated reference location, serving as the major-radius coordinate where
the vacuum toroidal magnetic field is specified in the right-handed
cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Major radius is the nonnegative perpendicular distance from the toroidal
symmetry axis to a geometric point or specified location. For this reference
quantity, the designated location is the radius at which the vacuum toroidal
magnetic field is specified, making it the reference specialization of
major_radius.

At the designated reference location, the major radius is defined
geometrically by:

$$
R_0 = \sqrt{X_0^2 + Y_0^2}
$$

where $R_0$ is the reference major radius, and $X_0$ and $Y_0$ are the
Cartesian coordinates of the reference location perpendicular to the
toroidal symmetry axis. The Cartesian basis is right-handed
$(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$ with $\hat{z}=\hat{Z}$; the corresponding
cylindrical frame is right-handed $(R,\phi,Z)$ with
$\hat{R}\times\hat{\phi}=\hat{Z}$.

This quantity is a single designated geometric reference value associated
with the vacuum toroidal magnetic field, represented by [toroidal vacuum
magnetic field](name:toroidal_vacuum_magnetic_field). It is not a pointwise
plasma-radius field, a flux-surface average, or a region integral, and it
has no species or plasma-population scope.

Unlike [flux-surface-averaged major
radius](name:flux_surface_averaged_major_radius), which averages the radius
over a nested magnetic flux surface, this quantity identifies one reference
radius. It is also distinct from a [radial
coordinate](name:radial_coordinate) assigned to an arbitrary geometric point
or measurement location.

The reference radius and the vacuum toroidal magnetic field form the
reference pair $R_0$ and $B_0$, where $B_0$ is the vacuum toroidal magnetic
field specified at the reference radius. Their product $R_0B_0$ supplies the
geometric-field scale used in normalized toroidal-flux and current-density
definitions.

NAMES.name: surface_area_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short:
Geometric area of a closed toroidal magnetic flux surface formed by
revolving its poloidal contour through one complete toroidal revolution in
the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the geometric area of a complete closed toroidal magnetic
flux surface. It includes the full surface swept out by the corresponding
poloidal contour during one toroidal revolution.

For an axisymmetric surface, the area is defined by

$$
A_{\mathrm{surf}}(\xi) = \oint_{C(\xi)} 2\pi R\,dl_p
$$

where $A_{\mathrm{surf}}(\xi)$ is the toroidal-surface area, $\xi$ is the
magnetic flux-surface label, $C(\xi)$ is the closed poloidal contour for
that surface, $R$ is the major radius, $dl_p$ is differential arc length
along the contour, and $\pi$ is the circular constant. The contour is
expressed in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is
major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The scope is one selected nested magnetic flux surface, with local surface
elements aggregated over the complete toroidal revolution. This is distinct
from the area enclosed by a poloidal contour, represented by the
[poloidal-plane cross-sectional area of a flux
surface](name:poloidal_plane_cross_sectional_area_of_flux_surface), and from
the enclosed [volume of a flux surface](name:volume_of_flux_surface).

As a specialization of the broader [area measure associated with a flux
surface], this quantity selects the total toroidal-surface area rather than
a poloidal cross-sectional area or an area derivative with respect to a flux
coordinate.

NAMES.name: toroidal_angle_of_measurement_position
NAMES.short:
Toroidal angular coordinate locating a measurement position around the
machine symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal angle is the azimuthal coordinate of a geometric point
designated as a measurement position, locating that point around the machine
symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

The angle may be defined from the transverse Cartesian coordinates by:

$$
\phi = \operatorname{atan2}(y,x)
$$

where $\phi$ is the toroidal angle, $x$ and $y$ are the transverse Cartesian
coordinates in the right-handed $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ basis, and
$\operatorname{atan2}$ returns the oriented azimuth relative to the defined
zero-angle direction. In the cylindrical frame, $R$ is major radius and $Z$
is vertical height.

This quantity applies to one geometric measurement position and has no
plasma-population, field, or region weighting. It is a point coordinate
rather than a line-of-sight integral, spatial average, or toroidal
displacement from a reference position.

The absolute angular coordinate differs from the signed displacement
represented by [toroidal offset at measurement
position](name:toroidal_offset_at_measurement_position). The same
toroidal-coordinate concept applied to another geometric locus is
represented by [toroidal coordinate of
aperture](name:toroidal_coordinate_of_aperture).

NAMES.name: toroidal_flux_coordinate
NAMES.short:
Non-negative, radius-like label of a nested magnetic flux surface, derived
from enclosed toroidal magnetic flux using a positive reference vacuum
toroidal field.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal flux coordinate is a non-negative, radius-like label assigned
to each nested magnetic flux surface. It orders surfaces outward from the
magnetic axis and approximates an effective minor radius without being a
geometric distance.

The coordinate is defined from the enclosed toroidal magnetic flux:

$$
\rho_{\rm tor} = \sqrt{\frac{\Phi_{\rm tor}}{\pi B_0}}
$$

where $\rho_{\rm tor}$ is the toroidal flux coordinate, $\Phi_{\rm tor}$ is
the toroidal magnetic flux enclosed by the surface relative to the magnetic
axis, $B_0$ is the positive reference vacuum toroidal magnetic field, and
$\pi$ is the circle constant.

The quantity applies to arbitrary nested magnetic flux surfaces, including
the magnetic axis, internal characteristic surfaces, and the plasma
boundary. Each value labels one surface; it has no species or population
scope and involves no population summation, charge-state aggregation, or
averaging convention. It is a flux-derived coordinate rather than a direct
geometric minor-radius measurement.

At the magnetic axis, the enclosed relative toroidal flux vanishes and the
coordinate is zero. Evaluations at particular loci, such as the [toroidal
flux coordinate at the plasma
boundary](name:toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_plasma_boundary) and the
[toroidal flux coordinate of the magnetic
axis](name:toroidal_flux_coordinate_of_magnetic_axis), are instances of this
same surface-labeling quantity. A [normalized toroidal flux coordinate at a
measurement
position](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_measurement_position)
is a dimensionless rescaling of a toroidal-flux label and is distinct from
this dimensional coordinate.

NAMES.name: toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short:
Dimensionful toroidal-flux radius labeling the outermost closed magnetic
flux surface and setting the boundary value for this radial coordinate.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal flux coordinate at the plasma boundary is the non-negative,
radius-like label assigned to the outermost closed magnetic flux surface. It
represents an effective flux radius rather than a geometric minor-radius
measurement.

At the plasma boundary, the coordinate is defined by

$$
\rho_{\mathrm{tor,b}} = \sqrt{\frac{\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,b}}}{\pi B_0}}
$$

where $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,b}}$ is the toroidal flux coordinate at the
boundary, $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,b}}$ is the toroidal magnetic flux enclosed by
the boundary, $B_0$ is the positive reference vacuum toroidal magnetic
field, and $\pi$ is the mathematical constant.

The quantity applies specifically to the plasma boundary, identified with
the outermost closed magnetic flux surface or last-closed flux surface in a
closed-boundary equilibrium. It is a single evaluation at that locus; no
spatial averaging, boundary integration, or summation over particle
populations is implied.

This boundary value is distinct from the [normalized toroidal flux
coordinate at the plasma
boundary](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_plasma_boundary),
which is dimensionless, and from the [toroidal magnetic flux at the plasma
boundary](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary), which is the
enclosed flux rather than its radius-like transformation.

The quantity is the boundary evaluation of the parent [toroidal flux
coordinate](name:toroidal_flux_coordinate) and supplies the outer radial
reference for flux-coordinate labels based on toroidal magnetic flux.

NAMES.name: toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude
NAMES.short:
Measure of how rapidly a toroidal magnetic-flux coordinate changes in space,
obtained from the magnitude of its spatial gradient.
NAMES.long:
This quantity represents the local geometric rate at which a toroidal
magnetic-flux coordinate changes through physical space. It is the
magnitude-based measure derived from the spatial gradient, independent of
any particular direction or projection.

The defining relation is

$$
\left|\nabla \chi\right| = \sqrt{\nabla\chi \cdot \nabla\chi}
$$

where $\chi$ is the toroidal magnetic-flux coordinate, $\nabla$ is the
spatial-gradient operator, and the dot denotes the Euclidean inner product
of the gradient with itself.

The local form is evaluated pointwise and is not intrinsically flux-surface
averaged or squared. The [flux-surface-averaged toroidal flux coordinate
gradient
magnitude](name:flux_surface_averaged_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude)
applies a flux-surface average to this measure, while [square of toroidal
flux coordinate gradient
magnitude](name:square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude)
applies the algebraic square. Both are derived from the underlying [toroidal
flux coordinate gradient](name:toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient), which
retains the full spatial-gradient quantity rather than its magnitude.

NAMES.name: flux_surface_averaged_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude
NAMES.short:
Geometric metric coefficient formed by averaging the local magnitude of the
toroidal-flux-coordinate gradient over each nested magnetic flux surface.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the flux-surface average of the local geometric rate at
which the toroidal flux coordinate changes through physical space. It is a
scalar metric coefficient associated with nested magnetic surfaces.

The defining relation is

$$
\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{S}) = \left\langle \left|\nabla \rho_{\mathrm{tor}}\right| \right\rangle_{\mathcal{S}}
$$

where $\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{S})$ is the averaged metric coefficient,
$\mathcal{S}$ is a magnetic flux surface, $\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the
toroidal flux coordinate labeling nested magnetic surfaces, $\nabla$ is the
spatial gradient, and the angle brackets with subscript $\mathcal{S}$ denote
averaging over that surface.

The quantity applies to the complete nested magnetic flux surface and is
aggregated over the surface rather than evaluated at a point, along a line,
or over a volume. It represents the average of the gradient magnitude, not a
directional component and not the local unaveraged value.

It is obtained by applying flux-surface averaging to the local [toroidal
flux coordinate gradient
magnitude](name:toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude). Unlike
[flux-surface-averaged square of toroidal flux coordinate gradient
magnitude](name:flux_surface_averaged_square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude),
it averages the magnitude itself rather than its square.

NAMES.name: square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude
NAMES.short:
Squared spatial gradient of a toroidal magnetic-flux coordinate, providing a
geometric coefficient for equilibrium descriptions in physical space.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the squared magnitude of the spatial gradient of a toroidal
magnetic-flux coordinate. It characterizes how rapidly the chosen flux
coordinate changes through physical space and serves as the geometric basis
for local and flux-surface equilibrium coefficients.

The underlying geometric measure is defined by

$$
G_\chi = \left|\nabla \chi\right|^2
$$

where $G_\chi$ is the squared flux-coordinate gradient magnitude, $\chi$ is
the toroidal magnetic-flux coordinate, $\nabla$ is the spatial gradient
operator, and the magnitude is taken with the physical-space metric.

The quantity applies to equilibrium magnetic geometry wherever the toroidal
flux coordinate and its spatial gradient are defined. Its aggregation is not
fixed at the parent level: concrete instances may be evaluated locally,
averaged over a magnetic flux surface, or formed into a ratio with another
geometric quantity.

It is distinct from the unsquared [toroidal flux-coordinate gradient
magnitude](name:toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude), and it does
not itself prescribe a denominator such as magnetic-field strength or major
radius. The [flux-surface-averaged
square](name:flux_surface_averaged_square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude)
is the averaged instance, while related ratio quantities compare this
squared geometric factor with the squared magnetic-field magnitude or
squared major radius.

NAMES.name: flux_surface_averaged_square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude
NAMES.short:
Flux-surface average of the squared magnitude of the gradient of the
normalized toroidal-flux radius. It is the averaged contravariant radial
metric coefficient for the flux coordinate rho_tor.
NAMES.long:
Flux-surface average of the squared magnitude of the gradient of the
toroidal flux coordinate is the average, over one magnetic flux surface, of
the squared norm of $\nabla \rho_\mathrm{tor}$. It is the
flux-surface-averaged contravariant radial metric coefficient associated
with the radial coordinate in the flux-coordinate system
$(\rho_\mathrm{tor}, \theta, \phi)$, where $\theta$ is a poloidal angle
label and $\phi$ is the toroidal angle.

The quantity is defined by the flux-surface average of the local radial
metric component:

$$
G_{\rho\rho}(\rho_\mathrm{tor}) = \left\langle |\nabla \rho_\mathrm{tor}|^2 \right\rangle_{\rho_\mathrm{tor}} = \frac{\int_{S(\rho_\mathrm{tor})} |\nabla \rho_\mathrm{tor}|^2\, dA / |\nabla \rho_\mathrm{tor}|}{\int_{S(\rho_\mathrm{tor})} dA / |\nabla \rho_\mathrm{tor}|}
$$

where $G_{\rho\rho}$ denotes this flux-surface-averaged metric coefficient,
$\rho_\mathrm{tor}$ is the normalized toroidal-flux radius,
$S(\rho_\mathrm{tor})$ is the magnetic flux surface with that label,
$\nabla$ is the spatial gradient operator, $dA$ is the surface-area element,
and $\langle\cdot\rangle_{\rho_\mathrm{tor}}$ denotes averaging over that
flux surface.

The coordinate $\rho_\mathrm{tor}$ is constituted by
$\rho_\mathrm{tor}=\sqrt{\Phi/\Phi_b}$, where $\Phi$ is the toroidal
magnetic flux enclosed by the flux surface and $\Phi_b$ is its value at the
plasma boundary. The scope is closed nested equilibrium flux surfaces; the
aggregation convention is an average over the entire surface at fixed
$\rho_\mathrm{tor}$.

This is not the pointwise quantity $|\nabla \rho_\mathrm{tor}|^2$, not the
flux-surface average of $|\nabla \rho_\mathrm{tor}|$, and not a volume or
time average. It belongs to the same flux-surface-averaged geometric-metric
family as the [flux-surface-averaged inverse major
radius](name:flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_major_radius), but it
characterizes the radial metric of the normalized toroidal-flux radius
rather than a major-radius factor.

NAMES.name: ratio_of_square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude_to_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude
NAMES.short:
Ratio of the square of the toroidal-flux-coordinate gradient magnitude to
the square of the local magnetic-field magnitude. It is the unaveraged
magnetic-geometry ratio whose flux-surface average defines the corresponding
averaged geometry coefficient.
NAMES.long:
Ratio of the square of the toroidal-flux-coordinate gradient magnitude to
the square of the local magnetic-field magnitude is a local scalar
magnetic-geometry coefficient. It expresses how the spatial metric of the
toroidal flux coordinate is weighted by the magnetic-field strength at the
same position.

The coefficient $K_{\rho B}$ is defined pointwise by:

$$
K_{\rho B}(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{|\nabla \rho_\mathrm{tor}(\mathbf{x})|^2}{|\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{x})|^2}
$$

where $K_{\rho B}$ is this ratio, $\mathbf{x}$ is spatial position,
$\rho_\mathrm{tor}$ is the toroidal flux coordinate, $\nabla
\rho_\mathrm{tor}$ is its spatial gradient, $\mathbf{B}$ is the
magnetic-field vector, and $|\mathbf{B}|$ is the [magnetic-field magnitude].

This quantity is the unaveraged, pointwise ratio evaluated where the
toroidal flux coordinate is differentiable and the magnetic-field magnitude
is nonzero. It does not include a flux-surface, volume, or time average, and
it is distinct from an averaged geometry coefficient.

The numerator is the [square of the toroidal flux-coordinate gradient
magnitude](name:square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude), and
the denominator is the square of the local magnetic-field magnitude at the
same position. The [flux-surface-averaged
ratio](name:flux_surface_averaged_ratio_of_square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude_to_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude)
is obtained by applying a flux-surface average to this local quotient
itself, not by separately averaging the numerator and denominator.

NAMES.name: flux_surface_averaged_ratio_of_square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude_to_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude
NAMES.short:
Flux-surface average of the squared toroidal-flux-coordinate gradient
magnitude divided by the squared local magnetic-field magnitude, a metric
coefficient for equilibrium geometry.
NAMES.long:
This coefficient describes the flux-surface-averaged geometric weighting of
a toroidal-flux radial coordinate by the inverse square of the local
magnetic-field magnitude.

The defining relation is

$$
\mathcal{G}_B = \left\langle \frac{|\nabla \rho_{\mathrm{tor}}|^2}{|\mathbf{B}|^2} \right\rangle_{\mathrm{FS}}
$$

where $\mathcal{G}_B$ is the averaged metric coefficient,
$\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the toroidal-flux radial coordinate, $\nabla$ is
the spatial gradient, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic-field vector, and
$\langle\cdot\rangle_{\mathrm{FS}}$ denotes the average over a magnetic flux
surface.

The quantity applies to nested equilibrium magnetic flux surfaces and uses
the average of the pointwise ratio, not the ratio of separately averaged
numerator and denominator. It is nonnegative because both the gradient
magnitude and magnetic-field magnitude are squared.

It is the flux-surface-averaged form of the local [ratio of squared
toroidal-flux-coordinate gradient magnitude to squared magnetic-field
magnitude](name:ratio_of_square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude_to_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude).
It shares the gradient-squared geometric factor with the
[flux-surface-averaged squared toroidal-flux-coordinate gradient
magnitude](name:flux_surface_averaged_square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude),
but additionally applies the pointwise inverse-square magnetic-field
weighting before averaging. It is distinct from the corresponding
major-radius denominator variant, [flux-surface-averaged ratio of squared
toroidal-flux-coordinate gradient magnitude to squared major
radius](name:flux_surface_averaged_ratio_of_square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude_to_square_of_major_radius).

NAMES.name: ratio_of_square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude_to_square_of_major_radius
NAMES.short:
Geometric equilibrium coefficient representing a squared flux-coordinate
gradient scaled by the inverse square of major radius.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is a geometric metric coefficient for nested magnetic flux
surfaces in toroidal plasma equilibrium. It measures spatial variation of a
flux coordinate after scaling by the inverse square of the major radius,
rather than representing a material, particle, or transport quantity.

For the gradient-ratio form represented by this family, the coefficient is
defined by:

$$
\mathcal{G}(\xi,R) = \frac{|\nabla \xi|^2}{R^2}
$$

where $\mathcal{G}$ is the geometric coefficient, $\xi$ is the relevant
flux-coordinate label, $\nabla \xi$ is its spatial gradient, $|\nabla \xi|$
is the gradient magnitude, and $R$ is the major-radius coordinate in the
right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

The scope is equilibrium magnetic geometry associated with nested flux
surfaces; no plasma population is selected, and the quantity is not a
density, magnetic-field strength, or transport coefficient. It is the
metric-ratio component of
[square_of_major_radius](name:square_of_major_radius), distinguished from a
bare reciprocal-square-radius factor by the flux-coordinate gradient in its
numerator. The parent quantity is not intrinsically flux-surface averaged;
averaging is an explicit aggregation applied by a child.

The representative [flux-surface-averaged gradient-ratio
coefficient](name:flux_surface_averaged_ratio_of_square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude_to_square_of_major_radius)
is the flux-surface average of this geometric ratio. This distinguishes it
from
[flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_square_of_major_radius](name:flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_square_of_major_radius),
which contains the reciprocal-square major-radius factor without the
flux-coordinate gradient factor.

NAMES.name: flux_surface_averaged_ratio_of_square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude_to_square_of_major_radius
NAMES.short:
Flux-surface-averaged magnetic-geometry coefficient measuring the squared
toroidal-flux-coordinate gradient relative to the squared major radius.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is a magnetic-geometry metric coefficient that characterizes
how a toroidal-flux radial coordinate varies across nested magnetic
surfaces, with the variation weighted by inverse squared major radius.

It is defined by

$$
g_2 = \left\langle \frac{|\nabla \rho|^2}{R^2} \right\rangle_{\mathrm{FS}}
$$

where $g_2$ is the flux-surface-averaged metric coefficient, $\rho$ is the
toroidal-flux radial coordinate, $\nabla\rho$ is its spatial gradient,
$|\nabla\rho|$ is the gradient magnitude, $R$ is the major radius, and the
subscript $\mathrm{FS}$ denotes the prescribed average over a complete
magnetic flux surface.

The quantity applies to an equilibrium magnetic flux surface and represents
an aggregate over that surface rather than a pointwise local value. It has
no species, population, or transport-channel restriction.

It is the flux-surface average of the local ratio defined by [ratio of
square of toroidal flux coordinate gradient magnitude to square of major
radius](name:ratio_of_square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude_to_square_of_major_radius).
Unlike [flux-surface-averaged square of toroidal flux coordinate gradient
magnitude](name:flux_surface_averaged_square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude),
it retains the inverse-square-major-radius weighting; the numerator is
constructed from the [toroidal flux coordinate gradient
magnitude](name:toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude).

NAMES.name: toroidal_flux_coordinate_of_magnetic_axis
NAMES.short:
Value of the radius-like toroidal-flux label on the magnetic surface passing
through the magnetic axis; it is zero because enclosed toroidal flux
vanishes there.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal flux coordinate at the magnetic axis is the value of the
radius-like flux-surface label on the magnetic-axis reference surface. It
identifies the origin of the toroidal-flux radial coordinate and is not a
geometric distance from the machine symmetry axis.

The coordinate is defined by

$$
\rho_{\mathrm{tor}} = \sqrt{\frac{\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}}{\pi B_0}}
$$

where $\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the toroidal flux coordinate,
$\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the toroidal magnetic flux enclosed by the magnetic
surface, and $B_0$ is the positive reference vacuum toroidal magnetic-field
strength. At the magnetic axis, the enclosed toroidal flux is zero, so this
value is zero.

The quantity applies to the single magnetic-axis locus and is neither a
flux-surface average nor an integral over a finite region. It is the axis
value of the parent [toroidal flux
coordinate](name:toroidal_flux_coordinate), not the coordinate of an
arbitrary flux surface or a geometric major- or minor-radius measurement.

The [toroidal magnetic flux](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux) supplies the
enclosed-flux quantity in the defining relation, while the corresponding
normalized toroidal-flux coordinate uses axis and boundary values to form a
dimensionless radial label.

NAMES.name: toroidal_flux_surface_averaged_current_density
NAMES.short:
Flux-surface-averaged toroidal current density is the toroidal conventional
current density assigned to a closed magnetic-flux surface. It is the
geometry-weighted total toroidal current-density component that acts as the
effective toroidal current source for the equilibrium poloidal magnetic-flux
distribution.
NAMES.long:
Flux-surface-averaged toroidal current density is the toroidal conventional
current density assigned to a closed magnetic-flux surface. It represents
the total toroidal current-density component on that surface, expressed with
the geometry weighting that provides the effective toroidal current source
for the equilibrium poloidal magnetic-flux distribution.

The defining flux-surface average is

$$
j_{\phi,\mathrm{FSA}} = \frac{\left\langle j_\phi/R \right\rangle}{\left\langle 1/R \right\rangle}
$$

where $j_{\phi,\mathrm{FSA}}$ is the flux-surface-averaged toroidal current
density, $j_\phi$ is the local toroidal component of the conventional
current-density vector projected on $\hat{\phi}$, $R$ is the major-radius
coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, and
$\langle \cdot \rangle$ denotes an average over the closed magnetic-flux
surface.

The scope is closed magnetic-flux surfaces in an axisymmetric equilibrium,
and the aggregation is over the total conventional current carried by the
plasma unless a population-specific qualifier is present. This quantity is
not the unweighted flux-surface average of $j_\phi$, not a local
current-density component at a point, and not a field-aligned or parallel
current density.

It is the toroidal counterpart of the [parallel flux-surface-averaged
current
density](name:parallel_flux_surface_averaged_current_density_due_to_wave_driven_current_drive)
and a member of the [flux-surface-averaged current
density](name:parallel_flux_surface_averaged_current_density_due_to_wave_driven_current_drive)
family. In equilibrium, this weighted toroidal average is the scalar source
coupled to the [poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux) in the
Grad-Shafranov balance.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the conventional current-density vector has a
positive projection on $\hat{\phi}$, the direction of increasing toroidal
angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_magnetic_field
NAMES.short:
Signed toroidal component of the local total magnetic induction, resolved
along increasing toroidal angle in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z)
frame.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal magnetic field $B_\\phi$ is the signed component of the local
total [magnetic induction](name:magnetic_field) resolved along the toroidal
direction. It represents directional field strength at a point before any
source selection, perturbation selection, spatial aggregation, magnitude
reduction, or locus restriction.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \\phi, Z)$ frame, the component is
defined by

$$
B_\\phi = \\mathbf{B} \\cdot \\hat{\\boldsymbol{\\phi}}
$$

where $B_\\phi$ is the toroidal magnetic-field component, $\\mathbf{B}$ is
the local total magnetic-induction vector, and $\\hat{\\boldsymbol{\\phi}}$
is the toroidal unit vector. Here, $R$ is major radius measured from the
symmetry axis, $\\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height; the
basis is right-handed with $\\hat{\\mathbf{R}} \\times
\\hat{\\boldsymbol{\\phi}} = \\hat{\\mathbf{Z}}$.

The quantity applies pointwise wherever the local total magnetic induction
is defined, including plasma and surrounding vacuum regions. It includes all
represented magnetic-field contributions and is neither a source-specific
field nor a perturbation-only field; it is also distinct from the unsigned
[poloidal magnetic-field strength](name:poloidal_magnetic_field).

Together with the [radial magnetic-field
component](name:radial_magnetic_field) and vertical component, $B_\\phi$
determines the local magnetic-induction vector in the cylindrical frame. The
toroidal component is one directional projection of the parent [magnetic
field](name:magnetic_field), not its full vector or magnitude.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when $B_\\phi$ points in the direction of
increasing toroidal angle $\\phi`.

NAMES.name: toroidal_magnetic_field_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.short:
Toroidal magnetic field at the magnetic axis is the signed toroidal
component of the total equilibrium magnetic field at the magnetic axis in
the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame. It includes externally applied
vacuum-field and plasma-current-generated contributions.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal magnetic field at the magnetic axis is the signed toroidal
component of the total equilibrium magnetic field evaluated at the magnetic
axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is
major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The
magnetic axis is the locus of the equilibrium flux surface with the
magnetic-axis value of poloidal magnetic flux. The total field includes
externally produced vacuum-field and plasma-current-generated contributions.

In an axisymmetric equilibrium, using the poloidal-current function
$F(\psi)=R B_\phi$, the defining relation is

$$
B_{\phi,\mathrm{axis}} = \mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{total}}(R_{\mathrm{axis}}, Z_{\mathrm{axis}}) \cdot \hat{\phi} = B_\phi(R_{\mathrm{axis}}, Z_{\mathrm{axis}}) = \frac{F(\psi_0)}{R_{\mathrm{axis}}}
$$

where $B_{\phi,\mathrm{axis}}$ is this quantity,
$\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{total}}$ is the total equilibrium magnetic field,
$B_\phi$ is the [toroidal magnetic field](name:toroidal_magnetic_field),
$\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal
angle $\phi$, $R_{\mathrm{axis}}$ and $Z_{\mathrm{axis}}$ are the
major-radius and vertical coordinates of the magnetic axis, $F(\psi)$ is the
[poloidal-current function](name:poloidal_current_function), and $\psi_0$ is
the [poloidal magnetic flux at the magnetic
axis](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis).

The scope is the local magnetic-axis value for the equilibrium state; it is
not an average over a flux surface, poloidal angle, toroidal angle, or
plasma volume. Because it is a component, not a magnitude, it retains the
sign of the toroidal projection and does not represent the absolute
magnetic-field strength.

This quantity is the on-axis specialization of [toroidal magnetic
field](name:toroidal_magnetic_field). It is distinct from [toroidal vacuum
magnetic field](name:toroidal_vacuum_magnetic_field), which excludes
plasma-current-generated contributions, and from [toroidal reference
magnetic field](name:toroidal_reference_magnetic_field), which denotes a
prescribed reference field rather than the local total field at the magnetic
axis even when numerical values coincide.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the total magnetic field at the magnetic axis
has a toroidal component in the direction of increasing toroidal angle
$\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_magnetic_flux
NAMES.short:
Toroidal magnetic flux is the signed surface integral of the magnetic field
over the poloidal cross-section enclosed by a nested magnetic flux surface.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal magnetic flux is the signed surface integral of the magnetic field
over the poloidal cross-section enclosed by a nested magnetic flux surface.
It is the toroidal member of the [magnetic flux](name:magnetic_flux) family
and is defined as a function of nested magnetic surfaces in axisymmetric
equilibrium.

The defining surface integral is:

$$
\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}(\mathcal{S}) = \int_{S_{\mathrm{pol}}(\mathcal{S})} \mathbf{B} \cdot d\mathbf{A}
$$

where $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}(\mathcal{S})$ is the toroidal magnetic flux
associated with the nested magnetic flux surface $\mathcal{S}$,
$S_{\mathrm{pol}}(\mathcal{S})$ is the poloidal cross-section bounded by
that surface at fixed toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical
$(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, $Z$ is
vertical height, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic-field vector, and
$d\mathbf{A}$ is the oriented area element whose positive normal is
$+\hat{\phi}$.

The scope is the total toroidal projection of magnetic flux through the
entire enclosed poloidal cross-section for each nested magnetic surface. It
is not a local magnetic-field value, not a flux-surface average, and not a
source-separated contribution; [toroidal magnetic flux at the plasma
boundary](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary) is the
boundary-specific value of the same quantity.

At the magnetic axis the enclosed poloidal cross-section shrinks to zero
area, so $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}=0$ there. Together with [poloidal magnetic
flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux) $\psi$, it provides a radial flux-surface
label; the [safety factor](name:safety_factor) $q$ is related to the two
fluxes by the differential relation $q = d\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}/d\psi$ for
consistent flux definitions.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the net magnetic flux through the poloidal
cross-section is directed along increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the
right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.
