NAMES.name: triangularity_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short:
Signed dimensionless shape parameter measuring the normalized horizontal
displacement of a nested magnetic flux surface’s upper or lower vertical
extremum.
NAMES.long:
Triangularity of a nested magnetic flux surface is the signed shape
parameter formed from the horizontal displacement of an upper or lower
vertical extremum, normalized by the surface’s horizontal half-width.

For a selected upper or lower vertical extremum, triangularity is defined in
the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame by

$$
\delta_s = \frac{R_c - R_s}{a}
$$

where $\delta_s$ is the triangularity, $s$ identifies the selected upper or
lower vertical extremum, $R_s$ is its radial coordinate, $R_c$ is the radial
midpoint of the flux surface’s horizontal extent, and $a$ is the
corresponding horizontal half-width.

This is a geometric parameter of an individual nested magnetic flux surface
in an equilibrium plasma. The unqualified quantity covers either vertical
extremum and carries no aggregation over multiple flux surfaces, plasma
volume, or the plasma boundary.

Triangularity characterizes the radial displacement of a vertical extremum;
it is distinct from [elongation of a flux
surface](name:elongation_of_flux_surface), which describes the ratio of
vertical to horizontal extent, and from [outer squareness of a flux
surface](name:outer_squareness_of_flux_surface), which describes corner
deformation.

The upper and lower branch-specific quantities are [upper triangularity of a
flux surface](name:upper_triangularity_of_flux_surface) and [lower
triangularity of a flux surface](name:lower_triangularity_of_flux_surface);
each is an instance of this parent quantity with $s$ fixed to the
corresponding vertical extremum.

NAMES.name: lower_triangularity_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless lower triangularity shape parameter for a nested magnetic flux
surface, given by the normalized inward radial displacement of its lower
vertical extremum.
NAMES.long:
Lower triangularity of a flux surface is the dimensionless triangularity
shape parameter defined at the lower vertical extremum of a nested magnetic
flux surface. It is the normalized inward displacement in major radius $R$
of that lower extremum relative to the magnetic-axis reference.

For the lower vertical extremum, the defining relation is:

$$
\delta_{\mathrm{lower}} = \frac{R_{\mathrm{axis}} - R_{\mathrm{lower}}}{a}
$$

where $\delta_{\mathrm{lower}}$ is lower triangularity, $R_{\mathrm{axis}}$
is the major-radius coordinate of the magnetic axis, $R_{\mathrm{lower}}$ is
the major-radius coordinate of the lower vertical extremum, and $a$ is the
minor radius of the same flux surface. These coordinates are defined in the
right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius
measured from the machine symmetry axis, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$
is vertical height.

This quantity applies independently to each nested magnetic flux surface and
is a geometrical property of the surface rather than a plasma-population
quantity. It resolves the lower vertical extremum only; it is not averaged
over flux surfaces or combined with the upper extremum. It is distinct from
[lower triangularity of a flux surface
boundary](name:lower_triangularity_of_plasma_boundary), which describes the
outer plasma boundary rather than an arbitrary nested surface.

It is the lower-extremum branch of [triangularity of a flux
surface](name:triangularity_of_flux_surface), whose parent quantity permits
the relevant upper or lower vertical extremum. The corresponding [upper
triangularity of a flux surface](name:upper_triangularity_of_flux_surface)
uses the upper vertical extremum, while [elongation of a flux
surface](name:elongation_of_flux_surface) describes vertical-to-horizontal
shaping rather than triangular displacement.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the lower vertical extremum lies at smaller
major radius $R$ than the magnetic-axis reference, corresponding to an
inward displacement.

NAMES.name: triangularity_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless shape parameter for the plasma-boundary poloidal
cross-section, expressing the aggregate inward radial displacement of its
upper and lower extrema relative to the geometric center.
NAMES.long:
Plasma-boundary triangularity is a dimensionless shaping parameter
describing the asymmetry of the boundary’s poloidal cross-section through
the inward displacement of its upper and lower radial extrema relative to
the geometric center. It characterizes the complete boundary rather than
either half-plane extremum alone.

For the upper and lower boundary extrema, the aggregate triangularity is
defined as

$$
\delta = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{R_0-R_u}{a}+\frac{R_0-R_l}{a}\right)
$$

where $\delta$ is the plasma-boundary triangularity, $R_0$ is the
major-radius coordinate of the geometric center, $R_u$ and $R_l$ are the
major-radius coordinates of the upper and lower boundary extrema, and $a$ is
the boundary minor radius. The coordinates refer to the right-handed
cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

This quantity applies to the entire plasma boundary and aggregates the upper
and lower extremal displacements into one shape parameter. It excludes the
separately resolved [upper triangularity of the plasma
boundary](name:upper_triangularity_of_plasma_boundary) and [lower
triangularity of the plasma
boundary](name:lower_triangularity_of_plasma_boundary), which retain only
one extremum. It also differs from [triangularity of a flux
surface](name:triangularity_of_flux_surface), which describes an individual
nested magnetic flux surface rather than the outer plasma boundary.

sources.leaf_definition: Triangularity of the plasma boundary
sources.parent_definition: Description of the plasma boundary. The boundary can be either the real separatrix (provided by a free boundary equilibrium solver) or the 0.99x psi_norm flux surface provided by a fixed boundary equilibrium

NAMES.name: lower_triangularity_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless shaping parameter equal to the normalized inward radial
displacement of the lower plasma-boundary extremum from the geometric
center.
NAMES.long:
Lower triangularity of the plasma boundary is a signed dimensionless measure
of the horizontal displacement of its lower poloidal extremum relative to
the geometric center. This component selects the lower extremum rather than
averaging the upper and lower contributions.

$$
\delta_l = \frac{R_0-R_l}{a}
$$

Here, $\delta_l$ is the lower triangularity; $R_0$ is the major-radius
coordinate of the geometric center; $R_l$ is the major-radius coordinate of
the lower vertical extremum; and $a$ is the minor radius of the plasma
boundary. These coordinates are defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,
\phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and
$Z$ is vertical height.

This quantity applies only to the lower extremum of the plasma boundary and
represents one term in the boundary-shaping description. It is not the upper
contribution or an average over both extrema; the corresponding upper
contribution is [upper
triangularity](name:upper_triangularity_of_plasma_boundary).

The parent [triangularity of the plasma
boundary](name:triangularity_of_plasma_boundary) is the arithmetic mean of
the upper and lower contributions: $\delta=(\delta_u+\delta_l)/2$, where
$\delta$ is the parent triangularity and $\delta_u$ is the upper
triangularity.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the lower extremum is displaced inward,
toward decreasing major radius $R$, relative to the geometric center.

NAMES.name: upper_triangularity_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless upper triangularity shape parameter for a nested magnetic flux
surface, given by the normalized inward radial displacement of its upper
vertical extremum.
NAMES.long:
Upper triangularity of a flux surface is the dimensionless triangularity
shape parameter defined at the upper vertical extremum of a nested magnetic
flux surface. It is the normalized inward radial displacement of that upper
extremum in a poloidal cross-section.

For the upper vertical extremum, the defining relation is:

$$
\delta_u = \frac{R_{\mathrm{axis}} - R_u}{a}
$$

where $\delta_u$ is upper triangularity, $R_{\mathrm{axis}}$ is the
major-radius coordinate of the magnetic axis, $R_u$ is the major-radius
coordinate of the upper vertical extremum, and $a$ is the minor radius of
the flux surface. These coordinates are defined in the right-handed
cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is
toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

This quantity applies separately to each nested magnetic flux surface
identified by its poloidal magnetic-flux label. It represents only the upper
extremum and is not an aggregate over the upper and lower extrema or over
multiple flux surfaces.

It is distinct from [lower triangularity of a flux
surface](name:lower_triangularity_of_flux_surface), which uses the lower
vertical extremum. It also differs from [upper triangularity of the plasma
boundary](name:upper_triangularity_of_plasma_boundary), which applies only
to the outer plasma boundary rather than to an arbitrary nested flux
surface.

Upper triangularity is the upper-extremum branch of [triangularity of a flux
surface](name:triangularity_of_flux_surface), whose definition permits the
relevant upper or lower vertical extremum. The upper and lower quantities
together describe the asymmetric triangular shaping of a flux-surface
cross-section.

NAMES.name: upper_triangularity_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless shape parameter for the plasma-boundary poloidal
cross-section, expressing the inward radial displacement of its upper
extremum relative to the geometric center.
NAMES.long:
Upper triangularity of the plasma boundary is a dimensionless shaping
parameter describing the inward radial displacement of the upper extremum of
the boundary’s poloidal cross-section relative to its geometric center. It
selects the upper extremum rather than combining the two vertical halves.

For the upper boundary extremum, it is defined as

$$
\delta_u = \frac{R_0-R_u}{a}
$$

where $\delta_u$ is the upper triangularity, $R_0$ is the major-radius
coordinate of the geometric center, $R_u$ is the major-radius coordinate of
the upper boundary extremum, and $a$ is the boundary minor radius. These
coordinates refer to the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where
$R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

This quantity applies to the outer plasma boundary and uses only its upper
poloidal extremum; it is not averaged over the upper and lower extrema. It
is a boundary-shape parameter rather than a local field value or the
triangularity of an individual nested magnetic flux surface.

The [triangularity of the plasma
boundary](name:triangularity_of_plasma_boundary) aggregates the upper and
lower components, with $\delta = (\delta_u+\delta_l)/2$, where $\delta$ is
the aggregate boundary triangularity and $\delta_l$ is the [lower
triangularity of the plasma
boundary](name:lower_triangularity_of_plasma_boundary). It differs from
[triangularity of a flux surface](name:triangularity_of_flux_surface), which
describes a nested magnetic flux surface rather than the outer plasma
boundary.

NAMES.name: vacuum_magnetic_field
NAMES.short:
Local magnetic-induction vector generated by currents external to the plasma
with plasma-current contributions omitted, retaining field strength and
direction before selecting a component in the right-handed cylindrical (R,
φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The vacuum magnetic field $\mathbf{B}_{\rm vac}$ is the local [magnetic
induction](name:magnetic_field) generated by currents external to the plasma
when plasma-current contributions are omitted. It represents a vector field
at a point, retaining field strength and direction rather than selecting a
cylindrical component or scalar magnitude.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, the vacuum field may be
resolved as

$$
\mathbf{B}_{\rm vac}=B_{R,{\rm vac}}\hat{R}+B_{\phi,{\rm vac}}\hat{\phi}+B_{Z,{\rm vac}}\hat{Z}
$$

where $\mathbf{B}_{\rm vac}$ is the vacuum magnetic field, $B_{R,{\rm vac}}$
is its signed radial component, $B_{\phi,{\rm vac}}$ is the [toroidal vacuum
magnetic field](name:toroidal_vacuum_magnetic_field), $B_{Z,{\rm vac}}$ is
its signed vertical component, and $\hat{R}$, $\hat{\phi}$, and $\hat{Z}$
are the basis vectors for increasing major radius, toroidal angle, and
vertical height.

This quantity is the externally sourced, plasma-current-omitted contribution
to the local field and may be evaluated inside the confined-plasma region as
well as in vacuum regions; it does not denote only the space outside the
plasma. It has no species population, and its aggregation convention is a
local point value, not a spatial average, flux-surface average, or
finite-volume reduction.

It is distinct from the [plasma magnetic field](name:plasma_magnetic_field),
which represents the magnetic-field contribution associated with the
confined plasma, and from the unrestricted local [magnetic
induction](name:magnetic_field), which does not by name isolate the vacuum
contribution. The [non-axisymmetric magnetic
field](name:non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field) is the toroidally varying part
of the external-coil vacuum field after its toroidally averaged component is
removed, while a [perturbed vacuum magnetic
field](name:perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field) denotes a perturbative vacuum
contribution rather than the full vacuum vector.

The [vacuum magnetic vector
potential](name:vacuum_magnetic_vector_potential) $\mathbf{A}_{\rm vac}$ is
a potential for this field, with $\mathbf{B}_{\rm
vac}=\nabla\times\mathbf{A}_{\rm vac}$, where $\mathbf{A}_{\rm vac}$ is the
vacuum magnetic vector potential and $\nabla$ is the spatial differential
operator. Different gage choices of $\mathbf{A}_{\rm vac}$ that have the
same curl represent the same vacuum magnetic field; in regions containing no
external current density, $\mathbf{B}_{\rm vac}$ is curl-free, and the field
is solenoidal.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when a resolved component of $\mathbf{B}_{\rm
vac}$ points along the corresponding positive basis vector of the
right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where the positive directions
are increasing major radius $R$, increasing toroidal angle $\phi$, and
increasing vertical height $Z$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_vacuum_magnetic_field
NAMES.short:
Signed toroidal component of the current-free vacuum magnetic field at a
reference major radius, defining the nominal externally generated field
strength.
NAMES.long:
The vacuum toroidal magnetic field $B_0$ is the signed toroidal component of
the equilibrium magnetic-field vector in the current-free region surrounding
the plasma, evaluated at a reference major radius.

The reference value is defined by

$$
B_0 = B_{\\phi,\mathrm{vac}}(R_0)
$$

where $B_0$ is the vacuum toroidal field at the reference major radius,
$B_{\phi,\mathrm{vac}}$ is the toroidal component of the vacuum magnetic
field, and $R_0$ is the major-radius coordinate of the reference location in
the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

This quantity applies to the equilibrium vacuum field generated by external
sources, with contributions from plasma currents omitted. It is a single
signed reference value rather than a spatial average, surface integral,
local total field, or Fourier perturbation coefficient. The vector quantity
it specializes is the [vacuum magnetic field](name:vacuum_magnetic_field);
it is distinct from the [toroidal perturbed vacuum magnetic field real
part](name:toroidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_real_part), which
describes a first-order perturbation. The normalization product $R_0 B_0$
represents the conserved major-radius-weighted toroidal field of an
axisymmetric vacuum field, for which $R B_{\phi,\mathrm{vac}}(R) = R_0 B_0$,
where $R$ is the major-radius coordinate.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the associated vacuum magnetic-field vector
has a toroidal component in the direction of increasing toroidal angle
$\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_geometric_axis
NAMES.short:
Signed vertical position of the plasma boundary’s geometric axis, defined as
the midpoint of its maximum and minimum Z extents in the right-handed
cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The geometric-axis vertical coordinate is the midpoint of the plasma
boundary’s maximum and minimum vertical positions in the right-handed
cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. Here $R$ is the major-radius coordinate,
$\phi$ is the toroidal angle, and $Z$ is the vertical coordinate. It
characterizes the boundary’s vertical placement rather than the location of
a magnetic-flux extremum.

For the specified plasma boundary, the defining relation is

$$
Z_{\mathrm{axis}} = \frac{Z_{\max}+Z_{\min}}{2}
$$

where $Z_{\mathrm{axis}}$ is the vertical coordinate of the geometric axis,
$Z_{\max}$ is the boundary’s maximum vertical coordinate, and $Z_{\min}$ is
its minimum vertical coordinate.

The quantity applies to the complete plasma boundary and uses the global
extrema with equal weighting; it is not a local boundary coordinate, an
arc-length average, or a flux-surface average. It is distinct from the
[vertical coordinate of the magnetic
axis](name:vertical_coordinate_of_magnetic_axis), which identifies the
vertical position of the interior poloidal-flux extremum rather than the
midpoint of the boundary extent.

sources.leaf_definition: Height
sources.parent_definition: Outboard point on the separatrix on which dr/dz = 0 (local maximum of the major radius of the separatrix). In case of multiple local maxima, the closest one from z=z_magnetic_axis is chosen.

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Z position of the geometric axis (defined as (Zmax+Zmin) / 2 of the boundary)

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_magnetic_axis
NAMES.short:
Signed vertical Z coordinate of the magnetic axis in the right-handed
cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, marking the interior extremum organizing nested
magnetic flux surfaces.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the signed vertical coordinate $Z_\mathrm{axis}$ of the
magnetic-axis point in a poloidal cross-section. The magnetic axis is the
interior extremum of the poloidal magnetic-flux function around which nested
magnetic flux surfaces are organized.

For an equilibrium with poloidal flux function $\psi(R,Z)$, the
magnetic-axis point satisfies the stationary-point condition

$$
\left.\frac{\partial \psi}{\partial R}\right|_{\mathrm{axis}}
=
\left.\frac{\partial \psi}{\partial Z}\right|_{\mathrm{axis}}
=0
$$

where $\psi$ is the poloidal magnetic-flux function, $R$ is the major-radius
coordinate, $Z$ is the vertical coordinate, and the subscript
$\mathrm{axis}$ denotes evaluation at the magnetic-axis point. The
derivatives are taken in the poloidal cross-section, and $0$ denotes a
vanishing derivative.

The coordinate is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$
frame, where $\phi$ is the toroidal angle. It applies to the single interior
magnetic-axis point, has no species or particle-population scope, and is
neither averaged nor integrated over a surface, region, or volume. It
records only the vertical coordinate; the corresponding radial coordinate is
required to locate the point fully.

This quantity is distinct from the [vertical coordinate of the geometric
axis](name:vertical_coordinate_of_geometric_axis), which describes a
boundary-derived geometric center, and from the [vertical coordinate of the
X-point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_x_point), which identifies a magnetic
null where separatrix branches meet.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the magnetic axis lies in the direction of
increasing vertical coordinate $Z$ from the origin of the right-handed
cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_measurement_position
NAMES.short:
Signed vertical coordinate of a generic measurement location, measured from
the machine midplane along the Z direction of the right-handed cylindrical
(R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate of a measurement position is its signed height
relative to the machine midplane in the right-handed cylindrical
$(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. Here $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and
$Z$ is vertical height.

The coordinate is defined by

$$
Z_{\mathrm{meas}} = \mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{meas}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{Z}}
$$

where $Z_{\mathrm{meas}}$ is the vertical coordinate,
$\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{meas}}$ is the position vector of the measurement
location relative to the machine-midplane origin, and $\hat{\mathbf{Z}}$ is
the vertical unit vector.

This quantity applies to the geometric measurement position independently of
the diagnostic type or physical quantity measured there. It represents one
coordinate of one position, with no averaging over positions, populations,
or physical regions, and it is not the value of a plasma field evaluated at
that location.

The generic position coordinate has the same geometric meaning as the
object-specific [vertical coordinate of a
camera](name:vertical_coordinate_of_camera) and [vertical coordinate of a
diagnostic aperture](name:vertical_coordinate_of_diagnostic_aperture); those
quantities differ only in the object whose position is identified.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_primary_x_point
NAMES.short:
Signed vertical position of the primary magnetic X-point, the poloidal-field
null where separatrix branches meet, in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ,
Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The primary X-point is the main poloidal magnetic-field null on the plasma
boundary, where separatrix branches meet. This quantity gives that point’s
vertical coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

$$
Z_{\mathrm{X,primary}} = \mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{X,primary}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{Z}}
$$

Here, $Z_{\mathrm{X,primary}}$ is the vertical coordinate of the primary
X-point, $\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{X,primary}}$ is its position vector relative
to the coordinate origin, and $\hat{\mathbf{Z}}$ is the vertical unit vector
of the cylindrical frame.

The locus is specifically the primary, or main, boundary X-point rather than
an unspecified or secondary X-point. This is a pointwise geometric
coordinate with no spatial averaging, surface integration, population
aggregation, or species dependence; it excludes the radial coordinate of the
same point.

The generic [vertical coordinate of an
X-point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_x_point) represents the same signed Z
coordinate without restricting the locus to the primary X-point, while the
[radial coordinate of an X-point](name:radial_coordinate_of_x_point)
supplies the corresponding major-radius coordinate.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the primary X-point lies in the direction of
increasing vertical coordinate $Z$.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_strike_point
NAMES.short:
Signed vertical (Z) coordinate of the inner divertor strike point, where the
inner separatrix leg intersects the divertor target in the right-handed
cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate of the inner divertor strike point is the signed Z
location where the inner leg of the plasma separatrix intersects the
divertor target. It identifies a boundary contact point in the poloidal
geometry, rather than the magnetic null.

This quantity applies specifically to the inner strike point and represents
one geometric coordinate value; it is not an average over strike points, a
target-surface extent, or a toroidal aggregation. It is distinct from the
corresponding outer strike-point location, which describes the outer
separatrix leg.

Together with the [major-radius coordinate of a magnetic strike
point](name:radial_coordinate_of_strike_point), this coordinate locates the
same strike point in the poloidal cross-section of the right-handed
cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. It must not be interpreted as the [vertical
coordinate of an X-point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_x_point), because an
X-point is a magnetic null rather than a separatrix–target intersection.

NAMES.name: vertical_magnetic_field
NAMES.short:
Vertical magnetic-field component of the local total magnetic induction,
resolved along increasing vertical height in the right-handed cylindrical
(R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The vertical magnetic field $B_Z$ is the signed component of the local total
[magnetic induction](name:magnetic_field) resolved along the vertical
direction. It represents directional field strength rather than the full
magnetic-induction vector or its magnitude.

The vertical component is defined by

$$
B_Z = \mathbf{B} \cdot \hat{Z}
$$

where $\mathbf{B}$ is the local total magnetic induction, $\hat{Z}$ is the
unit vector in the direction of increasing vertical height, and $B_Z$ is the
resulting vertical component.

This quantity is defined locally in the right-handed cylindrical
$(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and
$Z$ is vertical height. It does not select a plasma, vacuum, perturbed, or
other source contribution, and it has no restriction to a particular region
or species. At a point it is the local projection, not a sum or integral
over a region, source, or population; when a finite sensing volume defines
the value, the projected component is averaged over that volume.

It is distinct from the [radial magnetic field](name:radial_magnetic_field)
and [toroidal magnetic field](name:toroidal_magnetic_field), which are
projections onto the other cylindrical directions, and from the [poloidal
magnetic field](name:poloidal_magnetic_field), which is the magnitude in the
poloidal plane. Together, these component quantities resolve the local
[magnetic induction](name:magnetic_field) in the cylindrical frame.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when $B_Z$ points in the direction of increasing
vertical height $Z$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: volume_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short:
Geometric volume contained within a nested magnetic flux surface, cumulative
from the magnetic axis toward the outermost closed surface.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the three-dimensional volume enclosed inside a nested
magnetic flux surface. It characterizes the geometry of the region interior
to that magnetic surface.

The enclosed volume is defined by

$$
V(\chi) = \int_{\Omega_\chi} d^3x
$$

where $V(\chi)$ is the volume associated with flux-surface label $\chi$,
$\Omega_\chi$ is the region inside the corresponding magnetic surface
$S_\chi$, and $d^3x$ is the three-dimensional volume element.

The quantity applies to each nested magnetic surface across the modeled
plasma region, including confined-plasma and scrape-off-layer surfaces where
such surfaces are defined. It is a cumulative volume over the complete
interior of the surface, increasing outward from the magnetic axis; it is
not the volume of an infinitesimal shell.

It is distinct from [surface area of a flux
surface](name:surface_area_of_flux_surface) and from [poloidal-plane
cross-sectional area of a flux
surface](name:poloidal_plane_cross_sectional_area_of_flux_surface). The
[volume of the plasma boundary](name:volume_of_plasma_boundary) is the
boundary value of this enclosed-volume function, while [the derivative with
respect to poloidal magnetic flux coordinate of volume of flux
surface](name:derivative_with_respect_to_poloidal_magnetic_flux_coordinate_of_volume_of_flux_surface)
and [the derivative with respect to toroidal flux coordinate of volume of
flux
surface](name:derivative_with_respect_to_toroidal_flux_coordinate_of_volume_of_flux_surface)
describe its local change with different flux labels.

NAMES.name: derivative_with_respect_to_poloidal_magnetic_flux_coordinate_of_volume_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short:
Derivative of the enclosed volume of a nested magnetic flux surface with
respect to its signed poloidal magnetic-flux label.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the local geometric rate at which the volume enclosed by a
nested magnetic flux surface changes as the signed poloidal magnetic-flux
label changes. It describes the differential volume associated with an
increment of that label, rather than the enclosed volume itself.

The defining derivative is

$$
\frac{dV}{d\psi}(\psi) = \lim_{\Delta\psi \to 0} \frac{V(\psi + \Delta\psi) - V(\psi)}{\Delta\psi}
$$

where $V(\psi)$ is the volume enclosed by the nested magnetic flux surface
labeled by the signed poloidal magnetic flux $\psi$, and $\Delta\psi$ is an
increment of that flux label.

The quantity applies to nested closed magnetic flux surfaces and uses the
cumulative volume interior to each surface, ordered from the magnetic axis
toward the outermost closed surface. It is a scalar geometric metric based
on dimensional poloidal magnetic flux; it excludes volume outside the
selected surface and is not an integral over a finite range of flux labels.

It is the differential counterpart of the [volume of a flux
surface](name:volume_of_flux_surface), obtained by differentiating that
enclosed-volume quantity with respect to $\psi$. As a flux-coordinate
Jacobian factor, it contributes to flux-surface averages, pressure-balance
relations, and one-dimensional transport formulations. It must be
distinguished from a derivative with respect to the [normalized poloidal
flux coordinate](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate), which includes
the coordinate normalization in its chain rule.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the enclosed volume increases toward
increasing signed poloidal magnetic flux $\psi$; with positive plasma
current in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the
right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius,
$\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, $\psi$ decreases
outward and the outward increase of volume therefore gives a negative
derivative.

NAMES.name: derivative_with_respect_to_toroidal_flux_coordinate_of_volume_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short:
Radial rate of change of the volume enclosed by a nested magnetic flux
surface as its dimensionful toroidal flux coordinate increases.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the local derivative of the cumulative three-dimensional
volume enclosed by a nested magnetic flux surface with respect to its
dimensionful toroidal flux coordinate. It is a geometric metric coefficient
used in flux-surface-averaged equilibrium and transport relations.

The defining relation is

$$
\frac{dV}{d\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}}
=
\frac{d}{d\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}}
\left(\int_{\Omega(\rho_{\mathrm{tor}})} d^3x\right)
$$

where $V$ is the volume enclosed by the flux surface, $\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}$
is the dimensionful toroidal flux coordinate labeling that surface,
$\Omega(\rho_{\mathrm{tor}})$ is the region inside it, and $\mathbf{x}$ is
the spatial position whose volume element is $d^3x$.

This quantity applies to each nested magnetic flux surface, with the
enclosed volume accumulated from the magnetic axis outward and
differentiated locally with respect to the toroidal-flux-coordinate label.
It is a purely geometric scalar with no species, field-component, or process
aggregation; it is neither the enclosed volume itself nor a flux-surface
average.

It is the derivative of the [volume enclosed by a flux
surface](name:volume_of_flux_surface). It differs from the [derivative with
respect to toroidal flux coordinate of flux-surface
area](name:derivative_with_respect_to_toroidal_flux_coordinate_of_area_of_flux_surface),
which differentiates enclosed cross-sectional area, and from the [toroidal
flux coordinate gradient
magnitude](name:toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude), which
describes spatial variation of the coordinate rather than volume
accumulation.

NAMES.name: volume_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short:
Volume enclosed by the plasma boundary, representing the total
confined-plasma region inside the last closed magnetic flux surface.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the geometric volume of the confined plasma enclosed by the
plasma boundary, identified with the last closed magnetic flux surface. It
represents the full enclosed region rather than a local flux-surface shell
or material volume.

The volume is defined by

$$
V = \int_{\Omega_{\mathrm{plasma}}} d^3\mathbf{x}
$$

where $V$ is the enclosed plasma volume, $\Omega_{\mathrm{plasma}}$ is the
spatial domain inside the plasma boundary, and $d^3\mathbf{x}$ is the
differential volume element at position $\mathbf{x}$.

The integration domain is the entire confined-plasma region bounded by the
last closed magnetic flux surface, and the result is the total volume
aggregated over that domain. It excludes regions outside the plasma boundary
and volumes belonging to material structures or other non-confined regions.

This quantity is the terminal enclosed value of [volume of a flux
surface](name:volume_of_flux_surface) when the flux surface coincides with
the plasma boundary. It provides the integration domain for volume-averaged
quantities such as [volume-averaged ion
temperature](name:volume_averaged_ion_temperature).

NAMES.name: flux_surface_averaged_current_density_due_to_wave_driven_current_drive
NAMES.short:
Vector average on a magnetic flux surface of conventional plasma current
density generated non-inductively by electromagnetic-wave–particle
interactions, excluding inductive and non-wave current drive.
NAMES.long:
Flux-surface-averaged wave-driven current density is the vector average, on
a magnetic flux surface, of the conventional plasma current density
generated non-inductively by electromagnetic-wave–particle interactions. It
retains the vector character of the local current-density contribution while
averaging its resolved components over the surface.

The flux-surface average is defined componentwise by

$$
\left\langle \mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{wd}} \right\rangle_{\psi}
=
\frac{\displaystyle\int_{S_{\psi}} \mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{wd}}\,\frac{dS}{\lvert\nabla\psi\rvert}}
{\displaystyle\int_{S_{\psi}}\frac{dS}{\lvert\nabla\psi\rvert}}
$$

where $\mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{wd}}$ is the local conventional current-density
vector generated by wave–particle interactions, $\psi$ is the scalar
magnetic-flux label, $S_{\psi}$ is the corresponding magnetic flux surface,
$dS$ is its surface-area element, and $\nabla\psi$ is the spatial gradient
of the flux label.

The quantity applies to the plasma current on one magnetic flux surface and
includes the wave-driven contributions of the charged-particle populations
represented in the conventional current. Its aggregation convention is a
complete flux-surface average, not a local value, volume average, toroidal
current integral, or Fourier-mode-resolved contribution.

It excludes inductive current density and current contributions generated by
bootstrap, ohmic, or other non-wave current-drive mechanisms. No
field-aligned or other directional projection is imposed at this parent
level.

This quantity is obtained by applying flux-surface averaging to the local
[wave-driven current
density](name:current_density_due_to_wave_driven_current_drive). The
[parallel flux-surface-averaged wave-driven current
density](name:parallel_flux_surface_averaged_current_density_due_to_wave_driven_current_drive)
is a specialization that retains only the component projected along the
magnetic-field direction before or within the averaging operation.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when a resolved current-density component points
in the corresponding positive direction of the right-handed cylindrical
$(R,\phi,Z)$ basis, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and
$Z$ is vertical height, consistent with conventional positive-charge
transport.

NAMES.name: parallel_flux_surface_averaged_current_density_due_to_wave_driven_current_drive
NAMES.short:
Flux-surface-averaged field-aligned conventional plasma current density
generated non-inductively by electromagnetic-wave–particle interactions.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the scalar field-aligned component of the conventional
plasma current generated by electromagnetic-wave–particle interactions. It
represents the wave-driven contribution to current flowing along the
magnetic field on a magnetic flux surface.

For a magnetic flux surface labeled by the poloidal flux coordinate $\psi$,
the flux-surface-averaged parallel current density is defined by

$$
j_{\parallel,\mathrm{FSA}}(\psi) = \frac{\left\langle \mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{wave}} \cdot \mathbf{B} \right\rangle_{\psi}}{B_0(\psi)}
$$

where $j_{\parallel,\mathrm{FSA}}$ is this scalar current-density quantity,
$\mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{wave}}$ is the conventional current-density
contribution generated by wave–particle interactions, $\mathbf{B}$ is the
magnetic-field vector, $\langle\cdot\rangle_{\psi}$ denotes averaging over
the flux surface labeled by $\psi$, and $B_0(\psi)$ is the reference
magnetic-field magnitude used for the parallel-current normalization.

The quantity applies to the wave-driven current contribution from the plasma
populations participating in the electromagnetic-wave interaction and uses a
flux-surface average rather than a local value. It excludes inductive
current and current contributions from non-wave mechanisms, and it is
distinct from the full vector [flux-surface-averaged wave-driven current
density](name:flux_surface_averaged_current_density_due_to_wave_driven_current_drive).

It is the magnetic-field-aligned scalar projection of that vector parent,
retaining only the component parallel to the local magnetic field; [parallel
current density due to ohmic current
drive](name:parallel_current_density_due_to_ohmic_current_drive) instead
represents the inductive resistive contribution.

NAMES.name: flux_surface_averaged_magnetic_field_magnitude
NAMES.short:
Flux-surface average of the local magnetic-field strength, retaining the
pointwise modulus before averaging over each magnetic surface.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the flux-surface average of the magnitude of the total
equilibrium magnetic-field vector. It represents the mean field strength on
a magnetic surface, rather than a component or a vector average.

The flux-surface average is defined by

$$
\left\langle \lvert\mathbf{B}\rvert \right\rangle_{\psi} = \frac{\oint_{\psi} \lvert\mathbf{B}\rvert\,\mathrm{d}S/\lvert\nabla\psi\rvert}{\oint_{\psi} \mathrm{d}S/\lvert\nabla\psi\rvert}
$$

where $\mathbf{B}$ is the total equilibrium magnetic-field vector, $\psi$ is
the scalar label of the magnetic flux surface, $\mathrm{d}S$ is the
surface-area element, and $\nabla\psi$ is the spatial gradient of that
surface label. The aggregation is the normalized surface integral with
weighting $\mathrm{d}S/\lvert\nabla\psi\rvert$.

The quantity applies to all components of the equilibrium field on the
selected magnetic flux surface and is non-negative. It excludes any signed
field component, any species or source decomposition, and the magnitude of a
vector obtained by averaging $\mathbf{B}$ before taking its modulus.

It is the flux-surface-averaged transformation of [magnetic-field
magnitude]. It differs from [flux-surface-averaged square of magnetic-field
magnitude](name:flux_surface_averaged_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude),
which averages the squared field strength rather than the field strength
itself.

sources.leaf_definition: Flux surface averaged modulus of B (always positive, irrespective of the sign convention for the B-field direction).
sources.parent_definition: Equilibrium profiles (1D radial grid) as a function of the poloidal flux

NAMES.name: minimum_over_flux_surface_magnetic_field_magnitude
NAMES.short:
Smallest total magnetic-field strength attained along a specified nested
magnetic flux surface, using the field magnitude rather than a signed
component.
NAMES.long:
The minimum magnetic-field magnitude is the smallest total field strength
attained anywhere on a specified nested magnetic flux surface. It is
sign-invariant because it uses the modulus of the magnetic-field vector
rather than a signed component.

For a surface labeled by the magnetic-flux coordinate $\psi$, the quantity
is defined by

$$
B_{\min}(\psi) = \min_{\mathbf{x} \in S(\psi)} \left|\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{x})\right|
$$

where $B_{\min}(\psi)$ is the minimum magnetic-field magnitude, $\mathbf{x}$
is a position on the surface, $S(\psi)$ is the set of positions belonging to
the flux surface labeled by $\psi$, and $\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{x})$ is the
total magnetic-field vector at that position.

The minimum is taken over all positions on each nested magnetic flux surface
and includes the complete equilibrium field, including its poloidal and
toroidal contributions. It is not a signed component minimum, a flux-surface
average, or a minimum taken across multiple flux surfaces.

Unlike the [flux-surface-averaged inverse square of magnetic-field
magnitude](name:flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude),
this quantity reduces the field magnitude itself by a pointwise minimum
rather than averaging its reciprocal square.

sources.leaf_definition: Minimum(modulus(B)) on the flux surface (always positive, irrespective of the sign convention for the B-field direction)

NAMES.name: minimum_safety_factor
NAMES.short:
Signed safety-factor value on the closed magnetic flux surface where the
magnitude of field-line winding is smallest, distinct from that surface’s
location.
NAMES.long:
The minimum safety factor is the signed field-line winding number evaluated
on the nested closed magnetic flux surface where the magnitude of the safety
factor is smallest. It represents the extremal value of the safety-factor
function within the confined closed-surface domain.

The minimizing value is defined by

$$
q_{\min} = q(\rho_\ast), \qquad \rho_\ast \in \operatorname*{arg\,min}_{0 \leq \rho \leq 1} |q(\rho)|
$$

where $q(\rho)$ is the signed [safety factor](name:safety_factor) on the
flux surface labeled by $\rho$, $\rho_\ast$ is the label of a surface at
which the magnitude $|q(\rho)|$ is minimized, and $q_{\min}$ is the signed
value evaluated there. The label $\rho$ is a monotonic flux-surface
coordinate whose endpoints denote the magnetic axis and the last closed flux
surface. In flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, $\theta$ is the poloidal
angle and $\phi$ is the toroidal angle of the right-handed cylindrical
$(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height.

The extremum is taken over all nested closed magnetic flux surfaces and is
neither a flux-surface average nor a sum. The location-defining quantity is
separate: [poloidal magnetic flux at minimum safety
factor](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_minimum_safety_factor) identifies the
corresponding surface, while this quantity reports only the signed safety
factor. It is also distinct from a safety factor evaluated at a prescribed
locus, such as the magnetic axis.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the toroidal angle advance of a magnetic
field line is in the direction of increasing $\phi$ as the poloidal angle
$\theta$ increases.

sources.leaf_definition: Minimum q value
sources.parent_definition: Minimum q value and position

NAMES.name: normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short:
Radial flux-surface location of the selected plasma boundary, expressed by
the normalized poloidal flux coordinate. It is the linear normalized
poloidal flux value, increasing from zero at the magnetic axis to one at the
separatrix, of the closed flux surface taken as the plasma boundary;
fixed-boundary equilibrium calculations commonly set it slightly below one
to select a surface just inside the separatrix.
NAMES.long:
The normalized poloidal flux coordinate of the plasma boundary is the value
of the [normalized poloidal flux
coordinate](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate) on the closed flux
surface selected as the plasma boundary. It is the linear normalized
poloidal flux, labeling the boundary's radial position between the magnetic
axis and the last closed flux surface.

Its value is the poloidal flux difference from the magnetic axis normalized
to the axis-to-separatrix flux difference:

$$
\psi_{\mathrm{N}}^{\mathrm{boundary}} = \frac{\psi_{\mathrm{boundary}} - \psi_{\mathrm{axis}}}{\psi_{\mathrm{sep}} - \psi_{\mathrm{axis}}}
$$

where $\psi_{\mathrm{boundary}}$ is the [poloidal magnetic
flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux) on the selected plasma-boundary surface,
$\psi_{\mathrm{axis}}$ is the [poloidal magnetic flux at the magnetic
axis](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis), and
$\psi_{\mathrm{sep}}$ is the poloidal magnetic flux at the separatrix (last
closed flux surface).

The label equals zero at the magnetic axis and equals one when the selected
plasma boundary coincides with the separatrix; a value below one selects an
internal closed flux surface. Its defining role is to specify, for
fixed-boundary equilibrium representations, which closed flux surface is
taken as the plasma boundary, commonly a surface just inside the separatrix
so that the boundary remains strictly closed.

This is the linear normalized poloidal flux value itself, not its square
root, and it is a flux-surface label rather than a signed poloidal-flux
value or a geometric minor-radius measure. It is distinct from the
toroidal-flux-based boundary label [normalized toroidal flux coordinate at
the plasma
boundary](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_plasma_boundary), and
it belongs to the same locus-valued family as the [normalized poloidal flux
coordinate at minimum safety
factor](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_at_minimum_safety_factor)
and the [normalized poloidal flux coordinate of the
pedestal](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_of_pedestal).

sources.parent_definition: Description of the plasma boundary. The boundary can be either the real separatrix (provided by a free boundary equilibrium solver) or the 0.99x psi_norm flux surface provided by a fixed boundary equilibrium

NAMES.name: safety_factor_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.short:
Limiting signed field-line winding number on the innermost closed flux
surface, giving toroidal turns per poloidal circuit at the magnetic axis.
NAMES.long:
The safety factor at the magnetic axis is the limiting signed field-line
winding number as nested closed magnetic flux surfaces contract toward the
magnetic axis. It gives the toroidal transits per complete poloidal circuit
in that limit.

The axis value is defined by

$$
q_{\rm axis} = \lim_{\psi \to \psi_{\rm axis}} q(\psi)
$$

where $q_{\rm axis}$ is the safety factor at the magnetic axis, $q(\psi)$ is
the safety factor on the flux surface labeled by $\psi$, and $\psi_{\rm
axis}$ is the value of that flux-surface label at the magnetic axis.

This quantity applies only to the magnetic-axis limit of nested closed flux
surfaces in an equilibrium. It is a single equilibrium winding value with no
species, population, or charge-state aggregation, and it is distinct from
safety factor values on finite-radius surfaces such as the [safety factor at
the plasma boundary](name:safety_factor_at_plasma_boundary).

It is the magnetic-axis specialization of the [safety
factor](name:safety_factor): the parent quantity describes field-line
winding as a function of flux-surface label, while this quantity selects its
limiting value at $\psi_{\rm axis}$. The parent relation is the signed
flux-increment ratio $q = d\Phi_{\rm tor}/(d\Phi_{\rm pol}/2\pi)$, where
$\Phi_{\rm tor}$ is toroidal magnetic flux and $\Phi_{\rm pol}$ is poloidal
magnetic flux.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the toroidal magnetic-flux increment
$d\Phi_{\rm tor}$ and poloidal magnetic-flux increment $d\Phi_{\rm pol}$
have the same sign for the positively oriented field-line circuit, with
$\phi$ increasing in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where
$R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

sources.parent_definition: Safety factor (only positive when toroidal current and magnetic field are in same direction)

NAMES.name: safety_factor_at_normalized_poloidal_magnetic_flux_equal_to_0_95
NAMES.short:
Signed field-line winding number on the closed magnetic flux surface labeled
by normalized poloidal magnetic flux 0.95, near but inside the plasma
boundary.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the signed field-line winding number on the closed magnetic
flux surface labeled by normalized poloidal magnetic flux 0.95. It gives the
toroidal transits per complete poloidal circuit on that specific surface.

The locus-specific evaluation is

$$
q_{95}=q(\psi_N=0.95)
$$

where $q_{95}$ is the safety factor at the specified locus, $q$ is the
[safety factor](name:safety_factor), and $\psi_N$ is the normalized poloidal
magnetic-flux coordinate. The value 0.95 selects the surface at 95% of the
normalized poloidal-flux interval, with the magnetic axis and plasma
boundary serving as the inner and outer reference surfaces.

The quantity applies only to that single closed flux surface. It is a scalar
flux-surface value, with no summation, integration, or averaging over
neighboring surfaces. It is distinct from the [safety factor at the magnetic
axis](name:safety_factor_at_magnetic_axis) and the [safety factor at the
plasma boundary](name:safety_factor_at_plasma_boundary), which use different
evaluation loci.

Thus, this quantity is the normalized-poloidal-flux-locus specialization of
the parent [safety factor](name:safety_factor); the field-line winding
definition is unchanged, and only the evaluation surface differs. The
right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame has $R$ as major radius, $\phi$
as toroidal angle, and $Z$ as vertical height.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the signed toroidal and poloidal
magnetic-flux increments defining the field-line winding ratio have the same
sign in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: safety_factor_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short:
Signed field-line winding ratio evaluated on the outermost closed magnetic
flux surface, counting toroidal turns per poloidal circuit at the plasma
boundary.
NAMES.long:
The boundary safety factor is the signed helical winding of magnetic field
lines on the outermost closed magnetic flux surface, counting toroidal turns
per poloidal circuit at the plasma boundary.

It is defined by the differential ratio of toroidal to poloidal magnetic
flux:

$$
q_{\mathrm{b}} = \left.\frac{d\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}}{d\Phi_{\mathrm{pol}}}\right|_{\mathrm{b}}
$$

where $q_{\mathrm{b}}$ is the safety factor at the boundary,
$\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is toroidal magnetic flux, $\Phi_{\mathrm{pol}}$ is
poloidal magnetic flux, and the subscript $\mathrm{b}$ denotes evaluation on
the plasma-boundary flux surface.

The quantity applies to the single outermost closed flux surface defining
the plasma boundary. It is a flux-surface value, not a volume average,
region integral, or value at an interior normalized-flux surface; in
particular, it is distinct from the safety factor at normalized poloidal
magnetic flux 0.95, commonly represented by [safety factor at normalized
poloidal magnetic flux equal to
0.95](name:safety_factor_at_normalized_poloidal_magnetic_flux_equal_to_0_95).

This quantity is the boundary-specific instance of the general [safety
factor](name:safety_factor), obtained by evaluating the same flux-increment
relation on the plasma-boundary surface.

NAMES.name: energy_confinement_enhancement_factor
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless ratio comparing the plasma energy confinement time with the
IPB98(y,2) reference scaling prediction.
NAMES.long:
The energy confinement enhancement factor is the multiplicative departure of
a plasma’s global energy confinement time from the IPB98(y,2) reference
scaling prediction. It indicates whether energy is retained longer or
shorter than the reference predicts for the corresponding scaling inputs.

The factor is defined by:

$$
h_{98} = \frac{\tau_E}{\tau_{E,\mathrm{IPB98(y,2)}}}
$$

where $h_{98}$ is the energy confinement enhancement factor, $\tau_E$ is the
plasma energy confinement time, and $\tau_{E,\mathrm{IPB98(y,2)}}$ is the
energy confinement time predicted by the IPB98(y,2) reference scaling.

This is a global plasma quantity: the numerator represents the confinement
of the total stored plasma energy relative to the corresponding net
energy-loss power, aggregated over the plasma rather than assigned to a
local region or individual transport channel. It is not itself an energy
confinement time, stored energy, power, or local transport coefficient.

A value of one denotes agreement with the reference scaling; a value greater
than one denotes longer confinement, and a value less than one denotes
shorter confinement than the reference prediction.

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Energy confinement time enhancement factor over the IPB98(y,2) scaling

NAMES.name: ipb98y2_confinement_time
NAMES.short:
IPB98(y,2) empirical-scaling reference for global energy confinement time,
providing the denominator for the H98 confinement enhancement factor.
NAMES.long:
The IPB98(y,2) energy confinement time is the global energy-confinement
timescale predicted by the IPB98(y,2) empirical scaling law. It is an
energy-channel performance benchmark rather than a species-resolved or local
transport time.

The underlying global energy confinement time is defined by

$$
\tau_E = \frac{W}{P_{\mathrm{loss}}}
$$

where $\tau_E$ is the global energy confinement time, $W$ is the total
thermal energy stored in the plasma, and $P_{\mathrm{loss}}$ is the net
power leaving the plasma. The quantity documented here is the IPB98(y,2)
scaling prediction of this timescale, not the directly evaluated confinement
time for a particular plasma state.

The value applies to the complete plasma energy content and its global loss
balance; it is not a local profile quantity, a particle confinement time, or
a confinement time assigned to an individual species. It is a single
empirical reference value for the energy channel.

The [energy confinement enhancement
factor](name:energy_confinement_enhancement_factor) compares the actual
global energy confinement time with this reference through $H_{98} = \tau_E
/ \tau_{E,98}$, where $H_{98}$ is the dimensionless confinement enhancement
factor and $\tau_{E,98}$ is this IPB98(y,2) scaling prediction.

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Energy confinement time estimated from the IPB98(y,2) scaling

NAMES.name: krypton_density_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.subject: krypton
NAMES.short:
Number density of krypton ions at the plasma boundary, evaluated as the
local, intensive particle count per physical volume on the last closed
magnetic flux surface.
NAMES.long:
Number density of krypton ions at the plasma boundary is the local,
intensive particle count per physical volume for the krypton-ion population
evaluated on the last closed magnetic flux surface. The plasma boundary is
the limiting closed magnetic flux surface separating confined plasma from
the open-field-line scrape-off-layer region.

The local krypton ion number density is the sum of the zeroth velocity
moments over all krypton ionization states at a boundary point:

$$
n_{\mathrm{Kr}}(\mathbf{x}_b,t) = \sum_{q \in \mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{Kr}}} \int f_{\mathrm{Kr}^{q+}}(\mathbf{x}_b,\mathbf{v},t)\,d^3v
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{Kr}}$ is the krypton ion number density, $\mathbf{x}_b$ is
a point on the last closed magnetic flux surface, $t$ is time, $q$ is the
krypton ionization-state index, $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{Kr}}$ is the set of
all positively charged krypton ionization states, $f_{\mathrm{Kr}^{q+}}$ is
the phase-space distribution function for state $q$, $\mathbf{v}$ is
particle velocity, and $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element.

This quantity applies specifically to krypton ions and is summed over all
included ionization states. It excludes neutral krypton and all other ion
species, and it is a local boundary value with no averaging over the
boundary surface or over a volume.

It is the krypton-specific instance of [density at the plasma
boundary](name:density_at_plasma_boundary). The related [krypton
density](name:krypton_density) represents the same charge-state-summed ion
population at a general plasma location, whereas [flux-surface-averaged
krypton density at the plasma
boundary](name:flux_surface_averaged_krypton_density_at_plasma_boundary)
averages the krypton density over the complete last closed magnetic flux
surface rather than evaluating it locally.

NAMES.name: magnetic_field_at_pedestal_top_low_field_side
NAMES.short:
Magnetic field at the pedestal top on the low-field side is the scalar
magnetic-field quantity evaluated at the core-side end of the pressure
pedestal on the larger-major-radius side in the right-handed cylindrical (R,
φ, Z) frame. It fixes that locus; more specific names supply the scalar
reduction, such as magnitude.
NAMES.long:
Magnetic field at the pedestal top on the low-field side is the scalar
magnetic-field quantity associated with local magnetic induction evaluated
at the core-side end of the pressure pedestal on the low-field side. The
low-field side is the larger-major-radius side in the right-handed
cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is
toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

This quantity fixes the pressure-pedestal-top, low-field-side evaluation
locus and applies locally there with no flux-surface, volume, or spatial
averaging implied. It is not a magnetic-axis value, plasma-boundary value,
high-field-side value, or generic locus-independent magnetic field.

At parent scope it does not define the full vector [magnetic
field](name:magnetic_field), a signed cylindrical component, a projection,
or a source-specific contribution. Those narrower meanings require an
explicit more specific standard name.

A representative specialization is the [magnetic-field magnitude at the
pedestal top on the low-field
side](name:magnetic_field_at_pedestal_top_low_field_side_magnitude), which
applies the Euclidean norm to the local magnetic-induction vector at the
same pedestal-top low-field-side locus. Thus the locus is fixed by this
parent quantity, while the magnitude operation is supplied by the child
quantity.

NAMES.name: normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless magnetic-surface coordinate locating the internal transport
barrier between the magnetic axis and the last closed flux surface.
NAMES.long:
The normalized toroidal flux coordinate at the internal transport barrier is
the dimensionless magnetic-surface label assigned to the flux surface
containing the barrier. It locates that surface within the nested
closed-flux region rather than giving a cylindrical distance or vector
component.

The coordinate is defined by

$$
\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}(\mathrm{ITB}) = \left[\frac{\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}(\mathrm{ITB}) - \Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}}}{\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,LCFS}} - \Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}}}\right]^{1/2}
$$

where $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}(\mathrm{ITB})$ is the normalized toroidal
flux coordinate at the internal transport barrier,
$\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}(\mathrm{ITB})$ is the toroidal magnetic flux enclosed
by the flux surface containing the barrier, $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}}$ is
its value at the magnetic axis, and $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,LCFS}}$ is its value
at the last closed flux surface. The nonnegative square-root branch is used.

The value applies specifically to the flux surface assigned to the internal
transport barrier and is bounded from zero at the magnetic axis to unity at
the last closed flux surface for nested surfaces with monotonic toroidal
flux. It has no species, charge-state, or spatial averaging; it is a scalar
surface label.

This quantity is the internal-transport-barrier specialization of the
[normalized toroidal flux
coordinate](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate). Unlike the [toroidal
flux coordinate at the internal transport
barrier](name:toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_internal_transport_barrier), it
uses axis-to-last-closed-flux-surface normalization and is therefore
dimensionless.

sources.leaf_definition: Normalized toroidal flux coordinate. The normalizing value for rho_tor_norm, is the toroidal flux coordinate at the equilibrium boundary (LCFS or 99.x % of the LCFS in case of a fixed boundary equilibium calculation, see time_slice/boundary/b_flux_pol_norm in the equilibrium IDS)
sources.parent_definition: Radial position at which physics quantities are evaluated

NAMES.name: normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_pedestal_top
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless toroidal-flux label locating the top of the H-mode edge
pedestal on a nested magnetic surface relative to the magnetic axis and last
closed flux surface.
NAMES.long:
The normalized toroidal flux coordinate evaluated at the pedestal top is the
dimensionless magnetic-surface label assigned to the top of the H-mode edge
pedestal. It locates that position within the nested closed-flux-surface
family, rather than representing a cylindrical distance or a local vector
component.

For a nested equilibrium, the coordinate is defined by

$$
\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}(\mathrm{ped}) = \left[\frac{\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}(\mathrm{ped}) - \Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}(\mathrm{axis})}{\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}(\mathrm{LCFS}) - \Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}(\mathrm{axis})}\right]^{1/2}
$$

where $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}(\mathrm{ped})$ is the normalized toroidal
flux coordinate at the pedestal top, $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the toroidal
magnetic flux enclosed by a magnetic surface, $\mathrm{ped}$ denotes the
pedestal-top position, $\mathrm{axis}$ denotes the magnetic axis, and
$\mathrm{LCFS}$ denotes the last closed flux surface.

The value applies specifically at the top of the H-mode edge pedestal, the
inner shoulder of the edge transport barrier. Its position is defined by the
[normalized poloidal flux coordinate of the
pedestal](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_of_pedestal). This is a
single coordinate evaluation: no species, charge-state, or population
aggregation applies, and no surface averaging is implied. It is distinct
from a cylindrical radial distance and from the unnormalized [toroidal flux
coordinate at the pedestal
top](name:toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_pedestal_top).

This entry is the pedestal-top specialization of the [normalized toroidal
flux coordinate](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate), with the same
axis-to-boundary normalization. It should not be interpreted as the
corresponding [normalized poloidal flux
coordinate](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate), which labels surfaces
using poloidal rather than toroidal magnetic flux.

sources.leaf_definition: Normalized toroidal flux coordinate. The normalizing value for rho_tor_norm, is the toroidal flux coordinate at the equilibrium boundary (LCFS or 99.x % of the LCFS in case of a fixed boundary equilibium calculation, see time_slice/boundary/b_flux_pol_norm in the equilibrium IDS)
sources.parent_definition: Radial position at which physics quantities are evaluated

NAMES.name: normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless toroidal-flux surface label evaluated on the last closed
magnetic surface, serving as the outer reference for the normalized flux
coordinate.
NAMES.long:
The normalized toroidal flux coordinate at the plasma boundary is the
magnetic-surface label assigned to the last closed flux surface, also called
the separatrix. It identifies the outer boundary of the nested
closed-flux-surface region and is not a cylindrical distance or local vector
component.

The boundary value is defined by

$$
\left.\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}\right|_{\mathrm{plasma\ boundary}} = 1
$$

where $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ is the normalized toroidal flux coordinate
and the plasma boundary is the last closed magnetic flux surface.

This quantity is evaluated at the boundary itself, rather than averaged over
the boundary or assigned to an arbitrary spatial point. It is the boundary
specialization of the parent [normalized toroidal flux
coordinate](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate), whose value increases
outward from the magnetic axis; the corresponding unnormalized quantity is
the [toroidal flux coordinate at the plasma
boundary](name:toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_plasma_boundary).

sources.leaf_definition: Normalized toroidal flux coordinate. The normalizing value for rho_tor_norm, is the toroidal flux coordinate at the equilibrium boundary (LCFS or 99.x % of the LCFS in case of a fixed boundary equilibium calculation, see time_slice/boundary/b_flux_pol_norm in the equilibrium IDS)
sources.parent_definition: Radial position at which physics quantities are evaluated

NAMES.name: oxygen_density_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.subject: oxygen
NAMES.short:
Number density of oxygen ions at the plasma boundary, evaluated as the
local, intensive particle count per physical volume on the last closed
magnetic flux surface and summed over all charged oxygen ionization states.
NAMES.long:
Number density of oxygen ions at the plasma boundary is the local, intensive
particle count per physical volume for the oxygen-ion population evaluated
on the last closed magnetic flux surface. The plasma boundary is the
limiting closed magnetic flux surface separating confined plasma from the
open-field-line scrape-off-layer region.

The local charge-state-summed oxygen ion density at a boundary point is the
zeroth velocity moment of the oxygen-ion distribution functions:

$$
n_{\mathrm{O}}(\mathbf{x}_b,t)=\sum_{z=1}^{8}\int f_{\mathrm{O}^{z+}}(\mathbf{x}_b,\mathbf{v},t)\,d^3v
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{O}}$ is the oxygen-ion number density, $\mathbf{x}_b$ is a
point on the last closed magnetic flux surface, $t$ is time, $z$ is the
positive oxygen ionization state, $f_{\mathrm{O}^{z+}}$ is the phase-space
distribution function for that state, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity, and
$d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element.

This quantity applies specifically to oxygen ions and sums the populations
from singly ionized through fully stripped oxygen. It excludes neutral
oxygen and other ion species, and it is a local boundary value with no
averaging over the boundary surface or over a volume.

It is the oxygen-specific instance of [density at the plasma
boundary](name:density_at_plasma_boundary). The [flux-surface-averaged
oxygen density at the plasma
boundary](name:flux_surface_averaged_oxygen_density_at_plasma_boundary)
represents the same charge-state-summed oxygen-ion content averaged over the
last closed magnetic flux surface rather than evaluated locally.
