NAMES.name: perturbed_plasma_pressure
NAMES.short:
Perturbed plasma pressure is the Eulerian first-order variation of the
isotropic kinetic pressure of the plasma about an equilibrium, represented
as a complex normal-mode eigenfunction in linear magnetohydrodynamic
stability. For a specified toroidal Fourier mode, its real and imaginary
parts reconstruct the physical pressure disturbance.
NAMES.long:
Perturbed plasma pressure is the Eulerian first-order variation of the
isotropic kinetic pressure of the plasma in a linear fluid or
magnetohydrodynamic description. It represents the complex normal-mode
amplitude of the pressure disturbance about an equilibrium [plasma
pressure](name:plasma_pressure) and is not an equilibrium scalar pressure.

For a single toroidal Fourier mode, the real physical pressure disturbance
is reconstructed from the complex eigenfunction in the right-handed
cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame as:

$$
\delta p_{\mathrm{phys}}(R,\phi,Z,t) = \operatorname{Re}\left[\tilde{p}_n(R,Z)\exp\left(i(n\phi-\omega t)\right)\right]
$$

where $\delta p_{\mathrm{phys}}$ is the real physical pressure perturbation,
$\tilde{p}_n$ is the complex pressure-perturbation eigenfunction, $n$ is the
toroidal mode number, $(R,\phi,Z)$ are coordinates in the right-handed
cylindrical frame with $R$ major radius, $\phi$ toroidal angle, and $Z$
vertical height, $t$ is time, $\omega$ is the mode angular frequency, $i$ is
the imaginary unit, and $\operatorname{Re}$ denotes the real-part operation.

The quantity applies to one specified linear eigenmode and one specified
toroidal mode number. It is defined in the plasma region where the
equilibrium pressure and displacement perturbation are defined; its
population scope is the same set of plasma populations included in the
underlying equilibrium [plasma pressure](name:plasma_pressure) model, and
perturbations are additive over included population contributions. No
aggregation over toroidal mode numbers, independent eigenmodes, or Fourier
harmonics is implied.

It excludes equilibrium scalar pressure quantities such as [total plasma
pressure](name:total_plasma_pressure) and [thermal plasma
pressure](name:thermal_plasma_pressure), magnetic pressure, dynamic ram
pressure, anisotropic pressure-tensor components, any individual component
of the pressure tensor, and the Lagrangian pressure perturbation following a
displaced fluid element. It also excludes a real physical pressure
disturbance formed by superposing several toroidal modes.

[Perturbed plasma pressure real
part](name:perturbed_plasma_pressure_real_part) is
$\operatorname{Re}(\tilde{p}_n)$ and [perturbed plasma pressure imaginary
part](name:perturbed_plasma_pressure_imaginary_part) is
$\operatorname{Im}(\tilde{p}_n)$, where $\operatorname{Im}$ denotes the
imaginary-part operation; together they uniquely specify $\tilde{p}_n$ under
the chosen phase convention. The normal-mode phase convention is the one
shown in the reconstruction relation, and the complex eigenfunction has
arbitrary overall normalization and global phase: multiplying all
perturbation eigenfunctions for the same mode by a common nonzero complex
constant leaves the normalized mode identity unchanged unless an amplitude
normalization is separately defined. For adiabatic ideal magnetohydrodynamic
perturbations, the eigenfunction satisfies the linear pressure relation
$\tilde{p}_n=-\boldsymbol{\xi}_n\cdot\nabla p_0-\Gamma
p_0\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol{\xi}_n$, where $\boldsymbol{\xi}_n$ is the
plasma-displacement eigenfunction for the same mode, $p_0$ is the
equilibrium [plasma pressure](name:plasma_pressure), $\nabla p_0$ is its
spatial gradient, $\Gamma$ is the adiabatic index, and
$\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol{\xi}_n$ is the displacement divergence. It is the
pressure counterpart of [perturbed plasma mass
density](name:perturbed_plasma_mass_density) in the same toroidal
normal-mode representation.

NAMES.name: perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field
NAMES.short:
The perturbed vacuum magnetic field is the complex first-order vector
eigenfunction of the magnetic-field perturbation for a single toroidal
harmonic in the current-free vacuum region surrounding the plasma. It is
defined relative to the background vacuum magnetic field and excludes the
equilibrium field while retaining all spatial components.
NAMES.long:
The perturbed vacuum magnetic field $\tilde{\delta\mathbf{B}}_\mathrm{vac}$
is the complex first-order vector eigenfunction of the magnetic-field
perturbation for a single toroidal harmonic in the current-free exterior
domain surrounding the plasma. It is defined relative to the background
[vacuum magnetic field](name:vacuum_magnetic_field), retains all spatial
components, and excludes the equilibrium field itself.

For this single-toroidal-mode quantity, the real time-dependent perturbation
is reconstructed from the complex amplitude by

$$
\delta\mathbf{B}_\mathrm{vac}(R,\phi,Z,t) = \operatorname{Re}\!\left[\tilde{\delta\mathbf{B}}_\mathrm{vac}(R,Z)\exp\!\left(i n\phi - i\omega t\right)\right]
$$

where $\delta\mathbf{B}_\mathrm{vac}$ is the real magnetic-field
perturbation, $\tilde{\delta\mathbf{B}}_\mathrm{vac}$ is the complex
eigenfunction defined here, $(R,\phi,Z)$ is the right-handed cylindrical
frame with $R$ major radius, $\phi$ the toroidal angle increasing
counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ vertical
height, $t$ is time, $\operatorname{Re}$ takes the real part, $i$ is the
imaginary unit, $n$ is the [toroidal MHD mode
number](name:toroidal_mhd_mode_number), and $\omega$ is the angular
eigenfrequency. The chosen temporal factor fixes the phase convention; using
the opposite temporal factor complex-conjugates the eigenfunction, and the
overall complex scale and phase are set only by an explicit normalization.

In the current-free vacuum domain, absence of free current and magnetic
monopoles requires
$\nabla\times\tilde{\delta\mathbf{B}}_\mathrm{vac}=\mathbf{0}$ and
$\nabla\cdot\tilde{\delta\mathbf{B}}_\mathrm{vac}=0$, where $\nabla$ is the
spatial derivative operator and $\mathbf{0}$ is the zero vector.
Equivalently, $\tilde{\delta\mathbf{B}}_\mathrm{vac}=-\nabla\delta\Phi$ with
$\nabla^2\delta\Phi=0$, where $\delta\Phi$ is the scalar magnetic potential
of the perturbation; this potential is defined up to an additive constant.
At the plasma-vacuum interface, the normal component of this vacuum
perturbation is the exterior counterpart of the plasma-side perturbed
magnetic field used for interface matching.

The scope is the current-free vacuum region outside the plasma and inside
the relevant conducting or far-field boundary; it does not include
current-carrying plasma regions or free-current regions in material
structures. The quantity is one complex vector for one toroidal mode number,
with no averaging over phase, space, or mode number and no summation over
multiple toroidal harmonics. It is distinct from scalar field strength, from
the unperturbed [vacuum magnetic field](name:vacuum_magnetic_field), and
from any real physical perturbation before the normal-mode reconstruction is
applied.

The vector decomposes in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame as
projections on $\hat{R}$, $\hat{\phi}$, and $\hat{Z}$; the
[radial](name:radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field) and
[toroidal](name:toroidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field) quantities are
component projections of the same complex eigenfunction. The [poloidal
projection](name:poloidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field) is defined
relative to the explicitly chosen flux-coordinate system $(s,\theta,\phi)$
for that component and is not the cylindrical $Z$ projection. The
decomposition
$\tilde{\delta\mathbf{B}}_\mathrm{vac}=\tilde{\delta\mathbf{B}}_{\mathrm{vac},\mathrm{Re}}+i\tilde{\delta\mathbf{B}}_{\mathrm{vac},\mathrm{Im}}$
separates real and imaginary phase quadratures; component quantities such as
the [radial real
part](name:radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_real_part), [radial
imaginary part](name:radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_imaginary_part),
and [poloidal real
part](name:poloidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_real_part) are
projections or quadratures of this parent vector.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when a real component projection of the
reconstructed perturbation points along its positive basis direction, with
$+\hat{R}$ increasing major radius, $+\hat{\phi}$ increasing toroidal angle
$\phi$, and $+\hat{Z}$ increasing vertical height in the right-handed
cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: plasma_magnetic_field
NAMES.short:
Plasma magnetic-field strength of the local magnetic induction associated
with the confined plasma, including equilibrium and plasma-interior
perturbed contributions while excluding the separate vacuum-field
definition.
NAMES.long:
The plasma magnetic field $B_{\rm plasma}$ is the scalar magnitude of the
local [magnetic induction](name:magnetic_field) associated with the confined
plasma. It represents field strength at a plasma location, including
equilibrium and plasma-interior perturbed contributions when present, rather
than retaining vector direction or selecting a signed component.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, its value may be written
from the components of the associated plasma magnetic-induction vector as

$$
B_{\rm plasma}=\left|\mathbf{B}_{\rm plasma}\right|=\sqrt{B_{R,{\rm plasma}}^2+B_{\phi,{\rm plasma}}^2+B_{Z,{\rm plasma}}^2}
$$

where $B_{\rm plasma}$ is the plasma magnetic-field strength,
$\mathbf{B}_{\rm plasma}$ is the local plasma magnetic-induction vector,
$B_{R,{\rm plasma}}$ is its signed component along increasing major radius
$R$, $B_{\phi,{\rm plasma}}$ is its signed component along increasing
toroidal angle $\phi$, and $B_{Z,{\rm plasma}}$ is its signed component
along increasing vertical height $Z$.

This quantity applies locally within the confined plasma region and has no
species population. Its aggregation convention is a point value of
magnetic-field strength, not a spatial average, flux-surface average, volume
integral, or finite-volume reduction.

This scalar magnitude is distinct from the vector [magnetic
induction](name:magnetic_field) and from component-resolved fields such as
the [toroidal magnetic field](name:toroidal_magnetic_field), [radial
magnetic field](name:radial_magnetic_field), and [vertical magnetic
field](name:vertical_magnetic_field), which retain directional sign. It is
also distinct from the [vacuum magnetic field](name:vacuum_magnetic_field),
which excludes plasma-current and plasma-interior contributions, and from
the [perturbed plasma magnetic field](name:perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field),
which denotes the perturbation contribution rather than the total local
plasma-associated field strength.

NAMES.name: plasma_pressure_imaginary_part
NAMES.short:
Plasma pressure imaginary part is the scalar coefficient multiplying the
imaginary unit in a complex representation of isotropic plasma pressure. It
is a phase-quadrature part of the pressure representation, not the complete
complex pressure quantity.
NAMES.long:
Plasma pressure imaginary part is the scalar coefficient multiplying the
imaginary unit in a complex representation of isotropic plasma pressure. It
represents the imaginary phase quadrature of that pressure representation
and is not the complete complex pressure quantity.

A complex plasma-pressure quantity is decomposed into real and imaginary
quadratures as:

$$
p = p_\mathrm{R} + i\,p_\mathrm{I}
$$

where $p$ is the complex plasma-pressure quantity, $i$ is the imaginary
unit, $p_\mathrm{R}$ is its real-part quadrature, and $p_\mathrm{I}$ is the
plasma pressure imaginary part defined here.

This parent quantity applies to any complex scalar representation of
isotropic plasma pressure. It does not by itself specify perturbation order,
Fourier mode number, reference phase, eigenfunction normalization, or
spatial dependence.

The perturbation-specific [perturbed plasma pressure imaginary
part](name:perturbed_plasma_pressure_imaginary_part) is a specialization of
this parent in which $p$ is restricted to the complex first-order
plasma-pressure perturbation eigenfunction. The quantity is distinct from
[plasma pressure](name:plasma_pressure), which denotes the pressure scalar
itself rather than the imaginary quadrature of a complex representation.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the pressure phasor projects onto the $+i$
direction of the complex plane.

NAMES.name: plasma_pressure_real_part
NAMES.short:
Plasma pressure real part is the real quadrature of a complex scalar
representation of isotropic plasma pressure. For perturbation
eigenfunctions, it is the signed real component of the pressure
perturbation, not the full complex eigenfunction.
NAMES.long:
Plasma pressure real part is the scalar real quadrature of a complex
representation of isotropic plasma pressure. It represents the component
obtained after the phase convention for the complex pressure quantity has
been fixed, and it is distinct from the complete complex quantity.

The real part is defined by applying the real-part operator to the
corresponding complex plasma-pressure quantity:

$$
p_R = \operatorname{Re}(\tilde{p})
$$

where $p_R$ is the plasma pressure real part, $\tilde{p}$ is the
corresponding complex scalar plasma-pressure quantity, and
$\operatorname{Re}$ denotes extraction of the real component.

This parent quantity is restricted to real-part quantities of isotropic
plasma pressure and does not by itself specify perturbation order,
Fourier-mode labeling, phase normalization, or spatial locus. It applies to
the plasma scalar pressure field; it is not a species-resolved pressure, a
pressure-tensor component, or an anisotropic-pressure component.

It excludes the imaginary quadrature, modulus, phase, and complete complex
pressure quantity. More specific children add the physics qualifier while
preserving the same real-part operation; for example, [perturbed plasma
pressure real part](name:perturbed_plasma_pressure_real_part) is the real
component of a complex first-order plasma-pressure perturbation
eigenfunction. If the corresponding complex quantity is written as
$\tilde{p}=p_R+i p_I$, then $p_I$ is its imaginary quadrature and $i$ is the
imaginary unit, while this name denotes only $p_R$.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the selected real quadrature denotes an
increase of isotropic plasma pressure relative to the reference pressure
state.

NAMES.name: toroidal_flux_coordinate_of_neoclassical_tearing_mode_center
NAMES.short:
Non-normalized toroidal-flux radius locating the magnetic surface and radial
position of a neoclassical tearing-mode island center.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the toroidal-flux coordinate of the magnetic surface
passing through the center of a neoclassical tearing-mode island. It
provides a radius-like magnetic-surface label for the island’s radial
location, rather than a geometric distance.

It is a non-negative, dimensional coordinate evaluated at the neoclassical
tearing-mode center. The value represents a single locus on the nested
magnetic surfaces; it is neither a surface average nor a volume average.

The quantity is the locus-specific instance of the parent [toroidal flux
coordinate](name:toroidal_flux_coordinate). Unlike the [normalized toroidal
flux coordinate at the neoclassical tearing-mode
center](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_of_neoclassical_tearing_mode_center),
it retains the dimensional toroidal-flux-radius scale rather than mapping
the location to a normalized interval.

NAMES.name: accumulated_deposited_energy_of_plasma_facing_component
NAMES.short:
Pulse-integrated heat deposited in a plasma-facing component, including heat
recovered during post-discharge cooling as the component returns toward
thermal equilibrium.
NAMES.long:
Accumulated deposited energy is the total heat energy transferred to a
plasma-facing component during a complete plasma discharge and its
post-discharge return toward thermal equilibrium. It represents a
component-level thermal load rather than the plasma's stored thermal energy.

The accumulated quantity is defined by integrating the deposition-associated
power over the full interval:

$$
E_{\mathrm{dep}} = \int_{t_{\mathrm{start}}}^{t_{\mathrm{end}}} P_{\mathrm{dep}}(t)\,\mathrm{d}t
$$

where $E_{\mathrm{dep}}$ is the accumulated deposited energy,
$P_{\mathrm{dep}}(t)$ is the power associated with heat deposited in the
component at time $t$, and $t_{\mathrm{start}}$ and $t_{\mathrm{end}}$
define an interval covering the discharge and subsequent thermal return.

The quantity applies to the complete plasma-facing component and aggregates
all deposited contributions into one total; it is not resolved by particle
species or population. The accumulation includes heat recovered after the
plasma pulse and excludes instantaneous power, local energy flux density,
and plasma stored energy.

A mechanism-specific rate such as [power due to
convection](name:power_due_to_convection) may contribute to the integral,
but it is not itself the accumulated component-level energy.

NAMES.name: coolant_mass_flow_rate
NAMES.short:
Coolant mass throughput across a fluid-flow boundary, representing the rate
at which coolant mass passes through a port or cooling loop.
NAMES.long:
Coolant mass flow rate is the rate of coolant mass crossing a reference
section of a fluid-flow path. It represents fluid throughput for cooling
loops and plant-component ports without selecting one particular physical
location.

The defining mass flow rate is

$$
\dot{m} = \frac{\mathrm{d}m}{\mathrm{d}t}
$$

where $\dot{m}$ is the coolant mass flow rate, $m$ is the coolant mass
crossing the reference section, and $t$ is time.

This quantity applies to the aggregate coolant stream and is not a
volumetric flow rate, coolant temperature, transit time, or thermal power.
The enthalpy transport associated with the flow is
$\dot{m}(h_{\mathrm{out}}-h_{\mathrm{in}})$, where $h_{\mathrm{out}}$ and
$h_{\mathrm{in}}$ are the specific enthalpies of the coolant at the outlet
and inlet; the [coolant temperature at
outlet](name:coolant_temperature_at_outlet) helps characterize the outlet
state. The [coolant transit time of a plant component
port](name:coolant_transit_time_of_plant_component_port) is a related
elapsed-time quantity, not part of the mass flow rate itself.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when coolant crosses the reference section in the
designated positive flow direction from inlet toward outlet.

NAMES.name: coolant_transit_time_of_plant_component_port
NAMES.short:
Elapsed time for coolant to traverse the associated plant component from
inlet to outlet, defining the thermal delay between the two coolant states.
NAMES.long:
Coolant transit time is the elapsed travel time for the coolant stream to
pass through the plant component associated with the specified port, from
its inlet to its outlet. It represents the transport delay between the inlet
and outlet thermal states.

The transit time is defined as

$$
\tau_{\mathrm{c}} = t_{\mathrm{out}} - t_{\mathrm{in}}
$$

where $\tau_{\mathrm{c}}$ is the coolant transit time, $t_{\mathrm{in}}$ is
the instant when the coolant crosses the component inlet, and
$t_{\mathrm{out}}$ is the instant when the same coolant stream crosses the
component outlet.

The quantity applies to the coolant path through one associated plant
component and uses the inlet-to-outlet interval as its aggregation
convention. It is not a plant-wide sum over components or ports, and it
excludes transport outside the component, instrumentation or network
latency, and a thermal time constant of the component material.

The transit time establishes the temporal correspondence between inlet
conditions and the delayed outlet state represented by the [coolant
temperature at outlet](name:coolant_temperature_at_outlet). It is distinct
from the [coolant mass flow rate](name:coolant_mass_flow_rate), which
describes transported mass per time rather than travel duration, and it
provides the thermal-delay correction relevant to [total thermal coolant
absorbed power at wall](name:total_thermal_coolant_absorbed_power_at_wall).

NAMES.name: ion_current_of_mass_spectrometer_channel
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short:
Collected conventional electrical current carried by the ion population
assigned to one mass-resolved channel.
NAMES.long:
The collected ion current is the conventional electrical current delivered
to a detector by ions assigned to one selected atomic-mass or mass-to-charge
channel. It represents the channel-specific ion population rather than the
complete detector signal across all mass channels.

The defining charge-collection relation is

$$
I_{\mathrm{ion}} = \frac{dQ_{\mathrm{ion}}}{dt} = \sum_{k \in \mathcal{C}} q_k\frac{dN_k}{dt}
$$

where $I_{\mathrm{ion}}$ is the collected ion current, $Q_{\mathrm{ion}}$ is
the charge delivered by collected ions, $t$ is time, $\mathcal{C}$ is the
set of ion populations assigned to the selected channel, $q_k$ is the charge
carried by an ion in population $k$, and $N_k$ is the cumulative number of
ions from population $k$ collected by the detector.

The aggregation is over all ion arrivals assigned to the selected channel
and species, including any charge states represented by that channel; it is
not an aggregate over the full mass spectrum or over unrelated channels. The
quantity excludes neutral-gas pressure and the detector-bias potential
represented by the [voltage of a mass-spectrometer
channel](name:voltage_of_mass_spectrometer_channel).

Unlike [ion current density](name:ion_current_density), which is a local
vector charge flux per area, this quantity is the total collected current
associated with one channel. Its channel-specific value can therefore
contribute to determining the corresponding species abundance, while
remaining distinct from a current density.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when positive ion charge is collected by the
detector channel.

NAMES.name: toroidal_coordinate_of_aperture
NAMES.short:
Azimuthal angle locating the geometric center of an aperture about the
machine symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal coordinate of an aperture is the azimuthal angle locating the
aperture’s geometric center around the machine symmetry axis. It identifies
the center’s toroidal position in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$
frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is
vertical height.

This quantity applies specifically to the geometric center of the aperture
as a diagnostic component. It is a point coordinate, not the toroidal
coordinate of the aperture boundary, an angular extent, or an average over
the aperture or any plasma region.

Together with the [vertical coordinate of the
aperture](name:vertical_coordinate_of_aperture), it locates the aperture
center in the cylindrical frame. It is the aperture-specific member of the
geometric-center coordinate family represented by the [toroidal coordinate
of an optical element](name:toroidal_coordinate_of_optical_element).

NAMES.name: voltage_of_mass_spectrometer_channel
NAMES.short:
Signed bias potential applied between the photomultiplier detector electrode
and its electronics reference for one mass-resolved channel, setting
ion-signal gain.
NAMES.long:
The mass-spectrometer channel voltage is the detector-bias potential
difference associated with one channel assigned to a selected atomic mass.
It is an instrumental operating parameter of the photomultiplier detector
that controls the gain applied to the collected ion signal, rather than a
plasma thermodynamic or field quantity.

The defining potential difference is

$$
V_{\mathrm{ch}} = \phi_{\mathrm{det}} - \phi_{\mathrm{ref}}
$$

where $V_{\mathrm{ch}}$ is the channel detector-bias voltage,
$\phi_{\mathrm{det}}$ is the electric potential of the photomultiplier
detector electrode, and $\phi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the electronics reference
potential.

This quantity applies to one mass-resolved channel and its associated
detector circuit. It is not summed or averaged across channels, mass
assignments, detector electrodes, or ion populations, and it does not
represent a local plasma voltage.

The channel-level quantity specializes the device-level [mass-spectrometer
detector bias voltage](name:voltage_of_mass_spectrometer) to one channel. It
is distinct from the [ion current of a mass-spectrometer
channel](name:ion_current_of_mass_spectrometer_channel), which is the
collected electrical signal, and from the [voltage of a spectrometer
channel](name:voltage_of_spectrometer_channel), which denotes an electrical
output signal rather than the detector-bias potential.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the detector electrode potential exceeds the
electronics reference potential.

NAMES.name: line_averaged_effective_charge
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless line-averaged effective ionic charge of a plasma mixture,
obtained by averaging local effective charge along a prescribed plasma line
of sight.
NAMES.long:
Line-averaged effective ionic charge characterizes the charge composition of
a plasma mixture through the average of its local effective charge along a
prescribed line of sight.

The line average is defined by

$$
\overline{Z}_{\mathrm{eff}} = \frac{1}{L} \int_{0}^{L} Z_{\mathrm{eff}}(\ell)\,d\ell
$$

where $\overline{Z}_{\mathrm{eff}}$ is the line-averaged effective ionic
charge, $L$ is the total path length through the plasma, $\ell$ is distance
along the line of sight, and $Z_{\mathrm{eff}}(\ell)$ is the local effective
charge at position $\ell$.

This quantity applies to the complete included ion mixture along the line of
sight. At each position, the ionic contribution is summed over all
represented ion species and charge states, while the line aggregation is a
uniform average over physical path length.

The local integrand is the [effective charge](name:effective_charge),
defined from the second ionic charge moment divided by free-electron
density. This quantity is distinct from a local effective charge at a single
position and from the [volume-averaged effective
charge](name:volume_averaged_effective_charge), which uses volume weighting
rather than line-of-sight path-length weighting; it also differs from the
[flux-surface-averaged effective charge at the plasma
boundary](name:flux_surface_averaged_effective_charge_at_plasma_boundary),
which averages over a boundary surface.

sources.leaf_definition: Average effective charge along the line of sight
sources.parent_definition: Set of channels (detector or pixel of a camera)

NAMES.name: line_averaged_electron_temperature
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short:
Thermal energy of the bulk electron population expressed as an
energy-equivalent temperature, averaged along a plasma chord.
NAMES.long:
Line-averaged electron temperature is the energy-equivalent measure of the
mean random kinetic energy of the bulk electron population, averaged along a
plasma chord.

The defining path-length average is:

$$
T_{e,\mathrm{line}} = \frac{1}{L}\int_0^L T_e(l)\,dl
$$

where $T_{e,\mathrm{line}}$ is the line-averaged electron temperature,
$T_e(l)$ is the local [electron temperature](name:electron_temperature) at
path coordinate $l$, and $L$ is the total chord length. The coordinate $l$
measures distance along the specified plasma chord, and the averaging is
uniform with respect to path length.

This is an intensive quantity for the bulk electron population, aggregated
along the chord rather than summed over electron energies or particle
populations. It excludes ion temperatures and differs from the local
electron temperature because it combines values along the entire chord.

The line average is a chord-integrated representation of the parent
[electron_temperature](name:electron_temperature), whereas
[volume_averaged_electron_temperature](name:volume_averaged_electron_temperature)
applies a volume average over the confined plasma and is therefore a
distinct spatial aggregation.

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Electron temperature

NAMES.name: line_averaged_hydrogen_density
NAMES.subject: hydrogen
NAMES.short:
Line-averaged number density of hydrogen (protium) ions in the plasma,
giving the path-length-normalized H+ concentration along a specified chord.
NAMES.long:
The line-averaged hydrogen density quantifies the mean concentration of
protium ions along a specified chord through the plasma. It represents the
path-integrated hydrogen ion content normalized by the chord length.

The line average is defined as

$$
\overline{n}_H = \frac{1}{L}\int_{\mathcal{C}} n_H(\mathbf{r}(l))\,dl
$$

where $\overline{n}_H$ is the line-averaged hydrogen density,
$n_H(\mathbf{r}(l))$ is the local protium-ion number density at position
$\mathbf{r}(l)$ along the chord, $l$ is the path-length coordinate,
$\mathcal{C}$ is the specified chord, and $L$ is its total length.

The quantity applies to charged protium ions, with any included protium ion
charge states summed before the line average; neutral atomic hydrogen and
heavier hydrogenic isotopes are excluded. It is a chord average rather than
the local [hydrogen density](name:hydrogen_density) at a point or the volume
average represented by
[volume_averaged_hydrogen_density](name:volume_averaged_hydrogen_density).

Unlike
[line_averaged_total_ion_density](name:line_averaged_total_ion_density), it
does not include other ion species or hydrogen isotopes. The path-length
normalization preserves the same density meaning as the parent local
quantity while replacing its pointwise value with an average along the
chord.

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Hydrogen (H)

NAMES.name: motional_stark_photon_radiance_at_spectral_line
NAMES.short:
Photon-count radiance from a selected motional-Stark-split component of an
identified emission line, accumulated along the emitting line of sight.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the photon-number radiance associated with a selected
spectral component whose splitting is produced by the motional Stark effect.
It represents photon emission accumulated along the emitting line of sight
and resolved by projected collecting area and viewing solid angle.

The defining photon-count radiance is

$$
L_{\gamma,\mathrm{MS},\ell} = \frac{d^3 N_{\gamma,\mathrm{MS},\ell}}{dt\,dA_{\perp}\,d\Omega}
$$

where $L_{\gamma,\mathrm{MS},\ell}$ is the radiance of the selected
motional-Stark component, $N_{\gamma,\mathrm{MS},\ell}$ is its emitted
photon count, $t$ is time, $A_{\perp}$ is projected collecting area normal
to the viewing direction, and $\Omega$ is viewing solid angle. The subscript
$\mathrm{MS}$ identifies the motional-Stark component, and $\ell$ identifies
the selected emission line.

The quantity is integrated over the selected spectral-component interval and
accumulated along the emitting line of sight. It is restricted to the
motional-Stark-split component and excludes other spectral components and
wavelength-resolved radiance represented by [spectral radiance].

This quantity specializes [photon-count radiance at a spectral
line](name:photon_radiance_at_spectral_line) by isolating the motional-Stark
component of the identified transition; the parent represents the
corresponding line-integrated radiance without this component selection.

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_thomson_scattering_laser
NAMES.short:
Major-radius location of the Thomson-scattering laser endpoint, measured as
perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed
cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The radial coordinate of a Thomson-scattering laser is the major-radius
position of its laser-beam endpoint, measured from the toroidal symmetry
axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

$$
R_{\mathrm{end}} = \sqrt{x_{\mathrm{end}}^2+y_{\mathrm{end}}^2}
$$

where $R_{\mathrm{end}}$ is the endpoint major-radius coordinate, and
$x_{\mathrm{end}}$ and $y_{\mathrm{end}}$ are the endpoint coordinates along
the two horizontal axes of the right-handed Cartesian basis
$(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$, with $\hat{z}$ aligned with the vertical
direction $\hat{Z}$.

This quantity applies to one laser endpoint and is a geometric point
coordinate, not a path average, scattering-volume coordinate, beam
attribute, or plasma-population quantity. It is neither summed nor averaged
over lasers, endpoints, or plasma regions.

It is the Thomson-scattering-laser-specific realization of [radial
coordinate](name:radial_coordinate), providing the $R$ coordinate of the
endpoint. It is distinct from the [toroidal coordinate of the
Thomson-scattering
laser](name:toroidal_coordinate_of_thomson_scattering_laser), which
specifies the endpoint's toroidal angle $\phi$.

sources.leaf_definition: Major radius
sources.parent_definition: Position of the laser end point

NAMES.name: ratio_of_ion_density_to_electron_density
NAMES.short:
Local ion concentration relative to the electron population, defined as the
number-density ratio for a specified impurity or fuel ion species.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the local abundance of a specified impurity or fuel ion
species relative to the free-electron population. It compares particle
populations rather than electric charge density or mass density.

The local ion-to-electron concentration ratio is defined by

$$
\mathcal{R}_{i/e} = \frac{n_i}{n_e}
$$

where $\mathcal{R}_{i/e}$ is the ion-to-electron concentration ratio, $n_i$
is the local number density of the specified ion species, $n_e$ is the local
free-electron number density, $i$ identifies the selected ion species, and
$e$ identifies the electron population.

Both densities are evaluated at the same local plasma point. For a
species-level numerator without an explicitly selected charge state, $n_i$
is summed over all ionization states of that species; a
charge-state-resolved numerator applies only to the selected state. No
spatial average or line integration is implied.

The numerator is supplied by the corresponding [ion
density](name:ion_density), while [ion charge state
density](name:ion_charge_state_density) represents the density when one
charge state is isolated. A named-species example of the same construction
is the [ratio of iron density to electron
density](name:ratio_of_iron_density_to_electron_density). This quantity is
distinct from an ion charge-state fraction, electric charge-density ratio,
or mass-density ratio.

sources.leaf_definition: Ion concentration (ratio of the ion density over the electron density) at the channel measurement point
sources.parent_definition: Physical quantities related to ion species and charge stage (H+, D+, T+, He+2, Li+3, Be+4, C+6, N+7, O+8, Ne+10, Si+14, Ar+16 or Ar+18) derived from the measured charge exchange emission of each species, at the position of the measurement

NAMES.name: accumulated_total_particle_count_due_to_gas_injection
NAMES.short:
Cumulative equivalent-electron inventory of all gas particles delivered
since plasma breakdown, summed over every injected species and injection
location.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the cumulative inventory of gas delivered after plasma
breakdown, expressed as equivalent electrons. Each injected atom or molecule
contributes according to its total nuclear charge, so the quantity
represents delivered gas inventory rather than the free-electron population
currently present in the plasma.

$$
N_{\mathrm{eq}} = \sum_s Z_s N_s
$$

where $N_{\mathrm{eq}}$ is the cumulative equivalent-electron inventory, $s$
indexes the injected gas species, $Z_s$ is the total nuclear charge per
particle of species $s$, and $N_s$ is the cumulative number of particles of
species $s$ delivered after breakdown.

The aggregation includes all injected gas species and all injection
locations, producing one total inventory rather than a per-species or
per-inlet value. It excludes gas introduced during prefill before plasma
breakdown and does not represent the number of free electrons remaining in
the plasma or the ionization-state-resolved plasma content.

Species-specific accumulated inventories, such as
[accumulated_neon_count](name:accumulated_neon_count), contribute to this
total under the same equivalent-electron convention. The post-breakdown
quantity is distinct from
[accumulated_total_prefill_gas_count](name:accumulated_total_prefill_gas_count),
which accounts for gas introduced before plasma breakdown.

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Total accumulated injected gas (sum over species)

NAMES.name: coolant_temperature_at_inlet
NAMES.short:
Absolute thermodynamic temperature of coolant entering a cooling loop or
plant component, establishing the upstream state for enthalpy-based
heat-transfer balances.
NAMES.long:
The coolant inlet temperature is the absolute thermodynamic temperature of
the coolant or working fluid at the entrance to a cooling loop, plant
component, or cooling module. It specifies the upstream thermal state of the
fluid before heat transfer through the associated cooled volume.

The quantity is a local boundary value at the relevant inlet and is not an
average or aggregate over multiple components, loops, or inlet streams. It
applies to the coolant population crossing that inlet, rather than to the
cooled solid or the plasma.

It is distinct from the downstream [coolant temperature at
outlet](name:coolant_temperature_at_outlet) and does not represent the
temperature change across the cooled component or loop.

In an enthalpy balance, the inlet temperature supplies the upstream thermal
state and is used with the outlet temperature and [coolant mass flow
rate](name:coolant_mass_flow_rate) to determine thermal power transferred to
the coolant. The quantity itself is a temperature, not a power or a
coolant-flow measurement.

sources.parent_definition: Dynamic quantities at various time slices

sources.parent_definition: Set of cooling loops

sources.leaf_definition: Temperature of the coolant when entering the component
sources.parent_definition: Set of components on which calorimetry measurements are carried out

NAMES.name: coolant_temperature_at_outlet
NAMES.short:
Absolute thermodynamic temperature of coolant leaving a cooling component or
loop, specifying the fluid’s outlet thermal state for enthalpy-based heat
balance.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the absolute thermodynamic temperature of the coolant fluid
at the outlet of a cooling component, cooling loop, or comparable coolant
circuit. It describes the bulk fluid state at the exit boundary.

The scope is limited to coolant at an outlet and does not represent the
inlet temperature, a wall temperature, or an aggregate temperature over the
entire cooling system. It is an outlet state value for the selected cooling
path, not a mass-flow rate or a deposited-power quantity.

Together with the [coolant temperature at the
inlet](name:coolant_temperature_at_inlet) and the [coolant mass flow
rate](name:coolant_mass_flow_rate), this temperature determines the coolant
enthalpy change used to assess heat transferred into the fluid. The enthalpy
balance distinguishes thermal power deposited in the coolant from the outlet
temperature itself.

sources.parent_definition: Set of cooling loops

NAMES.name: gas_flow
NAMES.short:
Pressure-volume throughput of a gas stream, expressed as the product of gas
pressure and volumetric flow rate at a flow boundary.
NAMES.long:
Gas flow is the pressure-volume throughput of a gas stream crossing a
defined flow boundary. It represents the aggregate gas stream rather than a
particular molecular species, charge state, mass flow, or particle-number
rate.

The defining pressure-volume throughput is

$$
Q_g = p_g \frac{dV_g}{dt}
$$

where $Q_g$ is gas pressure-volume throughput, $p_g$ is the gas pressure at
the flow boundary, $V_g$ is the volume of gas crossing that boundary, and
$t$ is time.

This quantity applies to the gas stream delivered through an injection
system and is not itself restricted to an upper or lower operating limit.
The [maximum gas flow](name:maximum_gas_flow) is the largest reliably
deliverable value of this throughput, while the [minimum gas
flow](name:minimum_gas_flow) is the smallest reliably deliverable value;
both are limiting instances of the general quantity.

sources.leaf_definition: Flow rate at the exit of the pipe
sources.parent_definition: Set of gas injection pipes

sources.leaf_definition: Flow rate at the exit of the valve
sources.parent_definition: Set of valves connecting a gas bottle to pipes

sources.leaf_definition: Flow rate at the exit of the valve
sources.parent_definition: Response curve of the valve, i.e. gas flow rate obtained as a function of the applied voltage.

sources.parent_definition: Set of gas pumping ducts

sources.leaf_definition: Flow rate of the gas at the injector exit
sources.parent_definition: Description of the gas produced during fragmentation

NAMES.name: maximum_gas_flow
NAMES.short:
Maximum gas flow is the largest pressure-volume throughput that a gas
injection valve can reliably deliver, defining the upper bound of its
controllable range.
NAMES.long:
Maximum gas flow is the upper reliable operating limit of the
pressure-volume throughput delivered by a gas injection valve. It represents
the aggregate gas stream rather than a particular molecular species, charge
state, mass flow, or particle-number rate.

The defining pressure-volume throughput at the upper delivery limit is

$$
Q_g^{\max} = p_g \frac{dV_g}{dt}
$$

where $Q_g^{\max}$ is the maximum gas pressure-volume throughput, $p_g$ is
the gas pressure at the flow boundary, $V_g$ is the volume of gas crossing
that boundary, and $t$ is time.

This quantity applies to gas delivered through a gas injection valve for
fueling, impurity seeding, or disruption mitigation. The maximum qualifier
denotes a reliable upper delivery limit for the aggregate gas stream, not a
species-resolved flow, mass-flow rate, or particle-number rate.

The quantity is the upper-bound member of the [gas flow](name:gas_flow)
family: gas flow denotes the same pressure-volume throughput without an
upper-limit restriction, while [minimum gas flow](name:minimum_gas_flow)
denotes its lower reliable operating limit.

sources.leaf_definition: Maximum flow rate of the valve
sources.parent_definition: Set of valves connecting a gas bottle to pipes

NAMES.name: minimum_gas_flow
NAMES.short:
Minimum gas flow is the smallest pressure-volume gas throughput that a gas
injection valve can reliably deliver, defining the lower bound of its
controllable range.
NAMES.long:
Minimum gas flow is the lower reliable operating limit of the
pressure-volume throughput delivered by a gas injection valve. It identifies
the smallest controllable value of the aggregate gas stream throughput,
rather than a molecular-species flow or particle-number rate.

The pressure-volume throughput represented by this quantity is defined as

$$
Q_g = p_g \frac{dV_g}{dt}
$$

where $Q_g$ is gas pressure-volume throughput, $p_g$ is gas pressure at the
flow boundary, $V_g$ is the volume of gas crossing that boundary, and $t$ is
time.

This quantity applies to the aggregate gas stream delivered through an
injection system across a defined flow boundary. The stream is not
restricted to a particular molecular species or charge state, and this
quantity is distinct from mass flow and particle-number rate. Its defining
distinction is the lower reliable operating bound, rather than an
unrestricted instantaneous throughput.

The [gas flow](name:gas_flow) quantity defines the same pressure-volume
throughput without imposing a lower-limit condition; minimum gas flow is its
lower reliable operating bound. Conversely, [maximum gas
flow](name:maximum_gas_flow) is the upper reliable operating bound, so the
two quantities delimit the controllable range rather than represent
different throughput definitions.

sources.leaf_definition: Minimum flow rate of the valve
sources.parent_definition: Set of valves connecting a gas bottle to pipes

NAMES.name: total_neutral_source_rate_due_to_gas_injection
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short:
Instantaneous equivalent-electron source rate of neutral gas introduced into
the vessel by gas injection, summed over all injected species.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the instantaneous neutral-gas throughput supplied to the
vessel by gas injection, expressed as an equivalent-electron rate. It
combines all injected neutral species rather than representing one gas
species.

For the set of injected species, the equivalent-electron rate is defined by:

$$
\dot{N}_{\mathrm{eq}} = \sum_{s \in \mathcal{S}} Z_s\,\dot{N}_s
$$

where $\dot{N}_{\mathrm{eq}}$ is the total equivalent-electron source rate,
$\mathcal{S}$ is the set of injected neutral gas species, $\dot{N}_s$ is the
particle injection rate of species $s$, and $Z_s$ is the equivalent-electron
weighting per injected particle. For an atomic species, $Z_s$ is its atomic
number; for a molecule, it is the sum of the atomic numbers of its
constituent atoms.

The quantity applies to the vessel-level gas input and is aggregated by
summing over all injected neutral species. It is an instantaneous rate, not
a time-integrated inventory, and excludes ionization and subsequent plasma
particle sources. Species-resolved rates such as the [hydrogen source rate
due to gas injection](name:hydrogen_source_rate_due_to_gas_injection)
provide individual contributions to this total. Unlike the [total lower gas
source rate of the vacuum vessel due to gas
injection](name:total_lower_gas_source_rate_of_vacuum_vessel_due_to_gas_injection),
it is not restricted to the lower vessel region.

The corresponding accumulated quantity, such as the [accumulated hydrogen
count due to gas
injection](name:accumulated_hydrogen_count_due_to_gas_injection), is
obtained by time integration and represents delivered inventory rather than
instantaneous throughput.

sources.parent_definition: Total gas injection rate (sum over species)

NAMES.name: normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_pellet_path
NAMES.short:
Normalized toroidal magnetic-flux surface label assigned to each pellet
location, identifying the nested magnetic surface reached along the pellet’s
in-plasma ablation trajectory.
NAMES.long:
This quantity identifies the nested magnetic surface containing the pellet
at a specified location along its in-plasma ablation trajectory. It is a
magnetic-surface coordinate, not a cylindrical distance or a local vector
component.

At pellet position $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm p}$, the normalized toroidal flux
coordinate is defined by

$$
\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm p}) = \left[\frac{\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm p}) - \Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}}}{\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,boundary}} - \Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}}}\right]^{1/2}
$$

where $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ is the normalized toroidal flux coordinate,
$\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm p}$ is the pellet position,
$\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm p})$ is the toroidal magnetic flux
labeling the magnetic surface through that position,
$\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}}$ is its value at the magnetic axis, and
$\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,boundary}}$ is its value at the equilibrium boundary. The
position is interpreted in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame,
where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical
height.

The scope is the pellet’s in-plasma ablation trajectory, with the coordinate
evaluated pointwise at each pellet location. It does not represent distance
traveled along the path, a path integral, an average over the trajectory, or
an aggregate over multiple pellets.

This is the locus-specific realization of the [normalized toroidal flux
coordinate](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate). The axis and boundary
references set the coordinate endpoints, so the value increases outward
across nested magnetic surfaces while remaining distinct from a cylindrical
radial coordinate.

sources.leaf_definition: Normalized toroidal coordinate along the pellet path
sources.parent_definition: 1-D profiles of plasma and pellet along the pellet path

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_shatter_cone
NAMES.short:
Major-radius coordinate of the shatter-cone origin, locating its reference
point by perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis.
NAMES.long:
The radial coordinate of a shatter-cone origin is the major-radius location
of that geometric reference point relative to the toroidal symmetry axis. It
is the $R$ coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame,
with basis vectors $(\hat{R}, \hat{\phi}, \hat{Z})$ satisfying $\hat{R}
\times \hat{\phi} = \hat{Z}$.

This quantity applies specifically to the origin of the elliptic shatter
cone. It denotes one geometric coordinate of that reference point, with no
averaging, integration, or aggregation over the cone surface, its axis, or
injected fragments; it is distinct from radial coordinates assigned to other
injector features or positions.

It is a locus-specific specialization of [radial
coordinate](name:radial_coordinate): the parent defines the major-radius
coordinate generally, while this quantity evaluates it at the shatter-cone
origin.

sources.leaf_definition: Major radius
sources.parent_definition: Coordinates of the origin of the shatter cone

NAMES.name: radial_outline_of_limiter_tile
NAMES.short:
Major-radius coordinate R locating each point on the boundary outline of a
plasma-facing limiter tile in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The radial outline coordinate is the major-radius value $R$ of each point on
the geometric boundary outline of a plasma-facing limiter tile. It describes
tile geometry rather than a plasma field or a flux-surface coordinate.

In a right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, the major-radius
coordinate is defined from Cartesian coordinates by

$$
R = \sqrt{x^2+y^2}
$$

where $R$ is the perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis, and
$x$ and $y$ are Cartesian coordinate values along the $\hat{x}$ and
$\hat{y}$ axes of the right-handed $(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$ basis.

The quantity is evaluated pointwise for every contour point of the
limiter-tile outline. It is not an average, maximum, area, or integrated
boundary measure; for a closed contour, the first point is not repeated at
the end.

Together with the [vertical outline of the limiter
tile](name:vertical_outline_of_limiter_tile), it supplies the complementary
radial and vertical coordinates that locate the outline in a poloidal
cross-section. The related [radial coordinate](name:radial_coordinate)
expresses the same geometric coordinate concept without specifying the
limiter-tile outline locus.

sources.leaf_definition: Major radius
sources.parent_definition: Irregular outline of the limiting surface. Repeat the first point in case of a closed contour

NAMES.name: ratio_of_iron_density_to_electron_density
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless abundance ratio of charge-state-summed iron-ion number density
to local free-electron number density.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the local iron-to-electron abundance ratio in a plasma,
comparing the population of iron ions with unbound free electrons.

$$
R_{\mathrm{Fe}/e} = \frac{n_{\mathrm{Fe}}}{n_e}
$$

where $R_{\mathrm{Fe}/e}$ is the iron-to-electron abundance ratio,
$n_{\mathrm{Fe}}$ is the total [iron-ion number density](name:iron_density),
and $n_e$ is the local [free-electron number
density](name:electron_density).

The numerator is summed over all positive iron ionization states, while the
denominator counts free electrons and excludes electrons bound in atoms,
molecules, or ions. This is a local ratio with no volume averaging, maximum
operation, or specified spatial locus.

The ratio is the iron-specific counterpart of the general
[ion-density-to-electron-density
ratio](name:ratio_of_ion_density_to_electron_density); its numerator is the
charge-state-summed iron density and its denominator is the electron-density
parent quantity.

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Iron (Fe)

NAMES.name: ratio_of_volume_averaged_beryllium_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless beryllium abundance formed by dividing the volume-averaged
beryllium density by the volume-averaged electron density.
NAMES.long:
Dimensionless beryllium abundance formed by dividing the volume-averaged
beryllium density by the volume-averaged electron density. It represents the
abundance of ionized beryllium relative to free electrons in the confined
plasma volume.

The abundance is defined by the ratio of the two volume averages:

$$
a_{\mathrm{Be}} =
\frac{\langle n_{\mathrm{Be}} \rangle_V}{\langle n_e \rangle_V}
=
\frac{\left\langle \sum_{q=1}^{4} n_{\mathrm{Be}^{q+}} \right\rangle_V}{\langle n_e \rangle_V}
$$

where $a_{\mathrm{Be}}$ is the beryllium abundance ratio, $\langle \cdot
\rangle_V$ denotes averaging over the confined plasma volume,
$n_{\mathrm{Be}}$ is the charge-state-summed beryllium ion number density,
$n_{\mathrm{Be}^{q+}}$ is the number density of beryllium ions in charge
state $q$, and $n_e$ is the [electron density](name:electron_density).

The numerator is the [volume-averaged beryllium
density](name:volume_averaged_beryllium_density), summed over all ionized
beryllium charge states and excluding neutral beryllium atoms. The
denominator is the [volume-averaged electron
density](name:volume_averaged_electron_density) over the same confined
plasma volume.

This quantity is a ratio of two global volume averages, not a pointwise
impurity fraction and not the volume average of $n_{\mathrm{Be}}/n_e$. It is
not charge-weighted; a charge-weighted beryllium contribution to
quasineutrality would use terms proportional to $q n_{\mathrm{Be}^{q+}}$
rather than the unweighted ion sum. The local pre-averaged counterpart of
the numerator is [beryllium density](name:beryllium_density).

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Beryllium (Be)

NAMES.name: ratio_of_volume_averaged_boron_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless global boron abundance ratio using separately volume-averaged
boron and electron number densities, with neutral boron and every ionic
charge state included.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the global abundance of elemental boron relative to the
electron population. It characterizes plasma composition over the full
plasma volume rather than at a local point or along a line of sight.

The defining ratio is

$$
f_B = \frac{\overline{n}_B}{\overline{n}_e}
$$

where $f_B$ is the boron-to-electron abundance ratio, $\overline{n}_B$ is
the volume-averaged elemental boron number density, and $\overline{n}_e$ is
the volume-averaged electron number density. The overbar denotes averaging
over the plasma volume.

The numerator includes neutral boron and every ionic boron charge state,
while the denominator represents the complete electron population. For the
associated plasma-composition convention, the ratio is evaluated at the time
of peak electron density.

This quantity is distinct from local [boron density](name:boron_density) and
from [line-averaged boron density](name:line_averaged_boron_density): it is
a quotient of two separately volume-averaged densities, not a volume average
of a pointwise ratio or a line average. Its numerator is the
[volume-averaged boron density](name:volume_averaged_boron_density), making
this ratio the corresponding normalized composition measure.

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Boron (B)

NAMES.name: ratio_of_volume_averaged_carbon_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless plasma-wide carbon abundance defined as the ratio of
volume-averaged carbon number density to volume-averaged electron number
density. The carbon density is summed over all carbon charge states.
NAMES.long:
Dimensionless plasma-wide carbon abundance is the ratio of volume-averaged
carbon number density to volume-averaged electron number density. It
represents the elemental carbon abundance relative to electrons over the
same plasma volume.

The defining ratio is

$$
f_{C,V} = \frac{\langle n_C \rangle_V}{\langle n_e \rangle_V} = \frac{\left\langle \sum_{q=0}^{6} n_{\mathrm{C},q} \right\rangle_V}{\langle n_e \rangle_V}
$$

where $f_{C,V}$ is the ratio of volume-averaged carbon density to
volume-averaged electron density, $\langle n_C \rangle_V$ is the
[volume-averaged carbon density](name:volume_averaged_carbon_density),
$\langle n_e \rangle_V$ is the [volume-averaged electron
density](name:volume_averaged_electron_density), $n_C$ is the [carbon
density](name:carbon_density), $n_{\mathrm{C},q}$ is the local number
density of carbon nuclei in charge state $q$, $q$ is the carbon charge-state
index with $q=0$ for neutral carbon and $q=6$ for fully stripped carbon, and
$\langle\cdot\rangle_V$ denotes averaging over the same plasma volume for
numerator and denominator.

The population is elemental carbon in the plasma volume, with the numerator
summed over neutral carbon and all ionic charge states. The aggregation
convention is a ratio of two volume averages using the same volume
weighting; it is not the volume average of the local ratio $n_C/n_e$.

This quantity is not an ion-only carbon abundance, not a fraction of total
particle density, and not a charge-weighted impurity measure. It is the
carbon member of the same volume-averaged impurity-abundance family as the
[boron abundance
ratio](name:ratio_of_volume_averaged_boron_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density),
and it differs from the [ratio of total ion density to electron
density](name:ratio_of_total_ion_density_to_electron_density), which
aggregates over all ion species rather than isolating elemental carbon.

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Carbon (C)

NAMES.name: ratio_of_volume_averaged_oxygen_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density
NAMES.short:
Volume-averaged oxygen ion density relative to volume-averaged electron
density for the plasma, with oxygen summed over ionized charge states and
neutral oxygen excluded.
NAMES.long:
Volume-averaged oxygen ion density relative to volume-averaged electron
density is a scalar oxygen impurity fraction for the plasma. It compares the
charge-state-summed volume average of ionized oxygen number density with the
corresponding volume average of electron number density over the same
averaging volume.

The ratio is defined by

$$
f_O = \frac{\left\langle \sum_{q=1}^{8} n_{O^{q+}} \right\rangle_V}{\langle n_e \rangle_V}
$$

where $f_O$ is this oxygen-to-electron density ratio,
$\langle\cdot\rangle_V$ denotes a volume average over the averaging volume
$V$, $q$ is the oxygen charge-state index, $n_{O^{q+}}$ is the local number
density of oxygen ions in charge state $q+$, and $n_e$ is the local electron
number density. The denominator $\langle n_e\rangle_V$ is the
[volume-averaged electron density](name:volume_averaged_electron_density).

The numerator is summed over ionized oxygen charge states $O^{1+}$ through
$O^{8+}$ and excludes neutral oxygen. This quantity is a single scalar
composition fraction formed from volume-averaged populations; it is distinct
from a local [oxygen density](name:oxygen_density), from a [line-averaged
oxygen density](name:line_averaged_oxygen_density), and from a
neutral-inclusive [volume-averaged oxygen
density](name:volume_averaged_oxygen_density) when that quantity includes
neutral oxygen.

The essential relationship is normalization: the charge-state-summed
volume-averaged oxygen ion density is divided by the [volume-averaged
electron density](name:volume_averaged_electron_density), so the result
represents oxygen ion abundance relative to the electron population rather
than an absolute density.

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Oxygen (O)

NAMES.name: ratio_of_volume_averaged_tungsten_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless tungsten abundance ratio equal to the plasma-volume-averaged
elemental tungsten density divided by the plasma-volume-averaged electron
density.
NAMES.long:
Dimensionless tungsten abundance ratio equal to the plasma-volume-averaged
elemental tungsten density divided by the plasma-volume-averaged electron
density. It compares the charge-state-summed tungsten-ion population with
the free-electron population in the same plasma volume.

The ratio is defined from the two volume averages over the plasma volume $V$
as

$$
a_{\mathrm{W},V}
=
\frac{\langle n_{\mathrm{W}}\rangle_V}{\langle n_e\rangle_V}
=
\frac{V^{-1}\int_V \sum_{z=1}^{74} n_{\mathrm{W}^{z+}}(\mathbf{x})\, dV}{V^{-1}\int_V n_e(\mathbf{x})\, dV}
$$

where $a_{\mathrm{W},V}$ denotes this tungsten abundance ratio, $V$ denotes
the plasma volume enclosed by the last closed flux surface over which both
averages are formed, $\langle n_{\mathrm{W}}\rangle_V$ is the
[volume-averaged tungsten density](name:volume_averaged_tungsten_density),
$\langle n_e\rangle_V$ is the [volume-averaged electron
density](name:volume_averaged_electron_density),
$n_{\mathrm{W}^{z+}}(\mathbf{x})$ is the local number density of tungsten
ions in charge state $z$ at position $\mathbf{x}$, $n_e(\mathbf{x})$ is the
local free-electron number density, $z=1,\ldots,74$ indexes the positive
tungsten ionization states, and $dV$ is the volume element.

The scope is the confined plasma volume: both numerator and denominator use
the same volume and the same volume-averaging operation. The tungsten
population is elemental tungsten in positive ionization states, summed over
charge state; neutral tungsten is excluded. The aggregation is the ratio of
the two volume averages, not the volume average of the local ratio
$n_{\mathrm{W}}/n_e$, and the quantity is defined only when $\langle
n_e\rangle_V$ is nonzero.

This ratio is an unweighted tungsten-nucleus abundance relative to free
electrons; it is not a charge-weighted tungsten contribution to electron
density and is not an effective-charge measure. It is the tungsten member of
the same volume-averaged composition-ratio family as the [deuterium-tritium
abundance
ratio](name:ratio_of_volume_averaged_deuterium_tritium_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density)
and the [carbon abundance
ratio](name:ratio_of_volume_averaged_carbon_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density),
which replace the tungsten numerator with the corresponding species volume
average while retaining the same electron-density denominator.

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Tungsten (W)

NAMES.name: area_of_diagnostic_aperture
NAMES.short:
Geometric area of the designated diagnostic aperture surface that admits or
collects radiation or particles.
NAMES.long:
Diagnostic aperture area is the geometric extent of the designated limiting
surface through which radiation or particles are admitted or collected. It
may describe a clear aperture opening or a collecting face when that face
defines the aperture.

The area is defined by the surface integral

$$
A = \int_S dS
$$

where $A$ is the diagnostic aperture area, $S$ is the designated aperture
surface, and $dS$ is the differential area element on that surface.

This quantity applies to the specified aperture surface of the diagnostic
and is not an automatically aggregated area for unrelated apertures. It is a
geometric area, excluding surrounding housing, supports, and other
structures unless they form the designated aperture surface; it is not an
effective area weighted by transmission, sensitivity, or angular response.

The area is distinct from the [radius of a diagnostic
aperture](name:radius_of_diagnostic_aperture) and the [width of a diagnostic
aperture], which describe linear dimensions. For a circular aperture of
radius $r$, where $r$ is the geometric distance from the aperture center to
its boundary, the area satisfies $A = \pi r^2$, with $\pi$ denoting the
circle constant.

NAMES.name: cold_neutral_fraction
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless fraction of the cold recycled component of a hydrogen-isotope
neutral population relative to the total neutral atom population.
NAMES.long:
The cold neutral fraction is a dimensionless ratio bounded in $[0, 1]$
expressing the relative abundance of the cold, low-energy recycled component
of a hydrogen-isotope neutral population. It is a component of the broader
[neutral
fraction](name:ratio_of_neutral_state_density_to_total_hydrogenic_density),
distinct from the hot charge-exchange-born component.

The fraction is defined as:

$$
f_{\mathrm{cold}} = \frac{n_{\mathrm{cold}}}{n_{\mathrm{cold}} + n_{\mathrm{hot}}}
$$

where $f_{\mathrm{cold}}$ is the cold neutral fraction, $n_{\mathrm{cold}}$
is the number density of cold recycled neutral atoms, and $n_{\mathrm{hot}}$
is the number density of hot charge-exchange-born neutral atoms.

The quantity applies to a specified hydrogen isotope and uses the
two-component neutral-population model. Its denominator is the total neutral
population formed by the cold and hot components for that isotope; it is not
summed across different isotopes and does not represent the hot component
itself.

Within this model, the cold and hot fractions are complementary and sum to
unity. The [hot neutral fraction](name:hot_neutral_fraction) gives the
corresponding charge-exchange-born component, with the energy threshold
separating the two components defined by the applicable population model.

sources.leaf_definition: Fraction of cold neutrals for this isotope (n_cold_neutrals/(n_cold_neutrals+n_hot_neutrals))
sources.parent_definition: Set of isotopes

NAMES.name: etendue_of_hard_xray_detector
NAMES.short:
Geometric optical throughput of a hard X-ray detector’s optical system,
determined by its effective collecting area and accepted solid angle.
NAMES.long:
Étendue is the geometric throughput of the optical system associated with a
hard X-ray detector. It characterizes the angular and spatial acceptance
that determines how incident radiation is coupled into the detector.

The defining relation is

$$
G = A\Omega
$$

where $G$ is the detector étendue, $A$ is the effective collecting area, and
$\Omega$ is the accepted solid angle.

This quantity applies to the detector-level optical system and uses
effective area and angular acceptance for the associated detector; it does
not specify whether those properties arise from one or multiple optical
elements. It is distinct from the detector’s linear dimensions, such as its
[height](name:height_of_hard_xray_detector) and width, which do not
determine optical throughput alone.

Étendue provides the geometric factor relating incident [hard X-ray
brightness](name:hard_xray_brightness) to radiation coupled into the
detector and is the same physical optical-throughput concept represented by
[etendue_of_spectrometer](name:etendue_of_spectrometer), with the owning
optical system changed from a spectrometer to a hard X-ray detector.

sources.leaf_definition: Etendue (geometric extent) of the channel's optical system
sources.parent_definition: Set of channels (detector or pixel of a camera)

NAMES.name: etendue_of_spectrometer_channel
NAMES.short:
Optical phase-space acceptance of a radiation-collection system, determined
by effective collecting area and accepted ray directions and optionally
weighted by spectral response.
NAMES.long:
Optical étendue is the geometric phase-space acceptance of a
radiation-collection system. It describes how the collecting area and range
of accepted ray directions jointly determine the system's throughput for
radiation from an observed source.

For an effective area and accepted solid angle, the étendue $G$ is defined
by:

$$
G = A_{\mathrm{eff}}\Omega_{\mathrm{eff}}
$$

where $G$ is the optical étendue, $A_{\mathrm{eff}}$ is the effective
collecting area, and $\Omega_{\mathrm{eff}}$ is the accepted solid angle.

The quantity applies to radiation entering an optical collection system from
a plasma or other observed source and aggregates acceptance over the
collecting area and accepted ray directions. It is non-negative and does not
itself represent radiance, collected power, detector signal, or spectral
intensity. The [spectral étendue of a spectrometer
channel](name:spectral_etendue_of_spectrometer_channel) is a narrower
response-weighted form in which the optical acceptance is weighted by the
channel's wavelength response, while [étendue of a
spectrometer](name:etendue_of_spectrometer) represents the corresponding
unweighted spectrometer-level acceptance.

sources.leaf_definition: Etendue (geometric extent) of the channel's optical system
sources.parent_definition: Set of channels (detector or pixel of a camera)

NAMES.name: hard_xray_brightness
NAMES.subject: hard_xray
NAMES.short:
Band-integrated hard X-ray photon radiance received by a channel, normalized
by projected collecting area and accepted solid angle.
NAMES.long:
Hard X-ray brightness is the photon radiance received from a viewing
direction by a channel. It represents photon arrival rate with the
photon-energy dependence integrated over the selected hard X-ray band.

The band-integrated photon radiance is defined by

$$
B_{\mathrm{HX}} = \frac{dN_\gamma}{dt\,dA_{\mathrm{proj}}\,d\Omega}
$$

where $B_{\mathrm{HX}}$ is the hard X-ray brightness, $N_\gamma$ is the
number of received photons in the selected energy band, $t$ is time,
$A_{\mathrm{proj}}$ is projected collecting area, and $\Omega$ is accepted
solid angle.

This quantity applies to hard X-ray photons received by a channel and is
evaluated separately for each selected energy band. Its aggregation
convention is integration over photon energy within that band while
retaining normalization by projected area and solid angle. It is a received
radiometric quantity, not a local volumetric source term, and it counts
photons rather than their deposited or carried energy.

The local production counterpart is [hard X-ray emissivity], which describes
photon generation per unit volume and solid angle before propagation to the
channel. Integrating this brightness over the collecting geometry
represented by the [etendue of a hard X-ray
detector](name:etendue_of_hard_xray_detector) gives the received photon rate
under the corresponding angular and area acceptance. Unlike [incident soft
X-ray radiance](name:incident_soft_xray_radiance), which is energy-weighted,
this quantity is photon-count radiance; photon registration probability is a
separate detector property described by [spectral efficiency of a hard X-ray
detector](name:spectral_efficiency_of_hard_xray_detector).

sources.leaf_definition: Photons received by the detector per unit time, per unit solid angle and per unit area (i.e. photon flux divided by the etendue), in multiple energy bands if available from the detector
sources.parent_definition: Set of channels (detector or pixel of a camera)

NAMES.name: hot_neutral_fraction
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless fraction of the hot charge-exchange-born component of a
hydrogen-isotope neutral population relative to the total neutral atom
population.
NAMES.long:
The hot neutral fraction is a dimensionless ratio bounded in $[0, 1]$
expressing the relative abundance of the hot, charge-exchange-born component
of a hydrogen-isotope neutral population. It is a component of the broader
[neutral
fraction](name:ratio_of_neutral_state_density_to_total_hydrogenic_density),
distinct from the cold recycled component.

The fraction is defined as:

$$
f_{\mathrm{hot}} = \frac{n_{\mathrm{hot}}}{n_{\mathrm{cold}} + n_{\mathrm{hot}}}
$$

where $f_{\mathrm{hot}}$ is the hot neutral fraction, $n_{\mathrm{hot}}$ is
the number density of hot charge-exchange-born neutral atoms, and
$n_{\mathrm{cold}}$ is the number density of cold recycled neutral atoms.

The quantity applies to a specified hydrogen isotope and uses the
two-component neutral-population model. Its denominator is the total neutral
population formed by the cold and hot components for that isotope; it is not
summed across different isotopes and does not represent the cold component
itself.

Within this model, the hot and cold fractions are complementary and sum to
unity. The [cold neutral fraction](name:cold_neutral_fraction) gives the
corresponding recycled component, with the energy threshold separating the
two components defined by the applicable population model.

sources.leaf_definition: Fraction of hot neutrals for this isotope (n_hot_neutrals/(n_cold_neutrals+n_hot_neutrals))
sources.parent_definition: Set of isotopes

NAMES.name: incident_soft_xray_radiance
NAMES.short:
Incident soft X-ray power radiance gives received electromagnetic power per
projected detector area and solid angle, integrated over the selected energy
band.
NAMES.long:
Incident soft-X-ray power radiance is the energy-integrated radiant power
arriving at a receiving surface from the viewing direction, expressed per
projected area and per solid angle.

$$
L_{\rm inc} = \int_{\mathcal{E}} L_E^{\rm inc}\,dE = \frac{dP_{\rm inc}}{dA_\perp\,d\Omega}
$$

where $L_{\rm inc}$ is the incident power radiance, $L_E^{\rm inc}$ is the
incident spectral power radiance at photon energy $E$, $\mathcal{E}$ is the
selected photon-energy band or collection of bands, $P_{\rm inc}$ is
incident radiant power, $A_\perp$ is projected receiving area, and $\Omega$
is accepted solid angle.

The quantity applies to soft X-ray radiation incident on a detector channel,
with spectral dependence integrated over the selected energy band or bands.
It is an incoming radiometric quantity per area and solid angle, not a total
power integrated over the detector aperture or viewing directions, and it is
distinct from detector-registration efficiency.

Integrating this radiance over the relevant projected area and solid angle
gives the band-integrated received power represented by [power of soft X-ray
detector](name:power_of_soft_xray_detector). Unlike [hard X-ray
brightness](name:hard_xray_brightness), which is photon-number radiance,
this quantity is power radiance; [spectral efficiency of soft X-ray
detector](name:spectral_efficiency_of_soft_xray_detector) instead describes
the probability that incident photons are registered.

sources.leaf_definition: Power flux received by the detector, per unit solid angle and per unit area (i.e. power divided by the etendue), in multiple energy bands if available from the detector
sources.parent_definition: Set of channels (detector or pixel of a camera)

NAMES.name: intensity_at_spectral_line
NAMES.short:
Uncalibrated photoelectron detection rate obtained by integrating the
measured emission signal across an identified spectral line.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the uncalibrated photoelectron count rate associated with
one identified emission line. It represents the detector signal integrated
across the wavelength interval assigned to that line, rather than an
absolutely calibrated photon radiance.

The line-integrated count rate is defined by

$$
I_{\rm line} = \int_{\lambda_1}^{\lambda_2} i(\lambda)\,d\lambda
$$

where $I_{\rm line}$ is the integrated photoelectron count rate,
$i(\lambda)$ is the spectral photoelectron count-rate density, $\lambda$ is
wavelength, and $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$ delimit the interval assigned to
the identified emission line.

The quantity applies to a single identified spectral line and uses line
integration as its aggregation convention. It is non-calibrated and is not
background-subtracted; no aggregation over multiple spectral lines or
conversion to absolute photon radiance is included.

It is the uncalibrated line-integrated counterpart of [photon-count radiance
at a spectral line](name:photon_radiance_at_spectral_line), which
additionally represents an absolutely calibrated radiance and includes
background subtraction. Unlike [spectral flux of a spectrometer
channel](name:spectral_rate_of_spectrometer_channel), this quantity is
resolved at one identified line rather than describing the channel-level
spectral signal.

sources.leaf_definition: Non-calibrated intensity (integrated over the spectrum for this line)
sources.parent_definition: Set of processed spectral lines

NAMES.name: lower_bound_photon_energy
NAMES.short:
Lower boundary of an X-ray photon-energy band, specifying the minimum photon
energy included in the defined detection or emission band.
NAMES.long:
Lower boundary of an X-ray photon-energy band is the minimum photon energy
included in the specified detection or emission band. It defines the
low-energy cutoff of that band.

The photon-energy band defined by this lower boundary and its complementary
upper boundary satisfies:

$$
E_\mathrm{low} \le E \le E_\mathrm{up}
$$

where $E_\mathrm{low}$ is the lower-bound photon energy, $E$ is the photon
energy being classified, and $E_\mathrm{up}$ is the [upper photon
energy](name:upper_photon_energy).

The scope is an X-ray spectral band for photon detection, photon counting,
or energy-resolved emissivity. This quantity is a band boundary, not an
observed photon energy, photon-energy width, photon flux, count rate,
emissivity, or detector-response amplitude; it is a single boundary for one
specified band and implies no averaging or summation over photons.

Together with the [upper photon energy](name:upper_photon_energy), it
specifies the spectral interval of the band. The lower boundary must not
exceed the upper boundary, and any derived band width is their difference.

NAMES.name: photon_radiance_at_spectral_line
NAMES.short:
Photon-count radiance from an identified emission transition, integrated
over its spectral line interval and resolved by projected area and viewing
solid angle.
NAMES.long:
Photon-count line radiance is the photon emission rate from one identified
transition accumulated along the emitting line of sight, resolved by
projected collecting area and viewing solid angle.

The defining photon-count radiance is

$$
L_{\gamma,\ell} = \frac{d^3 N_{\gamma,\ell}}{dt\,dA_{\perp}\,d\Omega}
$$

where $L_{\gamma,\ell}$ is the line radiance, $N_{\gamma,\ell}$ is the
number of photons from transition $\ell$, $\ell$ identifies the emission
transition, $t$ is time, $A_{\perp}$ is collecting area projected normal to
the viewing direction, and $\Omega$ is viewing solid angle.

The quantity applies to one identified emission transition without imposing
a particular emitting species, charge state, or line-splitting mechanism.
Photon counts are integrated across the selected spectral-line interval and
accumulated along the viewing path; the result is not resolved per
wavelength.

Integrating [photon-number spectral radiance] over wavelength across the
selected line interval gives this line radiance under matching
projected-area and solid-angle conventions. The qualified [motional-Stark
photon radiance at a spectral
line](name:motional_stark_photon_radiance_at_spectral_line) is a specialized
instance restricted to an identified motional-Stark-split component. Unlike
energy radiance, this quantity counts photons without weighting them by
photon energy; conversion to energy radiance requires applying that energy
weighting before integration.
